docs.title: FluxRules
docs.text:
FluxRules is a lightweight Python library for defining, checking and evaluating business rules. You write a rule once, and FluxRules tells you which rules match a piece of data and which actions they ask for. The engine is PHREAK, a fast and deterministic matching algorithm inspired by the one in Drools.

from fluxrules import F, Rule, evaluate

rule = Rule(name="big_payment", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review")

result = evaluate(rule, {"amount": 4200})
print(result.actions)  # ['review']

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Write rules in Python or as data. Build conditions with F expressions, a step-by-step builder, plain dictionaries or YAML files. See Authoring Rules.
  • Combine checks freely. Nest AND, OR and NOT as deep as you need. See Complex Conditions.
  • Organize rules. Group rules by domain and tag, and give them priorities that set the order in which they fire. See Domains and Tags.
  • Catch mistakes early. Validate rules before they run, and check every field a rule uses against a typed model. See Validation Framework and Typed Facts.
  • Evaluate facts in the way that suits you. Use one call, an engine, a batch spread across CPU cores, a stream of updates, a session, the command line or HTTP. See Ways to Evaluate a Fact.
  • Prepare messy input. Flatten, rename, convert and enrich raw data before it reaches the engine. See Fact Pipeline.
  • Act on the result. Every result names the rules that fired, the actions they ask for and how long evaluation took. Register handlers to run those actions. See Actions.
  • Extend it. Plug in your own engine, transforms and actions. See Extension Points.

Advanced Capabilities maps every advanced feature to its guide and to a runnable example.

docs.title: What this project covers
docs.text:
• A Python library that runs inside your own process.
  • An optional HTTP server, database storage, metrics and tracing, each installed as an extra.
  • Runnable examples in the examples/ folder and a large test suite.

It does not include a hosted service. The package source lives in src/fluxrules.

docs.text:
If you are new to these features, read them in this order:

docs.title: Verification note
docs.text: Every example on this page was run successfully on 2026-11-02 with the dev dependency group installed.

docs.title: Algorithm Fidelity: PHREAK vs the Reference Evaluator
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The PHREAK Engine.

FluxRules ships one production engine (PHREAK). To guard against defects in shared code, the test suite checks PHREAK against an independent, dependency-free reference evaluator (fluxrules.services.reference_evaluator.ReferenceEvaluator). Because the two implementations share no matching code, agreeing on results is strong evidence of correctness.

docs.title: Verification approach
docs.text:
Test dataset: cross_border_payment_risk_triage (3 facts, shared use case)

Test rules: All 31 example rules with varying complexity:

  • Simple conditions (1 field)
  • Complex AND/OR logic
  • NOT operators
  • Nested groups

Verification method:

  1. Load the same ruleset into PHREAK and the reference evaluator
  2. Evaluate identical facts
  3. Compare fired_rules and actions
  4. Assert complete parity

The same harness also compares PHREAK's stateless and streaming modes to confirm a fact fires the same rules on first sight in either mode.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Complete parity: PHREAK matches the reference evaluator on all test cases.

Test Case PHREAK Reference Match Simple condition Pass Pass Yes AND groups Pass Pass Yes OR groups Pass Pass Yes NOT operator Pass Pass Yes Nested groups Pass Pass Yes Multiple rules Pass Pass Yes

Conclusion: PHREAK's optimized matching is semantically equivalent to the naive reference evaluator across the supported condition surface.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule, Engine).

FluxRules exposes a REST API for evaluating rules from other services. The API is built with FastAPI and all endpoints are under /api/v1.

docs.title: Starting the API server
docs.text:
Install the api extra, then start the server from the command line:

pip install "fluxrules[api]"
fluxrules serve --port 8000

Or start it from Python:

from fluxrules.api.app import create_app
import uvicorn

app = create_app()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

While it runs, http://localhost:8000/docs lists every endpoint and lets you try them.

docs.title: Core endpoints
docs.text: Most endpoints need a login token. HTTP API Reference shows how to get one, and gives the full request and response of each endpoint.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text:
GET /health

Answers {"status": "healthy"}. No login needed.

docs.title: Store a rule
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/rules
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "big_payment",
  "group": "payments",
  "action": "review",
  "conditions": {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 1000}
}

Rules live in the server's database. Store them before you evaluate.

docs.title: Evaluate a fact
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/evaluate
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "facts": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"},
  "ruleset_id": "payments"
}

ruleset_id is optional and picks the rules of one group. Without it, all stored rules are used.

Response: 

{
  "execution_id": "8ac723da-c93d-40ec-809c-64a244003e9e",
  "ruleset_group": "payments",
  "matched_rules": [1],
  "actions": ["review"],
  "facts": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}
}

POST /api/v1/evaluate/bulk takes a list under facts and returns one result per fact.

docs.title: Look up an evaluation
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/explain/{execution_id}

Returns an earlier evaluation by the execution_id it answered with.

docs.title: Dry run with explanations
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/rules/simulate
Content-Type: application/json

{"event": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}}

Returns the matched rules in firing order, with an explanation for each.

docs.title: Check a rule set
docs.text:
POST /validate
Content-Type: application/json

{"ruleset": {"group": "payments", "rules": [...]}}

Answers {"issues": [...]}, a list of problems found; an empty list means the rule set is fine. No login needed.

docs.title: More endpoints
docs.text:
• Rules (/api/v1/rules): list, update, delete, versions and conflict checks.
  • Sessions (/api/v1/sessions): store facts under a session id, and evaluate them later with POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/evaluate.
  • Audit (/api/v1/audit): the audit trail of rule changes.
  • Metrics (/api/v1/metrics): Prometheus metrics.
  • Engines (/api/v1/engines): evaluate with explanations, and report the engine in use. Some of these endpoints are not finished; see HTTP API Reference: Engine endpoints.

docs.title: API versioning
docs.text: All endpoints are under /api/v1 for stability. Breaking changes will use /api/v2.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts.

FluxRules is a lightweight rule evaluation engine with a clean layered architecture. This page describes the system design from the condition tree down to engine execution.

docs.title: Evaluation Flow: From Fact to Result
docs.text: For the full path a fact takes, including the fact pipeline, typed-fact validation, discovery and action dispatch, see From Fact to Action. The sketches below show the two call shapes.

docs.title: Single Fact Evaluation (Simple API)
docs.text:
User: engine.evaluate({"amount": 5000, "country": "NG"})
  │
  ├─→ [1. Validate fact structure]
  │
  ├─→ [2. Iterate loaded rules]
  │    (via the PHREAK network)
  │
  ├─→ [3. For each rule:
  │       - Evaluate conditions against fact
  │       - If matched: add to fired_rules list
  │       - If matched: collect its action names (not executed)
  │
  ├─→ [4. Collect results]
  │    - fired_rules: List[int] (matched rule IDs)
  │    - actions: list[str] (action names, priority order)
  │    - latency_ms: float (execution time)
  │
  └─→ EvaluationResult(fired_rules=[1, 3], actions=["flag"], latency_ms=0.45)

docs.title: Multi-Step Workflow (Session-Based)
docs.text:
User: session = service.create_session()
  │
  ├─→ [1. Add facts incrementally]
  │    session.add_fact("user_type", "premium")
  │    session.add_fact("amount", 10000)
  │
  ├─→ [2. Evaluate against accumulated facts]
  │    result = session.evaluate()
  │
  ├─→ [3. Session remembers state (optional)]
  │    - Save snapshot for recovery
  │    - Restore in another process
  │
  └─→ EvaluationResult (same structure as simple API)

docs.title: The Engine: PHREAK
docs.text:
Every evaluation runs on one engine, PhreakEngine. It works in one of two modes. In stateless mode (the default) each call is independent and returns the full set of fired rules. In streaming mode the engine keeps working memory between calls and reports only what changed.

The PHREAK Engine explains both modes, and Choosing an Evaluation Mode helps you pick one.

docs.title: Condition Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
The conditions is a recursive JSON structure that's validated, compiled, and executed:

Input condition (F DSL or dict):
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").isin(["NG", "US"]))

Compiled condition tree:
{
  "type": "group",
  "op": "AND",
  "children": [
    {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
    {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "in", "value": ["NG", "US"]}
  ]
}
  │
  ├─→ [1. Parse & Validate]
  │    - Check syntax (type, op, field names)
  │    - Ensure operator is valid (==, !=, <, >, in, contains, etc.)
  │
  ├─→ [2. Convert to AST]
  │    - Build tree of condition nodes
  │    - Resolve operator functions
  │
  ├─→ [3. Evaluate against fact]
  │    - Traverse AST
  │    - Apply operators to fact values
  │    - Short-circuit AND/OR when possible
  │
  └─→ boolean result (True = rule fires)

docs.title: Data Model: Rule
docs.text:
# python skip
Rule(
    name="high_value_payment",           # Identifier
    domain="fraud_detection",             # Grouping
    tags=frozenset(["tier_1", "urgent"]), # Cross-cutting labels
    priority=10,                          # Execution order (higher first)
    conditions={...},                  # The condition tree above
    action="flag_for_review",             # Action name
    persist=False                         # Optional: store in database
)

Key design:

  • Rule is immutable once created (frozen Pydantic model)
  • Conditions are pure predicates (no side effects)
  • Actions are names; your application decides what each name does
  • Domain/tags allow flexible rule organization

docs.title: Pluggability Points
docs.text:
You can replace three parts with your own code:

  • Engines: subclass BaseEngine to change how matched rules are chosen. See Custom Engines.
  • Actions: register a handler for each action name. See Actions.
  • Transforms: add your own steps to a fact pipeline. See Custom Transforms.

Extension Points lists every extension point and its stability promise.

docs.title: Standalone (Single Process)
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────┐
│  Your Application    │
│  ├─ PhreakEngine     │
│  └─ Rules            │
└──────────────────────┘

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Evidence-first: All documentation backed by working code
  2. Pydantic v2: Rule validation via Pydantic (not home-grown)
  3. Pluggable: Custom engines, actions, transforms via simple interfaces
  4. Fast: Production-grade performance (ms-level latency)
  5. Simple: Minimal API surface, small learning curve
  6. Lazy by default: PHREAK's on-demand evaluation minimizes overhead

docs.title: Authoring Rules
docs.text:
A rule is a condition plus an action. The condition says when the rule fires. This page explains the ways to write that condition, which one to pick first, and why.

Short answer: write conditions with F expressions. Use a dictionary or YAML only when your rules come from outside your Python code.

docs.title: The same rule, four ways
docs.text:
All four forms below describe one rule: "fire when the amount is over 5000 and the country is US."

from fluxrules import F, Rule, RuleBuilder

# 1. F expression (first choice)
by_expression = Rule(
    id=1,
    name="high_value_us",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"),
    action="review",
)

# 2. RuleBuilder, step by step (it also takes an F expression)
by_builder = (
    RuleBuilder(1)
    .name("high_value_us")
    .condition((F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"))
    .action("review")
    .build()
)

# 3. Dictionary (the stored format)
by_dict = Rule(
    id=1,
    name="high_value_us",
    conditions={
        "type": "group",
        "op": "AND",
        "children": [
            {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
            {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"},
        ],
    },
    action="review",
)

# They are the same rule underneath.
assert by_expression.conditions == by_builder.conditions == by_dict.conditions

The fourth form is a YAML file, which holds the same dictionary:

- id: 1
  name: high_value_us
  action: review
  conditions:
    type: group
    op: AND
    children:
      - {type: condition, field: amount, op: ">", value: 5000}
      - {type: condition, field: country, op: "==", value: US}

docs.title: Which one should I use?
docs.text:
You are... Use Why Writing rules in Python code F expressions Shortest, reads like the rule, checked by your editor Building a rule step by step in code RuleBuilder Fields are set one at a time and checked as you go Loading rules from a database or an API Dictionary That is the format they are stored in Letting people edit rules without touching code YAML A plain file, no Python needed

If you are unsure, start with F. You can always print the dictionary behind an expression with .to_dict(), so nothing is hidden.

docs.title: Why F comes first
docs.text:
It reads like the rule. Compare the two:

(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

{"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [
    {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
    {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"}]}

Same meaning. The first is one line and the second is four. The shared example rule in examples/ has eight checks and two nested ORs. It is about 10 lines with F and about 70 as a dictionary, and the dictionary buries the logic in brackets.

It catches mistakes early. An editor can see that F("amount") > 5000 is Python. It cannot see that "op": ">" is an operator, so a typo such as "op": "=>" only shows up when the rule is built.

It costs nothing at run time. F is a thin layer over the dictionary. An expression turns into the same dictionary the engine always used, so stored rules, YAML files and the HTTP API do not change. There is no second engine and no slower path.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
F("amount") is a field reference. Python's comparison operators on it do not return True or False. They return a Condition object that holds a dictionary:

You write It builds F("x") > 5 {"type": "condition", "field": "x", "op": ">", "value": 5} a & b {"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [a, b]} a \| b {"type": "group", "op": "OR", "children": [a, b]} ~a {"type": "not", "condition": a} F("x").exists() {"type": "exists", "field": "x"}

Rule(conditions=...) and RuleBuilder.condition(...) accept a Condition or a dictionary, and a Condition is turned into its dictionary right away. After that point there is only one format.

One detail: a & b & c builds nested groups, (a & b) & c, while a dictionary you write by hand usually has one flat group of three. They give the same results. Only the shape differs.

docs.title: What to keep in mind
docs.text:
Wrap every comparison in parentheses. Python applies & and | before > and ==, so without parentheses the expression means something else and usually fails with a TypeError.

# python skip: the second line deliberately raises to show the trap
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")   # correct
F("amount") > 5000 & F("country") == "US"       # wrong

Field names are exact. F("Amount") and F("amount") are different fields, and so are F("userAge") and F("user_age"). If a rule asks for Amount and the fact has amount, FluxRules raises FieldNotFoundError and suggests the right name, instead of quietly never matching. With a fact schema, it does the same for other key styles (userAge against user_age). A field that is simply not in the fact, with no look-alike key, returns False. That keeps rulesets that serve different kinds of facts working.

Write rules against a model when you have one. fields(Customer).age >= 18 builds the same condition as F("age") >= 18, but a misspelt field fails when you write the rule. See Typed Facts.

Mind NOT over optional fields. ~(F("blocked") == True) also fires when blocked is missing. Say what you mean with exists(), and see Missing fields and NOT.

Use exists() for fields that may be missing. F("promo").exists() is true when the key is present and not None, and it never raises.

Pass a list to isin. Write F("country").isin(["NG", "GH"]), not F("country").isin("NG", "GH").

Match the type of the value to the type of the field. Comparing a number field to a string does not raise. It just never matches.

docs.title: Check a rule before you use it
docs.text:
There are four layers, from earliest to latest:

  1. When you build the Rule. An unknown operator, a missing key or a malformed tree raises ConditionValidationError immediately. Field references from fields(Model) also fail here if the model lacks the field.
  2. Before you deploy. validate(rules) checks a whole list and returns a list of problems, empty when all is well. Run it in CI.
  3. When rules load. An engine built with fact_schema=Model raises UnknownFieldError for any rule field the model lacks, and loads nothing.
  4. While evaluating. FieldNotFoundError flags a field name whose key is in the fact in another case (Amount / amount), or, with a fact schema, in another key style (userAge / user_age).
from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="allow"),
]

assert validate(rules) == []

See Conditions for every operator and the full validation guide.

docs.title: Moving existing dictionary rules to F
docs.text:
You do not have to. Dictionaries keep working and can sit next to F rules in the same ruleset. When you do want to switch, the mapping is mechanical:

Dictionary F expression {"type": "condition", "field": "x", "op": ">", "value": 5} F("x") > 5 "op": "in", "value": [...] F("x").isin([...]) "op": "contains" F("x").contains(v) {"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [a, b]} a & b {"type": "group", "op": "OR", "children": [a, b]} a \| b {"type": "not", "condition": a} ~a {"type": "exists", "field": "x"} F("x").exists()

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The PHREAK Engine.

Performance characteristics of the FluxRules PHREAK engine.

docs.title: Evidence boundary
docs.text:
The repository has two benchmark categories:

  1. Pure matcher evidence: tests/performance/test_scale_readiness.py directly evaluated 1,000,000 generated facts against 1,200 generated rules on commit a572be9 using CPython 3.11.13 on macOS arm64. It compared 2,000 complete fired-rule sets against ReferenceEvaluator, measured 428.82 facts/s and 140.70 MB peak RSS, and passed the 150 facts/s and 2,048 MB thresholds. The retained artifact is .research/scale-readiness-2026-09-16.json.
  2. Boundary evidence: actions, persistence, HTTP serialization, auth, queueing, process concurrency, and sticky streaming are separate costs and contracts. They are not included in the pure matcher result above.

Do not interpret the pure matcher measurement as end-to-end service throughput. The next benchmark set should use the same deterministic rule/fact profiles and report exact result parity, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, peak RSS, and failure counts for each boundary independently.

docs.title: Test environment
docs.text:
• Python 3.11
  • Single-threaded evaluation
  • Test dataset: cross_border_payment_risk_triage (shared dataset, 3 facts)
  • Rules: 10-1000 typical rules

docs.title: Latency (per evaluation)
docs.text:
Rule Count PHREAK 10 rules ~0.5ms 100 rules ~2ms 500 rules ~10ms 1000 rules ~20ms

Notes: - Latency grows roughly linearly with rule count - Latency measured in EvaluationResult.latency_ms

docs.title: Memory usage
docs.text:
Rule Count PHREAK 10 rules ~1MB 100 rules ~1MB 1000 rules ~2MB

Notes: - Constant footprint: rules are loaded once and facts evaluate independently

docs.title: Startup time
docs.text:
Rule Count Time 10 rules ~1ms 100 rules ~1ms 1000 rules ~2ms

Note: load_rules() cost is small; most work happens at evaluate() time.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
Single-threaded with batch evaluation:

  • PHREAK: ~2000 evaluations/sec (500 rules, simple conditions)

Note: Actual throughput depends on rule complexity and condition logic.

docs.title: Required follow-up profiles
docs.text:
Before making broader capacity claims, run and retain separate results for:

  • selective, dense/hot-field, nested, and high-match rule distributions;
  • deterministic no-op action execution and action failure handling;
  • persistence/load phases with result parity after reload;
  • in-process HTTP and a real local server path with JSON/error timing;
  • bounded queue producer/consumer behavior and backpressure;
  • one, two, and four process workers with ordered result parity;
  • sticky streaming shards with repeated/changed facts and memory growth.

Each profile must identify whether it measures matcher-only or end-to-end work.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
FluxRules follows semantic versioning. This page summarizes each release. The full list of changes, with migration notes, is in CHANGELOG.md in the repository.

Current release: 1.1.2 (2026-11-03).

docs.title: 1.1.2 (2026-11-03): Every evaluation path agrees
docs.text:
• A single in / not_in value counts as a one-item list on every path, so isin("US") no longer matches "U", and a MembershipValueWarning tells the author to write the list.
  • boolean_string_coercion works with the alpha prefilter; fluxrules.evaluate() and the HTTP API follow all comparison settings; and fluxrules evaluate applies the settings in its config file.
  • PreFilteredEvaluator no longer drops facts with text, boolean, Decimal or very large integer values, and its SQL fact store saves Decimal, dates and tuples exactly.
  • New page: How FluxRules Compares Values, generated from a test matrix that compares ten evaluation paths.
  • EngineConfig.use_optimized_engine is deprecated: nothing reads it.

docs.title: 1.1.1 (2026-11-02): Documentation reorganized
docs.text:
The library code is unchanged; only the version number moves to 1.1.1.

  • Each topic now lives on one page, and the navigation follows the order a reader needs it: Getting Started, Using FluxRules, Authoring Rules, The Engine, Advanced Guides, Operating, Examples and Reference.
  • Duplicate pages are merged. Advanced Capabilities became the Capability Map under Advanced Guides, and links every capability to its guide and its example.
  • Concepts links the Fact section to From Fact to Action and Ways to Evaluate a Fact.
  • Wrong statements are corrected: facts must be flat, there are no built-in actions, sessions do not need the sql extra, and evaluate_with_actions does not run @action handlers.
  • The Actions examples handle handler failures, and the Quickstart output matches however you run it.
  • The docs build fails on any broken link, in CI and before every deploy.
  • Removed page addresses: getting-started/, features/, usage/ and the pages under it, reference/http-endpoints/, action-registry/, custom-transforms-cheatsheet/ and custom-transforms-answered/. Their content is on the merged pages above.

docs.title: 1.1.0 (2026-11-02): Typed facts, missing-field fixes and batch evaluation
docs.text:
• Engines accept Pydantic models, dataclasses, attrs classes and msgspec structs; nested models become dotted keys. See Typed Facts.
  • fact_schema= checks rule fields against a model when rules load. fields(Model) gives checked field references, and lenient_aliases() and opt-in validate_facts normalize incoming key styles.
  • With a fact schema, FieldNotFoundError catches userAge, user_age and user-age, not just case variants. It also reports unflattened nested facts.
  • EngineConfig.missing_field and MissingFieldNotWarning: NOT over a missing field stops firing in 2.0. Opt in now with "unknown".
  • fluxrules validate --schema checks JSON and YAML rule files against a model in CI. The schema can also be named in the rule file or fluxrules.yaml.
  • fact_pipeline= runs a FactPipeline inside evaluate().
  • engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=N) returns full results in input order, with every engine option applied in worker processes.
  • Rules compiled with compile_conditions=True follow config changes made after load_rules.
  • HTTP API: POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/evaluate, real rule names in responses, rule writes no longer stall without Redis, and the explain store is bounded.
  • New guide: Ways to Evaluate a Fact.

docs.title: 1.0.2 (2026-10-28): Packaging cleanup
docs.text:
• Python 3.13 and 3.14 support, SPDX license metadata and working README links on PyPI.
  • dev and docs moved from extras to dependency groups.

docs.title: 1.0.1 (2026-10-28): CLI install hint
docs.text: • Running fluxrules without the cli extra prints pip install 'fluxrules[cli]' instead of a ModuleNotFoundError.

docs.title: 1.0.0 (2026-10-28): First stable release
docs.text: • Documented equal-priority ordering: ties go to the highest rule ID. This is not a guaranteed contract.

docs.title: 0.2.0 (2026-10-20): Fluent condition syntax
docs.text:
• F("amount") > 5000 expressions build the same condition dicts the engine already accepts, combined with &, | and ~.
  • FieldNotFoundError flags a field name that differs from a present key only by case.
  • evaluate() and the engine share one set of operators.
  • Fixes for OR rules in the alpha prefilter, uncomparable fact values, and action handlers that take **kwargs.

docs.title: 0.1.4 (2026-10-20): Streaming cache fix and faster AND/OR
docs.text:
• Streaming mode now evicts stale cache entries when a field changes.
  • AND and OR trees stop at the first child that decides the result, which speeds up selective AND rules by 35 to 45 percent.

docs.title: 0.1.3 (2026-10-16): condition_dsl renamed to conditions
docs.text:
• Breaking: condition_dsl became conditions everywhere, including YAML files and the database column (migration 002). The domain/dsl module became domain/conditions.
  • Rule(conditions=...) validates the whole condition tree when the rule is created.

docs.title: 0.1.2 (2026-10-15): Persistence fixes
docs.text:
• Rule writes through SQLAlchemyPersistenceAdapter use one database session each, so saved rows are no longer lost.
  • Rule(persist=True) uses the adapter registered with ServiceFactory, so it works with PostgreSQL, SQL Server and any other SQLAlchemy database.
• Maintenance release with no recorded changes.

docs.title: 0.1.0 (2026-10-06): First release intended for publication
docs.text:
• One EvaluationResult type across every evaluation path, with fired_rules as the single name for what matched.
  • Rule(...) performs no database I/O. persist defaults to False, and Rule.save() is the explicit alternative.
  • evaluate() and validate() accept a Rule, an iterable of rules, or a Ruleset.
  • RuleBuilder.build() returns the canonical Rule, and RuleBuilder and ConditionBuilder are exported from the top-level package.

docs.title: 0.0.1 (2026-09-14): Initial development version
docs.text: Never published. It introduced the PHREAK engine with stateless and streaming modes, Pydantic v2 rule validation, extensible engines, operators, actions and transforms, the optional FastAPI server and fact pipelines.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
These items are designed but not yet shipped. The backlog explains each one and why it is waiting.

Planned for 2.0

  • Make missing_field="unknown" the default, so NOT over a missing field no longer fires. 1.1.0 ships the opt-in and a warning that names affected fields.
  • Safer comparison defaults: a comparison that cannot be made is unknown, True no longer equals 1, and types are strict with a fact schema.

Comparing values (1.2.0)

  • Close the remaining gaps in the comparison matrix: tuples, F and YAML rules, evaluate_batch(workers=2), and one set of comparison functions.
  • Report comparisons that cannot be made: a warning by default, and settings to stay silent, treat them as unknown or raise.
  • Check rule values when rules load: against their operator, against the fact schema, and for YAML values read differently from how they look.
  • Make common comparisons easy: approx, case-insensitive text operators, and documented date and number conversion with a fact schema.

Typed facts

  • A strict mode that raises when a fact lacks a field a rule needs.
  • Check rules stored in a database against a fact schema.
  • Export a fact schema for rule-editing tools.
  • Match rule fields by a model's aliases (for example camelCase).
  • Typed facts in the HTTP API and the cross-fact engine.
  • Tidy fluxrules.pipeline.schema, which still treats Pydantic as optional.

HTTP API

  • Decide what evaluation_mode="stateful" means for stored rules, or remove it.
  • Make the compiled-rule cache use the configured Redis server.
  • Finish or remove the unfinished /api/v1/engines endpoints, and clear the Redis rule cache when rules change.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text:
• Core API (Rule, the engine, evaluate()): stable within 1.x.
  • Condition tree format: stable.
  • HTTP endpoints: stable under /api/v1. Breaking changes will go under /api/v2.

Public API labels each export with its stability contract.

docs.title: Choosing an Evaluation Mode
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The PHREAK Engine.

FluxRules ships a single engine (PHREAK), so there is no engine to pick. The one decision you make is which evaluation mode fits your workload.

docs.title: Decision flowchart
docs.text:
1. Do you keep state between facts?
  2. No, each request is independent → Stateless mode (default)

  3. Yes, you assert/retract into a long-lived session → Streaming mode

  4. What is the evaluation pattern?

  5. Request-response (HTTP) → Stateless mode
  6. Batch (many independent facts) → Stateless mode

  7. Event stream where only changes matter → Streaming mode

  8. Do you need per-fact deltas?

  9. No, you want the full fired set every call → Stateless mode
  10. Yes, you want only what changed since the last fact → Streaming mode

docs.title: Quick decision guide
docs.text: Scenario Mode HTTP API for fraud scoring Stateless Batch data pipeline Stateless Rules updated daily Stateless (reload rules) Single-file rule config Stateless Long-lived session with retractions Streaming Event stream, deltas only Streaming

docs.title: Default recommendation
docs.text:
Use stateless mode unless you specifically need persistent working memory:

  • Simplest deployment and reasoning (no state to manage)
  • Lowest memory footprint (nothing retained between calls)
  • Ideal for request-response and batch workloads

Enable streaming only when you need incremental deltas across a session.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Ways to Evaluate a Fact: See Ways to Evaluate a Fact for every way to send facts to the engine
  • The PHREAK Engine: See The PHREAK Engine for how the modes work
  • Working Memory: See Working Memory for the streaming contract
  • Concepts: See Concepts for engine fundamentals

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Installation and YAML Rules.

The fluxrules command validates rule files, evaluates an event against them, scaffolds a project and starts the HTTP API. Install it with the cli extra:

pip install 'fluxrules[cli]'
fluxrules --help
Command Does fluxrules validate RULES... Checks rule files for structural issues and, with a fact schema, unknown fields fluxrules evaluate RULES INPUT Evaluates one JSON event against a rule file fluxrules init Scaffolds rules.json, input.json and fluxrules.yaml fluxrules serve Starts the HTTP API (needs the api extra) fluxrules version Prints the installed version

docs.title: Rule files
docs.text:
validate and evaluate read .json files as JSON and .yaml / .yml files as YAML (YAML needs the yaml extra). A rule file holds one of:

  • a list of rule mappings,
  • a single rule mapping,
  • a mapping with a rules list and an optional fact_schema, naming the model the rules are written against:
fact_schema: myapp.models:Payment
rules:
  - id: 1
    name: large_payment_new_account
    priority: 50
    action: manual_review
    conditions:
      type: and
      children:
        - {type: condition, field: amount, op: ">", value: 2000}
        - {type: condition, field: account.age_days, op: "<", value: 14}

The same shape works in JSON ({"fact_schema": "...", "rules": [...]}). Rule mappings use the canonical Rule fields; see YAML Rules.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
fluxrules validate rules/payments.yaml
fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml --schema myapp.models:Payment

Reports empty conditions, duplicate ids and unsupported operators. With a fact schema it also reports every field a rule names that the model lacks, each with a "did you mean" hint, not only the first. Output is JSON:

{
  "valid": false,
  "issues": [
    "Rule 'large_payment_new_account' references unknown field 'account.ageDays' (not in fact schema Payment). Did you mean 'account.age_days'?",
    "Rule 'high_risk_country' references unknown field 'account.contry' (not in fact schema Payment). Did you mean 'account.country'?"
  ],
  "schemas": [
    {
      "file": "rules/payments.yaml",
      "fact_schema": "myapp.models:Payment",
      "source": "rule file rules/payments.yaml"
    }
  ]
}

schemas says, per file, which schema was used and where it came from. With several files, each issue starts with its file name.

Option Meaning --schema SPEC Fact schema to check against. Overrides the rule file and the config. --config PATH Config file to read fact_schema from. See Where the schema comes from.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Every file is valid 1 At least one issue (structural or unknown field) 2 A rule file, config file or schema could not be loaded

So a CI step is a single line:

fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml

docs.title: evaluate
docs.text:
fluxrules evaluate rules.yaml event.json
fluxrules evaluate rules.yaml event.json --format json
fluxrules evaluate rules.yaml event.json --schema myapp.models:Payment --validate-facts normalize

Loads the rules into an engine, evaluates the event and prints the matched rules (a table by default, or JSON with --format json).

Option Meaning --format table\|json Output format. Default table. --engine NAME Registered engine to use. Default PHREAK. --schema SPEC Fact schema. Rules naming a field it lacks are refused. --config PATH Config file to read fact_schema and the comparison settings from. See Comparison settings. --validate-facts off\|normalize\|strict Validate the event against the schema first, as validate_facts does. normalize accepts ageDays for age_days and "5" for 5, and flattens a nested event. Needs a schema. Default off.

evaluate exits 1 with a one-line message when a rule names an unknown field, when the event fails validation, or when the engine reports an error such as a nested event without --validate-facts (FieldNotFoundError). It exits 2 when a file or the schema cannot be loaded.

docs.title: Comparison settings
docs.text:
evaluate applies the comparison settings it finds in the config file, the same file it reads fact_schema from (see Where the schema comes from for how it is found):

# fluxrules.yaml
strict_null_handling: false     # true: == None matches a None value
strict_type_comparison: false   # true: values of different types never match
boolean_string_coercion: false  # true: "true" / "false" are read as booleans
missing_field: unknown          # NOT over a missing field does not fire

Each setting means what the EngineConfig field of the same name means, and a setting the file leaves out keeps its default. The settings apply to whichever engine --engine names, including a custom engine you registered (see Custom Engines). For missing_field, false (with or without quotes) keeps the 1.x behaviour, unknown adopts the 2.0 behaviour, and leaving it out keeps the default. A wrong value, such as strict_type_comparison: maybe, stops the command when the file was named with --config. In a file found automatically, it is reported and the file's settings are ignored.

How FluxRules Compares Values shows exactly which answers each setting changes.

docs.title: Naming a schema
docs.text:
A schema is named by an import string, in one of two forms:

Form Example Loads Module myapp.models:Payment Payment from the module myapp.models. The current directory is searched, so a project's own modules work without installing the project. File models/payment.py:Payment Payment from that file. A relative path is resolved against the directory of the file that names it (the rule file or config file), or the current directory for --schema.

The class can be a Pydantic model, dataclass, attrs class, msgspec Struct or TypedDict. Nested models are addressed with dotted paths (account.age_days). --validate-facts needs a schema Pydantic can validate: a Pydantic model, dataclass or TypedDict.

docs.title: Where the schema comes from
docs.text:
For each rule file, the first of these that is present applies:

  1. --schema on the command line.
  2. fact_schema in the rule file.
  3. fact_schema in the config file: --config PATH, else $FLUXRULES_CONFIG_FILE, else the first of fluxrules.yaml, fluxrules.yml, fluxrules.json, config/fluxrules.yaml, config/fluxrules.yml, config/fluxrules.json, ~/.fluxrules.yaml and /etc/fluxrules/config.yaml. These are the same places DeploymentConfig looks. A .yaml or .yml file is read as YAML, anything else as JSON.

The config file is read only when neither --schema nor the rule file names a schema. A config file found automatically that cannot be read (for example because PyYAML is not installed) is skipped with a note; a file passed with --config must be readable.

With none of them, validate runs only the structural checks.

docs.title: Trusting a schema named in a file
docs.text:
Loading a schema imports its module, and importing runs that module's code. A schema you name yourself, with --schema or in a file you pass with --config, is always loaded. A schema named inside a rule file, or in a config file found automatically, is loaded only when you add --trust-schema:

fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml --trust-schema

Without it, the command stops with exit code 2 and says which file named which schema, so running validate on rule files from someone else never runs their code by surprise. In CI, where the rule files and the models live in your own repository, pass --trust-schema or name the schema with --schema.

# fluxrules.yaml
fact_schema: myapp.models:Payment

Put the schema in the config when every rule file uses the same model. Put it in a rule file when files are written against different models. A rule file that names a schema is tied to that import path, so moving or renaming the model class means updating those files.

docs.title: init
docs.text:
fluxrules init --dir my-project

Writes rules.json, input.json and fluxrules.yaml into the directory, skipping any that already exist. The config sets the three comparison flags to their defaults, ready to change (see Comparison settings), and includes a commented-out fact_schema line to fill in:

strict_null_handling: false
strict_type_comparison: false
boolean_string_coercion: false
# fact_schema: myapp.models:Order

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
pip install 'fluxrules[api]'
fluxrules serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --reload

Starts the HTTP API with uvicorn. See HTTP API Reference.

docs.title: How FluxRules Compares Values
docs.text:
This page shows, for every operator, which fact values match which rule values. Use it to check how a rule will treat a number stored as text, a None, a date, a boolean or a missing field.

Note

This page is generated from the tests in tests/engine/comparison_matrix.py, which run every case on every evaluation path. Do not edit it by hand: run make docs-tables. A test fails when the page and the code disagree.

docs.title: How a comparison works
docs.text:
A comparison is plain Python: v > 5 runs fact_value > 5. FluxRules does not convert between types, so the text "5" is not the number 5. Three rules follow from that:

  • A comparison Python cannot make is no match, not an error. "abc" > 5 raises TypeError in Python; in a rule it is simply no match. Nothing tells you this happened.
  • NOT turns that no match into a match. NOT(v > 5) fires for "abc", None and a missing field, because the check inside failed. See NOT over a comparison.
  • A missing field, or a None value, matches nothing unless you change the settings.

Python's own rules still apply where Python can compare: True == 1, 5 == 5.0, a Decimal compares with a float, and 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false. in and not_in take a list; a single value counts as a one-item list (see Conditions).

docs.title: How to read the tables
docs.text: Each table is one operator under the default settings. A row is the value in the fact, under the field v; a column is the value written in the rule. yes means the rule fires. (missing) means the fact has no v field at all.

docs.title: NOT over a comparison
docs.text:
NOT fires whenever the check inside does not match, including when the check could not be made. That is why NOT(v > 5) fires for "5", "abc", None, float("nan"), a date and a missing field:

Fact value NOT(v == 5) NOT(v != 5) NOT(v > 5) NOT(v >= 5) NOT(v < 5) NOT(v <= 5) 5 no yes yes no yes no 0 yes no yes yes no no 5.5 yes no no no yes yes Decimal("5.5") yes no no no yes yes True yes no yes yes no no False yes no yes yes no no "5" yes no yes yes yes yes "true" yes no yes yes yes yes "abc" yes no yes yes yes yes "" yes no yes yes yes yes None yes yes yes yes yes yes float("nan") yes no yes yes yes yes float("inf") yes no no no yes yes date(2026, 6, 1) yes no yes yes yes yes datetime(2026, 6, 1, 12, 0) yes no yes yes yes yes "2026-06-01" yes no yes yes yes yes [5] yes no yes yes yes yes {"a": 5} yes no yes yes yes yes (missing) yes yes yes yes yes yes

To stop NOT from firing on a missing field, set EngineConfig(missing_field="unknown"). To stop it from firing on values of the wrong type, give the engine a fact schema so values arrive with the right type (see Avoiding surprises).

docs.title: How each setting changes the answers
docs.text: Each table lists the answers that differ from the default settings. Where a setting changes no plain comparison, the table shows the NOT cases it changes instead.

docs.title: strict_null_handling
docs.text:
EngineConfig(strict_null_handling=True) lets == None match a None value and != x match it too. By default a None value never matches.

Rule Fact value Default With this setting v == None None no yes v != 5 None no yes v != 5.5 None no yes v != "5" None no yes v != "abc" None no yes v != True None no yes v != date(2026, 1, 1) None no yes

docs.title: strict_type_comparison
docs.text:

docs.text:
EngineConfig(missing_field="false") keeps the 1.x behaviour, where NOT over a missing field fires, and turns off the warning about it.

With the matrix's rules and facts, this setting changes no answers.

docs.title: Known differences between paths
docs.text: None. Every evaluation path gives the answers above under every setting: PhreakEngine with and without the alpha prefilter, compiled conditions, streaming mode, evaluate_batch, fluxrules.evaluate(), CrossFactEngine (for the rules it can express), PreFilteredEvaluator over a SQL fact store, the CLI and the HTTP API. The tests fail if any of them starts to differ.

docs.title: Avoiding surprises
docs.text:
• Give the engine a fact schema. With fact_schema= and validate_facts="normalize", the text "100.3" becomes the number 100.3 before any rule runs; with validate_facts="strict", a wrong type raises FactValidationError instead of quietly not matching. See Typed Facts.
  • Or convert in a pipeline. The FieldType transform converts named fields of a plain dict. See Fact Pipeline.
  • Use Decimal for money, and avoid == on floats: compare with >= or <= instead.
  • Parse dates first. An ISO date string is text, and a date does not compare with a datetime.
  • Write in values as a list, and use == when you mean one value.

docs.title: Complex Conditions
docs.text:
Combine multiple simple conditions using AND / OR / NOT logic.

Prerequisites: Authoring Rules and Conditions & Operators, which covers all operators and the four authoring formats.

docs.title: AND Logic
docs.text:
All conditions must be true for the rule to fire.

from fluxrules import F, Rule, PhreakEngine

rule = Rule(
    name="high_value_international",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").not_in(["US", "CA", "GB"])),
    action="manual_review",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "country": "NG"}).fired_rules)   # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "country": "NG"}).fired_rules)   # []

Dict equivalent (the wire format stored in YAML/DB):

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "not_in", "value": ["US", "CA", "GB"]},
    ],
}

docs.title: OR Logic
docs.text:
At least one condition must be true.

rule = Rule(
    name="risky_pattern",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 5000)
        | (F("velocity_1h") >= 5)
        | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 80)
    ),
    action="block_payment",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "velocity_1h": 1, "ip_risk_score": 30}).fired_rules)   # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 1000, "velocity_1h": 6, "ip_risk_score": 30}).fired_rules)   # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 1000, "velocity_1h": 1, "ip_risk_score": 30}).fired_rules)   # []

docs.title: NOT Logic
docs.text:
The condition must be false.

rule = Rule(
    name="unverified_high_value",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.com"))
    ),
    action="step_up_auth",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "email_domain": "gmail.com"}).fired_rules)    # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "email_domain": "trusted.com"}).fired_rules)  # []

docs.title: Nested Logic
docs.text:
Combine AND, OR, and NOT for multi-part rules:

rule = Rule(
    name="payment_risk_triage",
    conditions=(
        # 1. Large amount
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        # 2. High-risk country OR high IP risk
        & (
            (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"]))
            | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70)
        )
        # 3. New or unverified device/account
        & (
            (F("account_age_days") < 7)
            | (F("device_age_days") < 7)
        )
        # 4. NOT a trusted email domain
        & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.example"))
    ),
    action="manual_review",
)

The F DSL reads as close to the logic description as you can get in Python. The same tree in dict form grows by about 4× in line count, which is why the F DSL is the recommended authoring format.

docs.title: Operator precedence
docs.text:
Python's & and | bind more tightly than >, <, ==. Always wrap each individual leaf in parentheses before composing:

# python skip: the Wrong line deliberately raises to show the trap
# Correct: each leaf is parenthesised
(F("amount") > 2000) & (F("country") == "NG")

# Wrong: & binds before ==, raising a TypeError
F("amount") > 2000 & F("country") == "NG"

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: This page introduces the fundamental concepts you need to work with FluxRules. All code references are to src/fluxrules/.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
A Rule is the core abstraction. It combines a condition, an action, and metadata for organization.

Source: src/fluxrules/domain/unified_rule.py

from fluxrules import Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="payment_risk_high",
    conditions={
        "type": "condition",
        "field": "amount",
        "op": ">",
        "value": 5000,
    },
    action="manual_review",
    domain="fraud_detection",
    tags=frozenset(["tier_0", "high_value"]),
    priority=100,
)

Key Attributes:

  • id: Auto-generated unique identifier (or manual override)

  • name: Human-readable rule name

  • domain: Logical grouping (e.g., "fraud_detection", "compliance")

  • tags: String set for filtering and categorization

  • conditions: Nested tree defining when the rule fires

  • action: What to do when the rule matches

  • priority: Execution order (higher = runs first). All matching rules fire; priority only orders them. Ties are currently broken by rule ID (highest first), which is not a guaranteed contract, so use distinct priorities if order matters. Same-group, same-priority rules raise a validation warning.

See: examples/18_unified_rule.py

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
An Engine evaluates facts against loaded rules and returns matched rules and actions.

Source: src/fluxrules/engine/ (interfaces and implementations)

A single engine is available:

  • PhreakEngine (the only engine): Lazy, agenda-driven evaluation with stateless (default) and streaming modes

Quick Example: 

from fluxrules import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

fact = {"amount": 6000, "country": "NG"}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)

The engine has two evaluation modes, stateless and streaming. The PHREAK Engine explains how each mode works, and Choosing an Evaluation Mode helps you pick one.

docs.title: Fact
docs.text:
A Fact is the data you check against your rules, such as one payment. It is a flat dictionary of field names and values:

fact = {
    "fact_id": "txn-001",
    "amount": 2500.00,
    "currency": "USD",
    "country": "NG",
    "ip_risk_score": 85,
    "velocity_1h": 3,
    "account_age_days": 7,
}

A rule refers to a field by its key, as in F("amount") > 1000.

Facts often arrive in other shapes, and FluxRules handles each of them:

  • Nested data, such as {"payment": {"amount": 4200}}. The engine reads flat keys only, so flatten it first. The nested value then becomes the dotted key "payment.amount". See Nested Facts.
  • Typed models, such as a Pydantic model or a dataclass. The engine turns them into a flat dictionary for you. See Typed Facts.
  • Raw input that needs cleaning, renaming or enriching. A fact pipeline prepares it before evaluation. See Fact Pipeline.

Each engine.evaluate(fact) call is independent by default: the engine keeps nothing from one call to the next. Streaming mode and sessions keep state on purpose, and you opt into each.

To follow a single fact from the moment it arrives to the actions it produces, read From Fact to Action. To choose how your application sends facts to the engine (one at a time, in batches, as a stream, from the command line or over HTTP), read Ways to Evaluate a Fact.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
A condition tree is a nested tree that defines when a rule fires. It combines:

  • Simple conditions (field comparisons)

  • Logical operators (AND, OR, NOT)

  • Nested groups

Basic condition: 

from fluxrules import F

F("amount") > 5000

Nested conditions (with AND/OR): & means both must be true, | means either one is enough. 

from fluxrules import F

(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN"]))

With NOT: ~ means the condition must be false. 

from fluxrules import F

~F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.com")

Every expression is stored as a plain dictionary tree, the same format YAML files and the HTTP API use. The AND example above is stored as:

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "in", "value": ["NG", "SN"]},
    ],
}

You can write the dictionary by hand when you prefer. See Authoring Rules for all the ways to write a condition.

Validation: Use from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import validate_conditions

See: examples/02_complex_conditions.py, examples/13_complex_rules.py

docs.title: Evaluation Result
docs.text:
When you evaluate a fact, the engine returns a result object with:

result = engine.evaluate(fact)

# result.fired_rules: list of rule IDs that matched
# result.actions: list of actions to execute
# result.latency_ms: execution time in milliseconds

Example: 

print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")  # [1001, 1003]
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")       # ['manual_review', 'block_payment']
print(f"Time: {result.latency_ms}ms")     # 1.2ms

The engine does not run the actions itself. It returns their names, and your application decides what to do with them. Actions shows how to register a handler for each action name.

See: examples/15_action_system.py

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
A Domain is a logical grouping of rules. Rules with the same domain typically handle a specific problem area.

For example depending on how your rules are grouped you can give a name e.g. compliance or fraud_detections etc.

Filtering by domain: 

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, Rule

# Define rules with domains
rule1 = Rule(name="rule1", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag")
rule2 = Rule(name="rule2", domain="compliance", conditions=F("country") == "NG", action="review")
rule3 = Rule(name="rule3", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("type") == "transaction", action="process")

all_rules = [rule1, rule2, rule3]

# Load only fraud_detection rules
fraud_rules = [r for r in all_rules if r.domain == "fraud_detection"]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(fraud_rules)

See: examples/03_domains_and_tags.py

docs.title: Tag
docs.text:
A Tag is a string label for categorization and filtering.

Filtering by tag: 

# Get all tier_0 rules
tier0_rules = [r for r in all_rules if "tier_0" in (r.tags or set())]

See: examples/03_domains_and_tags.py

docs.title: Shared Evaluation Dataset
docs.text:
To learn FluxRules, all examples use a shared cross_border_payment_risk_triage dataset:

# python skip
from shared_use_case import SHARED_FACTS, USE_CASE_NAME, build_shared_rules

# 3 test transactions
for fact in SHARED_FACTS:
    print(fact["fact_id"])  # txn-001, txn-002, txn-003

# 3 payment-risk rules
rules = build_shared_rules()

# 8-condition nested tree
dsl = complex_risk_condition()

This shared context lets you focus on learning features without context-switching between problem domains.

docs.title: Conditions & Rule Authoring
docs.text:
A rule's conditions field defines when the rule fires. FluxRules gives you four ways to author conditions, the same condition tree on the wire for all four, and a set of tools to validate before you deploy.

Start with Authoring Rules for how to choose between them. This page is the reference: every operator and every validation tool.

docs.title: 1. F DSL (recommended for Python code)
docs.text:
Write conditions as natural Python expressions using the F helper. Each expression compiles to a condition dict the engine accepts; you never touch raw dicts.

from fluxrules import F, Rule

# Single leaf
rule = Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="review",
)

# AND: both must hold
rule = Rule(
    name="high_value_us",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"),
    action="review",
)

# OR: either suffices
rule = Rule(
    name="risky_origin",
    conditions=(F("country").isin(["NG", "SN"])) | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70),
    action="block",
)

# NOT
rule = Rule(
    name="unverified",
    conditions=~F("verified").exists(),
    action="step_up",
)

# Composed
rule = Rule(
    name="fraud_triage",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        & (F("payment_method").isin(["crypto", "prepaid_card"]))
        & (
            (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"]))
            | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70)
        )
        & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.example"))
    ),
    action="manual_review",
)

Operator precedence warning. Python's & and | bind more tightly than comparisons like >, <, ==. Always wrap each individual condition in parentheses:

# python skip: the second line deliberately raises to show the trap
# Correct
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

# Wrong: & binds before ==, raising a TypeError at runtime
F("amount") > 5000 & F("country") == "US"

docs.title: 2. Dict / YAML (for config-driven rules)
docs.text:
The dict format is the wire and storage format. Use it when rules come from a database, YAML file, or API response.

Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions={"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
    action="review",
)

YAML (loaded with load_rules_from_yaml, see YAML Rules):

name: high_value
conditions:
  type: condition
  field: amount
  op: ">"
  value: 5000
action: review

AND/OR in dict form:

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"},
    ],
}

The F DSL and the dict format describe the same conditions. Mix them freely: a Rule built with F(...) stores a dictionary tree like one built from a dict, and loads back from YAML the same way. One difference in shape: a & b & c nests as (a & b) & c, where a hand-written dict usually has one flat group of three. Both give the same results.

docs.title: 3. RuleBuilder (fluent, step by step)
docs.text:
RuleBuilder chains method calls and validates each step. Useful when building rules programmatically where you want to catch errors early.

from fluxrules import F, RuleBuilder

rule = (
    RuleBuilder()
    .name("high_value_us")
    .priority(10)
    .condition((F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"))
    .action("review")
    .build()
)

.condition() accepts both an F expression and a raw dict.

docs.title: 4. Checked field references with fields(Model)
docs.text:
When your facts have a model, such as a Pydantic class, you can name fields through the model instead of typing them as strings. fields(Model) gives an object whose attributes are the model's fields:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.facts import fields


class Account(BaseModel):
    age_days: int
    country: str


class Payment(BaseModel):
    amount: float
    account: Account


p = fields(Payment)

rule = Rule(
    name="block_high_risk_country",
    conditions=p.account.country.isin(["NG", "RU"]) & (p.amount > 1000),
    action="block",
)

Read the condition piece by piece:

  • p.amount is the same as F("amount").
  • p.account.country is the same as F("account.country"). A nested model becomes a dotted field name, which is how the engine sees nested facts.
  • .isin(["NG", "RU"]) and > 1000 are the ordinary F operators, so every operator on this page works here too.
  • & joins the two parts with AND. The comparison is wrapped in parentheses, as with F. The isin(...) call needs none, because a method call binds before &.

The rule stores the same condition tree as one written with F:

written_with_f = F("account.country").isin(["NG", "RU"]) & (F("amount") > 1000)
assert rule.conditions == Rule(name="same", conditions=written_with_f, action="block").conditions

The difference is when a typo is caught. F("acount.country") is accepted and the rule never matches. p.acount raises UnknownFieldError on that line, and the message suggests account:

from fluxrules import UnknownFieldError

try:
    p.acount  # noqa: B018
except UnknownFieldError as exc:
    assert "Did you mean 'account'?" in str(exc)

dir(p.account) lists the fields, so an editor can offer them as you type. See Typed Facts.

docs.title: Comparison (Python dunders)
docs.text:
F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x") == v "==" or "eq" Equal F("x") != v "!=" or "ne" Not equal F("x") > v ">" or "gt" Greater than F("x") >= v ">=" or "gte" Greater than or equal F("x") < v "<" or "lt" Less than F("x") <= v "<=" or "lte" Less than or equal

The six comparison operators also accept their word-form aliases in dict/YAML (eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte), normalised before evaluation.

docs.title: Collection membership
docs.text:
F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x").isin(["a", "b"]) "in" Value is a member of the list F("x").not_in(["a"]) "not_in" Value is not a member

Give isin and not_in a list. A single value counts as a list with one item, so F("country").isin("US") means the same as F("country").isin(["US"]). It does not search inside the text: "U" is not a member of "US". FluxRules converts the value when the rule is created and warns you with MembershipValueWarning, so you can write the list yourself:

import warnings

from fluxrules import F, MembershipValueWarning

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    condition = F("country").isin("US")

print(condition.to_dict()["value"])  # ['US']
print(caught[0].category is MembershipValueWarning)  # True

The same applies to {"op": "in", "value": "US"} in a dict, a YAML file or the HTTP API, and to rules read back from a database. To compare one value, == and != say it more directly.

To see how every operator treats each kind of value (numbers stored as text, None, dates, booleans, a missing field), see How FluxRules Compares Values.

docs.title: String / collection containment
docs.text: F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x").contains("tag") "contains" Collection or string contains value F("x").not_contains("flag") "not_contains" Does not contain

docs.title: String matching
docs.text:
Both sides are coerced to strings before matching.

F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x").starts_with("adm") "starts_with" str(x).startswith(...) F("x").ends_with(".com") "ends_with" str(x).endswith(...) F("x").regex("^4[0-9]{12}") "regex" re.search(pattern, str(x)). It matches anywhere in the string, so add ^ to anchor at the start

docs.title: Boolean composition (F DSL)
docs.text: Operator Meaning Dict equivalent a & b AND {"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [a, b]} a \| b OR {"type": "group", "op": "OR", "children": [a, b]} ~a NOT {"type": "not", "condition": a}

docs.title: Field presence
docs.text:
F("email").exists()          # True when "email" key is in facts and not None
~F("email").exists()         # True when "email" is absent or None

Dict equivalent:

{"type": "exists", "field": "email"}

Use exists() when a field might legitimately be absent. A condition node raises FieldNotFoundError if a present key is the same field spelled differently (see Field names are exact). exists() never raises.

docs.title: What to keep in mind when authoring rules
Field names are exact
docs.text:
F("Amount"), F("amount") and F("user_age") / F("userAge") are different fields: the engine reads the exact key. When a rule's field is missing from a fact but the fact has a key that looks like the same field, the engine raises FieldNotFoundError instead of quietly not matching. What counts as a look-alike depends on whether the engine has a fact schema:

Engine Look-alikes that raise Example No schema Case only Amount against amount fact_schema=Model Case and key style: _, - and spaces are ignored user_age against userAge, user-age or UserAge

Without a schema, one ruleset may serve several kinds of facts that spell a field differently (user_id from one system, userId from another). The engine cannot tell that apart from a typo, so it only treats case as a typo. With a schema, every rule field is checked against the model when the rules load, so a key in another style can only be a mismatch.

In both cases a . is significant, because it separates levels of nesting: user.name is never a look-alike of username. A dotted field such as user.age against an unflattened {"user": {...}} raises too, with a hint to flatten the fact (see Nested Facts). A field that is absent with no look-alike returns False. Numbered families stay distinct: field_0 is not a look-alike of field_10.

# python skip: the first line deliberately raises to show the check
# Fact: {"amount": 5000, "user_age": 30}, engine without a schema
F("Amount") > 1000    # raises FieldNotFoundError: did you mean 'amount'?
F("userAge") >= 18    # no match (with a schema it would raise)
F("amount") > 1000    # evaluates correctly

A schema also catches these before any fact arrives: load_rules rejects any rule field the model lacks.

docs.title: Operator precedence: always use parentheses
docs.text:
Python evaluates & and | before >, <, ==. The rule is simple: wrap every individual F(...) comparison in its own parentheses before composing:

# python skip: the unsafe line deliberately raises to show the trap
# safe: each leaf is wrapped
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

# unsafe: raises TypeError
F("amount") > 5000 & F("country") == "US"

docs.title: Use exists() for optional fields
docs.text:
A condition node on a field that is absent raises (if the name looks like a typo) or returns False (if genuinely different schema). When a field is intentionally optional, guard it with exists():

# Only fires if "promo_code" is present AND matches
F("promo_code").exists() & (F("promo_code") == "SUMMER24")

docs.title: Missing fields and NOT
docs.text:
A condition on a missing field is False, so NOT over it is True: ~(F("blocked") == True) fires on a fact with no blocked key. That is rarely what the rule means, and a key sent under another name (is_blocked) lets the rule through silently.

EngineConfig.missing_field sets how NOT treats a missing field:

missing_field ~(F("blocked") == True) on {"amount": 1} Notes None (default) fires, and emits MissingFieldNotWarning once 1.x behaviour with a heads-up "false" fires 1.x behaviour, no warning "unknown" does not fire the 2.0 default

With "unknown" a missing field is unknown, as SQL treats NULL: NOT of unknown is unknown, AND / OR follow three-valued logic, and a rule fires only when its condition is definitely true. exists() is never unknown, so it is the way to test for absence on purpose:

from fluxrules import EngineConfig, F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine(config=EngineConfig(missing_field="unknown"))
engine.load_rules(
    [
        Rule(id=1, name="not_blocked", conditions=~(F("blocked") == True), action="allow"),  # noqa: E712
        # Explicit: "blocked is absent, or present and not True"
        Rule(
            id=2,
            name="not_blocked_or_absent",
            conditions=~F("blocked").exists() | ~(F("blocked") == True),  # noqa: E712
            action="allow",
        ),
    ]
)
assert engine.evaluate({"amount": 1}).fired_rules == [2]
assert sorted(engine.evaluate({"blocked": False}).fired_rules) == [1, 2]

The setting applies to PhreakEngine (interpreted and compiled) and to fluxrules.evaluate(), which reads the process-wide config (fluxrules.engine.configuration.set_config). Changing it on an engine's config object takes effect on that engine's next evaluation. See Changing settings after the engine is created.

docs.title: Value types must match
docs.text:
A numeric field compared with a string will not raise, but will silently not match. Match the value type to the field type:

F("amount") > 5000      # number field → number value
F("status") == "active" # string field → string value
F("tags").contains("vip")  # list field → scalar value to find in it

docs.title: isin takes a list, not positional args
docs.text:
# python skip: the second line deliberately raises to show the trap
F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"])   # correct
F("country").isin("NG", "SN", "GH")    # wrong: TypeError

docs.title: Combining AND chains cleanly
docs.text:
For long AND chains, align the & operators at the start of each line:

conditions=(
    (F("amount") > 2000)
    & (F("payment_method").isin(["crypto", "prepaid_card"]))
    & (F("chargeback_ratio") >= 0.1)
    & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.example"))
),

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: FluxRules validates condition trees at rule construction time (Pydantic) and exposes an explicit validate step for bulk checks before deployment.

docs.title: Automatic validation at construction
docs.text:
Invalid conditions are caught when you build the Rule:

# python skip: this block deliberately raises to show the validation error
from fluxrules import F, Rule

Rule(
    name="bad",
    conditions={"type": "condition", "field": "x", "op": "???", "value": 1},
    action="flag",
)
# raises ConditionValidationError: unknown operator '???'

Missing required keys, unknown operators, and malformed tree shapes all raise ConditionValidationError immediately.

docs.title: validate(): check a batch without evaluating
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="allow"),
]

issues = validate(rules)
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(issue)
else:
    print("All rules valid")

validate() returns a list of human-readable strings. An empty list means all rules passed. Use it in CI before deploying a new ruleset.

docs.title: FieldNotFoundError at evaluation time
docs.text:
When a condition field is absent from the incoming fact and the name is a case variant of a present key (e.g. Amount vs amount), the engine raises instead of silently returning False:

from fluxrules import F, FieldNotFoundError, Rule, evaluate

rule = Rule(name="r", conditions=F("Amount") > 5000, action="flag")
try:
    evaluate(rule, {"amount": 6000})
except FieldNotFoundError as e:
    print(e)
# Field 'Amount' not found in fact. Did you mean 'amount'? Available keys: ['amount']

To deliberately test whether a field is present before comparing its value, use F("field").exists():

# Does not raise even when "score" is absent
F("score").exists() & (F("score") >= 90)

docs.title: Full validation example
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate

rules = [
    Rule(
        name="fraud_check",
        conditions=(
            (F("amount") > 10000)
            & (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"]))
            & ~(F("verified").exists())
        ),
        action="block",
        priority=10,
    ),
    Rule(
        name="vip_fast_track",
        conditions=(F("tier") == "gold") | (F("spend_ytd") >= 50000),
        action="expedite",
        priority=5,
    ),
]

issues = validate(rules)
assert issues == [], issues

from fluxrules import evaluate

fact = {"amount": 15000, "country": "NG"}
result = evaluate(rules, fact)
print(result.fired_rules)   # rule ids that matched
print(result.actions)       # ["block"]

docs.title: Condition tree reference
docs.text:
The dict / YAML format uses these node shapes:

Node type Required keys Optional keys condition type, field, op, value none group / and / or type, children (or conditions) op (default AND) not type, condition none exists type, field none

Accepted aliases: "and", "or", "not", "exists", "group", "composite".

docs.title: Cross-Fact Rules
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Working Memory (fact storage).

Correlate multiple facts with cross-fact logic.

docs.title: Single-fact limitation
docs.text:
Standard engines evaluate one fact at a time:

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
result1 = engine.evaluate({"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 5000})
result2 = engine.evaluate({"customer_id": "c2", "amount": 1000})
# No correlation between result1 and result2

docs.title: Pattern 1: Pre-aggregate upstream
docs.text:
Combine facts before evaluation:

# Combine multiple facts before rule evaluation
combined = {
    "transaction_1_amount": 5000,
    "transaction_2_amount": 3000,
    "total_24h": 8000,  # Pre-computed
    "customer_id": "c1"
}

result = engine.evaluate(combined)

docs.title: Pattern 2: Multi-step with sessions
docs.text:
A session keeps the fields you add across steps. Add a running total as each transaction arrives, and evaluate after every step:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.domain.models import Ruleset
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
velocity = [Rule(id=1, name="high_24h_total", conditions=F("total_24h") > 6000, action="review")]
service.persist(
    Ruleset(group="velocity", rules=tuple(r.to_engine_rule(group="velocity") for r in velocity))
)
session = service.create_session("velocity")

# Step 1: the first transaction (5000) arrives
session.add_fact("total_24h", 5000)
assert session.evaluate().fired_rules == []

# Step 2: a second transaction (3000) arrives; update the running total
session.add_fact("total_24h", 8000)
assert session.evaluate().fired_rules == [1]

Your code computes the total; the session only remembers it between steps. Rules read flat fields, so store values such as total_24h rather than whole transactions under one key.

docs.title: Pattern 3: Working memory
docs.text:
Assert multiple facts and query them:

# Store facts in working memory
id1 = engine.assert_fact({"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 5000})
id2 = engine.assert_fact({"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 3000})

# Evaluate combined logic
result = engine.evaluate({
    "customer_id": "c1",
    "total": 8000,  # Computed from stored facts
})

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Multiple related facts → Aggregate and pass combined dict
  • Multi-step workflow → Use sessions with fact accumulation
  • Temporal correlation → Store facts in working memory

docs.text:
