docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule, Evaluation Result).

An action is the name of what should happen when a rule fires, such as "manual_review" or "block". The engine does not run actions. It returns their names in result.actions, and your application decides what each name means. This keeps rules free of side effects, so you can evaluate them in a test, a dry run or a batch job without sending emails or blocking payments.

When you want FluxRules to keep track of the code behind each name, register a handler in the action registry, described below.

docs.title: Actions in rules
docs.text:
A rule takes one action with action, or several with actions:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule1 = Rule(
    name="check_high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="require_approval",
)

rule2 = Rule(
    name="check_fraud",
    conditions=F("ip_risk_score") > 80,
    actions=("block", "notify_security"),
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule1, rule2])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500, "ip_risk_score": 90})
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")
  • action="require_approval" gives the rule a single action name.
  • actions=("block", "notify_security") gives it several, in the order they should run.

result.actions lists the actions of every fired rule, in firing order. Any string is a valid action name.

docs.title: Registering a handler
docs.text:
The @action decorator registers a function under an action name:

from fluxrules.plugins.actions import action, action_registry


@action(
    name="send_approval_request",
    description="Send an approval request to the team",
    category="notifications",
)
def send_approval_request(transaction_id: str, amount: int) -> dict:
    print(f"Sending approval request for {transaction_id} ({amount})")
    return {"sent": True}


outcome = action_registry.execute("send_approval_request", transaction_id="TXN-123", amount=7500)
print(outcome)  # {'success': True, 'action': 'send_approval_request', 'result': {'sent': True}}

The decorator takes these options:

  • name: the action name that rules use. Registering the same name again replaces the earlier handler without a warning, so keep names unique.
  • description: a short text that tools and listings show.
  • category: a label for grouping related actions. The default is "general".
  • async_handler: marks the handler as async. You do not need it for an async def function, which the registry detects on its own. Set it only for a plain function that returns an awaitable.

action_registry.execute(name, **kwargs) calls the handler with the keyword arguments you pass. Before calling, it checks that every required parameter is present and that no unknown ones are passed, and raises ValueError if not. It returns a dictionary with success, action, and either result or error. A handler that raises does not stop your program: the error is logged and returned under error with success set to False.

docs.title: Running the actions of a result
docs.text:
A common pattern is to evaluate a fact and then run the handler for each fired action. A handler that declares **fact accepts every field of the fact, so you can pass the whole fact to it. A handler with fixed parameters, such as send_approval_request above, rejects the extra fields with ValueError, so catch it and carry on with the next action:

@action(name="notify_security", category="notifications")
def notify_security(**fact) -> dict:
    return {"notified": True, "amount": fact.get("amount")}


fact = {"amount": 7500, "ip_risk_score": 90}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)

for name in result.actions:
    if not action_registry.has(name):
        print(f"No handler for {name!r}; the application handles it")
        continue
    try:
        print(action_registry.execute(name, **fact))
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"Could not run {name!r}: {e}")

action_registry.has(name) tells you whether a handler is registered, so action names without a handler can fall through to your own code. The try block keeps one action with the wrong parameters, or an async handler passed to execute, from stopping the rest.

docs.title: Async handlers
docs.text:
Register an async def function as usual, and run it with execute_async:

import asyncio


@action(name="log_to_database", category="logging")
async def log_to_database(event_id: str) -> dict:
    return {"logged": True, "event_id": event_id}


outcome = asyncio.run(action_registry.execute_async("log_to_database", event_id="evt-1"))
print(outcome["result"])  # {'logged': True, 'event_id': 'evt-1'}

execute refuses an async handler, and execute_async refuses a plain one. Each raises ValueError that says which method to use instead.

docs.title: Inspecting the registry
docs.text:
Every registered action keeps its metadata:

print(action_registry.list_actions())  # every registered name

info = action_registry.get("send_approval_request")
print(info.name, info.category, info.description)

notifications = action_registry.get_actions_by_category("notifications")
print([a.name for a in notifications])

print(action_registry.get_action_signature("send_approval_request"))
# send_approval_request(transaction_id: str, amount: int) -> dict
  • list_actions() returns every registered name.
  • get(name) returns the metadata of one action, or None.
  • get_actions_by_category(category) returns the metadata of every action in that category.
  • get_action_signature(name) returns the handler's parameters and return type as text.

docs.title: Choosing behavior from the fact
docs.text:
A handler can read the fact and decide what to do:

@action(name="escalate", description="Escalate by amount")
def escalate(**fact) -> dict:
    amount = fact.get("amount", 0)
    if amount > 50000:
        level = "executive"
    elif amount > 10000:
        level = "manager"
    else:
        level = "standard"
    return {"escalated_to": level}

docs.title: Chaining actions
docs.text:
A handler can run other registered actions in a fixed order:

@action(name="block_transaction")
def block_transaction(**fact) -> dict:
    return {"blocked": True}


@action(name="notify_then_block")
def notify_then_block(**fact) -> dict:
    for step in ("notify_security", "block_transaction"):
        outcome = action_registry.execute(step, **fact)
        if not outcome["success"]:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{step} failed: {outcome['error']}")
    return {"status": "complete"}

execute reports a failed handler in its return value instead of raising, so check success after each step. Raising here marks the whole chain as failed, and the error reaches whoever called notify_then_block.

Often it is simpler to list both names in the rule with actions=("notify_security", "block_transaction") and let the dispatch loop above run them in order.

docs.title: Custom Engines
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Engine) and The PHREAK Engine.

FluxRules provides one standard engine: PhreakEngine (lazy, agenda-driven). You can implement a custom engine by subclassing BaseEngine.

docs.title: Why custom engines?
docs.text:
• Specialized algorithms: Implement domain-specific matching logic
  • Performance optimization: Tailor to your data patterns
  • Integration: Wrap external rule systems

docs.title: Custom engine structure
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine import BaseEngine
from fluxrules.domain import Rule
from fluxrules.domain.conditions.evaluator import evaluate_conditions
from typing import Any


class MyCustomEngine(BaseEngine):
    """Custom rule evaluation engine."""

    def _evaluate_rules(
        self, rule_ids: list[int], facts: dict[str, Any]
    ) -> tuple[list[int], list[str], dict[int, str]]:
        """Evaluate discovered rules and return fired IDs, actions, explanations."""
        fired_ids = []
        actions = []
        explanations = {}
        for rule_id in rule_ids:
            rule = self.rule_repository.get(rule_id)
            if rule and evaluate_conditions(rule.conditions, facts):
                fired_ids.append(rule_id)
                actions.extend(rule.actions)
                explanations[rule_id] = f"Rule {rule.name} matched"
        return fired_ids, actions, explanations

docs.title: Using a custom engine
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F

rule = Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
    action="review",
    persist=False,
)
engine = MyCustomEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 5000, "country": "US"})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Required methods
docs.text: Method Purpose load_rules(rules) Initialize engine with rules _evaluate_rules(rule_ids, facts) Evaluate discovered rule IDs and return fired IDs, actions, and explanations assert_fact(fact) Store fact in working memory retract_fact(fact_id) Remove fact from working memory

docs.title: Standard interfaces
docs.text:
Your custom engine should:

  1. Inherit from BaseEngine: Provides working memory and utilities
  2. Return EvaluationResult: Consistent result format
  3. Preserve the result contract: Return fired IDs, actions, and explanations from _evaluate_rules
  4. Use BaseEngine.evaluate(): It supplies discovery, filters, grouping, and latency measurement

docs.title: Evaluating many facts
docs.text:
Every engine gets evaluate_batch(facts) from BaseEngine. Without workers, it calls your engine's evaluate() on each fact and returns the results in order, so it works for a custom engine with no extra code:

results = engine.evaluate_batch([{"amount": 5000}, {"amount": 10}])
assert [len(r.fired_rules) for r in results] == [1, 0]

workers=N (more than 1) runs the facts in N worker processes, and each worker must build its own copy of your engine. BaseEngine cannot know how to build yours, so by default it raises NotImplementedError and asks you to use workers=1. To allow workers, override _clone_settings() and return your engine class plus the keyword arguments its constructor needs:

class BatchReadyEngine(MyCustomEngine):
    def __init__(self, threshold: int = 0) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.threshold = threshold

    def _clone_settings(self) -> tuple[type, dict[str, Any]]:
        return type(self), {"threshold": self.threshold}


assert BatchReadyEngine(threshold=5)._clone_settings() == (BatchReadyEngine, {"threshold": 5})

Each worker then calls BatchReadyEngine(threshold=5) and loads your rules into it. The class and its arguments are sent to the workers by pickling, so define the class at the top level of a module (not inside a function), and call evaluate_batch(facts, workers=4) under if __name__ == "__main__":. See Many facts at once for the other rules that apply to workers.

docs.text:

  • Example: See Example 09: Custom Engines

docs.title: Custom Transforms
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Fact Pipeline (transforms and pipelines).

The built-in transforms (Flatten, Rename, FieldType, Defaults, Require and the rest) cover most cleaning work. When you need logic of your own, such as looking up a risk score or normalizing a phone number, write a custom transform. This page shows how, and lists the mistakes people make most often.

docs.title: The rule to remember
docs.text: A pipeline accepts only objects whose class inherits from Transform. A plain function or a class that does not inherit from Transform fails when the pipeline runs, with an AttributeError. Subclassing Transform is what gives a step its metadata, its error handling and the >> and | operators.

docs.title: Writing a transform
docs.text:
A transform is a class with two members:

  • __call__(self, fact), which takes a fact and returns the new fact.
  • metadata, a property that describes the transform.
from typing import Any

from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Transform, TransformMetadata


class GeoEnricher(Transform):
    """Add a region and a risk score based on the country."""

    def __init__(self, geo_db: dict[str, dict[str, Any]]):
        self.geo_db = geo_db

    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="geo_enricher",
            description="Add geographic risk scores",
            required_input_fields=["country"],
            output_fields=["geo_risk_score", "geo_region"],
        )

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        enriched = dict(fact)
        info = self.geo_db.get(fact.get("country"))
        if info:
            enriched["geo_risk_score"] = info["risk"]
            enriched["geo_region"] = info["region"]
        return enriched


pipeline = FactPipeline([GeoEnricher({"NG": {"risk": 8, "region": "Africa"}})], name="enrich_geo")

print(pipeline({"country": "NG", "amount": 5000}))
# {'country': 'NG', 'amount': 5000, 'geo_risk_score': 8, 'geo_region': 'Africa'}

TransformMetadata takes these fields:

  • name: a short name, shown in metrics, traces and error messages.
  • description: a sentence that says what the transform does.
  • required_input_fields: the fields the transform reads.
  • output_fields: the fields the transform adds or changes.

Only name is required. The field lists are documentation: tools read them to show what each step needs and produces.

If you leave out __call__ or metadata, Python refuses to create the object and raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class.

docs.title: Mixing custom and built-in transforms
docs.text:
A custom transform goes into a pipeline next to the built-in ones:

from fluxrules.pipeline import Defaults, FieldType, Flatten, Rename, Require


class LogStep(Transform):
    """Print the fact and pass it on unchanged."""

    def __init__(self, label: str):
        self.label = label

    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(name="log_step", description=f"Log the fact ({self.label})")

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        print(f"{self.label}: {fact}")
        return fact


normalize = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),
        Rename({"user_id": ["user.id", "userId"]}),
        LogStep("after rename"),
        FieldType({"amount": float}),
        Defaults({"country": "US"}),
        Require(["user_id", "amount"]),
    ],
    name="normalize",
)

fact = normalize({"user": {"id": "u_1"}, "amount": "1500"})
# after rename: {'user.id': 'u_1', 'amount': '1500', 'user_id': 'u_1'}
print(fact)
# {'country': 'US', 'user.id': 'u_1', 'amount': 1500.0, 'user_id': 'u_1'}

docs.title: Rejecting a bad fact
docs.text:
To reject a fact, raise ValueError from __call__. The pipeline passes the error on to you, or to its error policy if you set one (see Fact Pipeline):

class RequirePositiveAmount(Transform):
    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(name="require_positive_amount", required_input_fields=["amount"])

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        if fact.get("amount", 0) <= 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
        return fact


checked = FactPipeline([RequirePositiveAmount()])

try:
    checked({"amount": -5})
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Rejected: {e}")

docs.title: Composing transforms
docs.text:
Transforms combine with >>, which runs the left side and then the right side:

enrich_then_check = GeoEnricher({"NG": {"risk": 8, "region": "Africa"}}) >> RequirePositiveAmount()
print(enrich_then_check({"country": "NG", "amount": 5000}))

You do not need to wrap each transform in its own FactPipeline first. a >> b and FactPipeline([a, b]) do the same thing.

For branching, use Conditional instead of an if inside one large transform. It runs then_transform when the predicate is true, and else_transform otherwise:

from fluxrules.pipeline import Conditional

by_source = Conditional(
    predicate=lambda f: f.get("source") == "legacy",
    then_transform=Rename({"id": ["legacy_id"]}),
    else_transform=Rename({"id": ["modern_id"]}),
)

print(by_source({"source": "legacy", "legacy_id": 7}))  # {'source': 'legacy', 'legacy_id': 7, 'id': 7}

Each branch stays small, and each one can be tested on its own.

docs.title: When you do not need a class
docs.text:
If you only want to apply a function to some fields, MapValues does that without a custom class:

from fluxrules.pipeline import MapValues

clean = FactPipeline([MapValues(str.upper, fields=["country"])])
print(clean({"country": "de", "amount": 10}))  # {'country': 'DE', 'amount': 10}

MapValues(fn, fields=[...]) calls fn on the value of each listed field. Without fields, it calls fn on every value.

docs.title: Saving a pipeline that uses your transform
docs.text:
A pipeline can be saved as a dictionary with to_dict() (and from there to JSON or YAML), then rebuilt with FactPipeline.from_dict(). For your transform to survive that round trip, give it to_dict and from_dict, and register the class so the loader can find it by name:

from fluxrules.pipeline import register


class LowercaseEmail(Transform):
    def __init__(self, field: str = "email"):
        self.field = field

    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(name="LowercaseEmail", required_input_fields=[self.field])

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        out = dict(fact)
        if isinstance(out.get(self.field), str):
            out[self.field] = out[self.field].lower()
        return out

    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"type": "LowercaseEmail", "field": self.field}

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, spec: dict[str, Any]) -> "LowercaseEmail":
        return cls(field=spec["field"])


register(LowercaseEmail)

saved = FactPipeline([LowercaseEmail(field="email")]).to_dict()
restored = FactPipeline.from_dict(saved)
print(restored({"email": "Ana@Example.COM"}))  # {'email': 'ana@example.com'}

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Changing the input fact. Always copy the fact with dict(fact) before you change it. Error policies and retries rely on the original fact staying as it was:

class AddFlag(Transform):
    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(name="add_flag", output_fields=["flag"])

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        out = dict(fact)  # copy first, never write to `fact`
        out["flag"] = True
        return out

Assuming a field is present. fact["name"] raises KeyError when the field is missing. Use fact.get("name"), or raise ValueError on purpose so the error policy can deal with the fact.

Passing a plain function. FactPipeline([my_function]) fails when the pipeline runs. Wrap the logic in a Transform subclass, or use MapValues.

Empty pipeline. FactPipeline([]) raises ValueError: Pipeline must have at least one transform.

docs.title: Which approach to use
docs.text: You want to Use Apply a function to some fields MapValues(fn, fields=[...]) Pick different steps for different facts Conditional(...) Reject facts that break a rule of yours A Transform that raises ValueError Add data from a lookup table or service A Transform that holds the lookup Save the pipeline to JSON or YAML A Transform with to_dict and from_dict, registered with register

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts.

This page helps you make the first design choices for a project that uses FluxRules. Each section asks one question and points to the page that covers the answer in depth.

docs.title: Is FluxRules a good fit?
docs.text:
FluxRules fits well when you need to:

  • decide what to do with a piece of data based on business rules,
  • combine many checks with AND, OR and NOT,
  • change or review those rules separately from the code that uses them.

If all three apply, read on.

docs.title: Library or HTTP service?
docs.text:
As a library, FluxRules runs inside your own Python process:

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, Rule

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([Rule(name="adult", conditions=F("age") >= 18, action="allow")])
result = engine.evaluate({"age": 21})

There is no network call and nothing extra to deploy.

As an HTTP service, FluxRules runs as its own server, and other services send facts to it:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/evaluate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"facts": {"age": 21}}'

Each call adds network latency, but many services can share one set of rules, and you can scale the server on its own.

Choose the library for a single application or when latency matters most. Choose the HTTP service when several services, possibly not written in Python, must use the same rules. See HTTP API to start the server.

docs.title: Rules in code or in a database?
docs.text:
In code is the default. You build rules in Python, or load them from a YAML file, every time the application starts. Nothing else is needed. See YAML Rules for keeping rules in files.

In a database, rules are saved once and loaded on startup, and several processes can share them. This needs the sql extra. See Persistence and Rule Lifecycle.

Start with rules in code while you prototype. Move them to a database when rules change more often than you deploy, or when several processes must share them.

docs.title: Independent facts or state across steps?
docs.text:
Most applications check each fact on its own: one payment, one order, one request. Use the engine as it is; this is stateless mode, the default.

Some applications collect data over several steps, such as an onboarding flow that learns one field at a time. For that, use a session: it gathers the fields of one fact and evaluates them when you ask. A session lives in memory, and you can save it as a JSON snapshot and restore it later. See Sessions.

If you process a long stream of updates and only care about what changed since the last update, use streaming mode. See Choosing an Evaluation Mode.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Quickstart: See Quickstart to write your first rules
  • Ways to Evaluate a Fact: See Ways to Evaluate a Fact for every way to send facts to the engine
  • Architecture: See Architecture for how the parts fit together

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Actions and Custom Engines.

FluxRules is designed for manual dependency injection via constructor parameters.

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Inject dependencies
logger = get_logger("fluxrules")
metrics = get_metrics_collector()
database = get_database_connection()

# Pass to engine
engine = PhreakEngine(metrics_collector=metrics, logger=logger)


# Or to action
@action(name="log_and_store")
def log_and_store(database=database, logger=logger, **kwargs):
    logger.info(f"Storing: {kwargs}")
    database.insert(kwargs)
    return {"stored": True}

docs.title: No framework dependency
docs.text:
FluxRules has zero framework dependencies. Integrate with your existing DI setup:

# python skip
# FastAPI
from fastapi import Depends


@app.post("/evaluate")
def evaluate(request: Request, engine: Engine = Depends(get_engine)):
    return engine.evaluate(request.facts)


# Django
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404


def evaluate_view(request):
    engine = get_engine()  # From your service layer
    return engine.evaluate(request.POST)

docs.title: ServiceFactory and persistence
docs.text:
When you register a persistence adapter via ServiceFactory.create_persistence_adapter(), Rule(persist=True) and Rule.save() automatically delegate to that adapter rather than the built-in SQLite default. This is the recommended pattern for production deployments that use PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or another provider:

# python skip: requires a live database and session provider
from fluxrules.di import ServiceFactory
from fluxrules.config import RuntimeConfig, PersistenceConfig

ServiceFactory.create_persistence_adapter(
    session_provider=SessionLocal,          # your SQLAlchemy sessionmaker
    config=RuntimeConfig(
        persistence=PersistenceConfig(backend="postgres")
    ),
)

See Persistence for a full example.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Persistence: See Persistence for database configuration
  • Custom Engines: See Custom Engines
  • Actions: See Actions

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Prerequisites: API and Persistence.

Deploy FluxRules as a service for production rule evaluation.

docs.title: Minimal deployment (development)
docs.text:
from fluxrules.api.app import create_app
import uvicorn

app = create_app()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Single worker, no persistence
    uvicorn.run(
        app,
        host="127.0.0.1",
        port=8000,
        workers=1,
    )

docs.title: Production deployment (Docker)
docs.text:
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app

# Install FluxRules with all extras
RUN pip install fluxrules[all]

# Copy rules (if stored as files)
COPY rules/ /app/rules/

# Start API server
CMD ["python", "-m", "fluxrules.api.app"]

Run: 

docker run -p 8000:8000 -e FLUXRULES_ENV=prod fluxrules:latest

docs.title: Production configuration
docs.text:
Set environment variables for production:

# Database
export FLUXRULES_ENV=prod
export FLUXRULES_DB_URL=postgresql://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules

# API
export API_HOST=0.0.0.0
export API_PORT=8000
export API_WORKERS=4

# How many recent evaluations GET /api/v1/explain can find (default 10000)
export EXPLAIN_STORE_MAX_RECORDS=10000

# Optional: Prometheus metrics
export OTEL_ENABLED=true
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317

docs.title: Redis (optional)
docs.text:
The server works without Redis. When a Redis server is reachable, the API uses it to share work between server processes:

  • POST /api/v1/event puts events on a queue for the event worker instead of evaluating them during the request.
  • The rule cache and the compiled rules used for conflict checks are shared between server processes. Without Redis, each process keeps its own copy in memory.
  • Runtime analytics are kept in Redis instead of in each process's memory.

The API connects with REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT and REDIS_DB (defaults localhost, 6379, 0). The compiled-rule cache always connects to localhost:6379 for now.

Without Redis, the server checks once at startup and then stops trying, so requests are not slowed down. The compiled-rule cache tries again at most every 30 seconds, and always tries when it must clear old rules after a rule change.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
For high-throughput production:

# python skip
import uvicorn

app = create_app()

uvicorn.run(
    app,
    host="0.0.0.0",
    port=8000,
    workers=4,  # CPU cores × 2-4
)

Place behind a load balancer (nginx, AWS ALB, etc.):

upstream fluxrules {
    server 127.0.0.1:8000;
    server 127.0.0.1:8001;
    server 127.0.0.1:8002;
    server 127.0.0.1:8003;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name rules.example.com;

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://fluxrules;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
    }
}

docs.title: Health monitoring
docs.text:
Use the health endpoint for readiness checks:

curl http://localhost:8000/health
# {"status": "healthy"}

GET /api/v1/system/status also reports the version and the state of each part of the server (queue, cache, persistence).

Add to Docker/K8s liveness probes:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Security: See Security for authentication & authorization
  • Observability: See Observability for monitoring
  • Troubleshooting: See Troubleshooting for common issues

docs.title: Domains and Tags
docs.text:
Organize and filter rules using domains (logical grouping) and tags (multi-dimensional labeling).

Prerequisites: Familiarity with Rules and rule creation (see Getting Started).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As your rule systems grow, you need ways to: - Organize rules by business area (fraud, compliance, marketing) - Filter rules at evaluation time (only evaluate tier_1 rules) - Manage rules by team or feature - Query rules without loading everything

Domains and tags enable this organization:

  • Domain: Single category each rule belongs to (mutually exclusive)
  • Tags: Multiple labels per rule (cross-cutting concerns)

docs.title: Domains
docs.text: A domain is a logical grouping. Each rule belongs to exactly one domain.

docs.title: Define a Domain
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F
from fluxrules.domain import Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="fraud_check",
    domain="fraud_detection",  # Single domain per rule
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="flag_for_review"
)

Default domain is "default" if not specified:

from fluxrules import F

rule_no_domain = Rule(
    name="simple_rule",
    conditions=F("status") == "active",
    action="process"
)
# rule_no_domain.domain == "default"

docs.title: Query by Domain
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", domain="compliance", conditions=F("country") == "US", action="block"),
    Rule(name="r3", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="review"),
]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Evaluate against a fact
fact = {"status": "active", "country": "US", "amount": 6000}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)
print(f"Fired rules: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tags are labels you add to rules for cross-cutting organization. A rule can have unlimited tags.

docs.title: Add Tags to a Rule
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F
from fluxrules.domain import Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="vip_fast_track",
    domain="marketing",
    tags=frozenset(["vip", "urgent", "auto_action"]),  # Multiple tags
    conditions=F("customer_tier") == "vip",
    action="fast_track_checkout"
)

Tags must be passed as frozenset[str]. Rule automatically converts lists to frozensets:

# python skip
# Both work:
# Rule(name="r1", conditions={...}, tags=frozenset(["tag1", "tag2"]))
# Rule(name="r2", conditions={...}, tags=["tag1", "tag2"])  # Converted to frozenset

docs.title: Query by Tags
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", tags=frozenset(["urgent", "vip"]), conditions=F("priority") == "high", action="action1"),
    Rule(name="r2", tags=frozenset(["low_priority"]), conditions=F("priority") == "low", action="action2"),
    Rule(name="r3", tags=frozenset(["urgent"]), conditions=F("type") == "alert", action="action3"),
]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Evaluate against a fact
fact = {"priority": "high", "type": "notification"}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)
print(f"Fired: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Real Example: Shared Payment Risk Dataset
docs.text:
The shared payment-risk use case demonstrates domains and tags in action:

from examples.shared_use_case import build_shared_rules

rules = build_shared_rules()

# Rule 1: Fraud detection domain, tier_1 and manual_review tags
# Rule 2: Compliance domain, tier_2 and block tags
# Rule 3: Risk operations domain, tier_1 and step_up tags

for rule in rules:
    print(f"{rule.name}: domain={rule.domain}, tags={rule.tags}")

Output: 

triage_for_manual_review: domain=fraud_detection, tags=frozenset({'tier_1', 'manual_review', 'cross_border'})
triage_for_hard_block: domain=compliance, tags=frozenset({'tier_2', 'block', 'geo_risk'})
triage_for_step_up_auth: domain=risk_ops, tags=frozenset({'tier_1', 'step_up', 'identity'})

See Example 03: Domains and Tags for complete working code.

docs.title: Evaluate Specific Domain Only
docs.text:
# python skip
# Demonstration using shared dataset (run from examples/ directory)
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
from fluxrules.engine import EvaluationFilter
from shared_use_case import SHARED_FACTS, build_shared_rules

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(build_shared_rules())

# Evaluate only fraud_detection rules
for fact in SHARED_FACTS:
    result = engine.evaluate(
        fact,
        filters=EvaluationFilter(domains=frozenset(["fraud_detection"]))
    )
    print(f"Fraud rules: {result.fired_rules}")

# Evaluate only compliance rules
for fact in SHARED_FACTS:
    result = engine.evaluate(
        fact,
        filters=EvaluationFilter(domains=frozenset(["compliance"]))
    )
    print(f"Compliance rules: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Evaluate Specific Tags Only
docs.text:
# Evaluate only tier_1 priority rules
result = engine.evaluate(
    fact,
    filters=EvaluationFilter(tags=frozenset(["tier_1"]))
)

# Evaluate only rules with both "manual_review" and "cross_border" tags
result = engine.evaluate(
    fact,
    filters=EvaluationFilter(tags=frozenset(["manual_review", "cross_border"]))
)

docs.title: 1. Use Clear Domain Names
docs.text:
Choose domain names that map to business areas:

# Good: Clear business areas
domains = ["fraud_detection", "compliance", "marketing", "risk_ops"]

# Confusing: Too broad or vague
domains = ["rules", "checks", "business_logic"]

docs.title: 2. Use Consistent Tag Naming
docs.text:
Establish tag conventions within your organization:

# Tag naming patterns:
# Priority: tier_0, tier_1, tier_2
# Action: auto_action, manual_review, informational
# Status: experimental, stable, deprecated
# Scope: vip, enterprise, new_customer

tags_good = frozenset(["tier_1", "auto_action", "stable"])
tags_confusing = frozenset(["high", "auto", "new"])

docs.title: 3. Document Tag Meanings
docs.text:
Create a tag reference for your team:

TAG_MEANINGS = {
    "tier_0": "Highest priority, critical business logic",
    "tier_1": "High priority, reviewed and tested",
    "tier_2": "Standard priority, production ready",
    "auto_action": "Can execute automatically",
    "manual_review": "Results must be reviewed by human",
    "experimental": "Still being tested",
    "stable": "Production-ready, well-tested",
}

docs.title: 4. Combine Domains and Tags for Powerful Queries
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Create diverse set of rules
all_rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", domain="fraud_detection", tags=frozenset(["tier_1"]), conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", domain="fraud_detection", tags=frozenset(["tier_2"]), conditions=F("country") == "NG", action="review"),
    Rule(name="r3", domain="compliance", tags=frozenset(["tier_1", "stable"]), conditions=F("type") == "transfer", action="log"),
]

# Get all tier_1 rules in fraud_detection domain
tier1_fraud = [
    r for r in all_rules
    if r.domain == "fraud_detection" and "tier_1" in r.tags
]

# Load and evaluate
engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(tier1_fraud)
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "country": "NG"})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Domain mutations: Rules cannot change domain after creation
  • Tag mutation: Tags cannot be modified after creation
  • Query combinations: Filters use OR for multiple tags/domains (all matching are evaluated)

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Complex Conditions: AND/OR/NOT boolean logic for rules
  • Actions: Run custom code when rules match
  • Examples 03: Working code example

docs.title: The PHREAK Engine
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Engine).

FluxRules is built on a single production engine: PHREAK, a lazy, agenda-driven matching algorithm. There is no engine to choose. The design goal is one fast, memory-efficient engine that covers every supported use case.

PHREAK exposes two evaluation modes on the same engine, plus a dependency-free reference evaluator used internally as a correctness oracle.

docs.title: Modes at a glance
docs.text:
Property Stateless mode Streaming mode Call shape Full re-evaluation per call Delta-driven (incremental) Return value Full fired set every call Fired delta since last fact State None kept between calls Working memory persists Best for HTTP/request-response, batch Long-lived sessions, event streams Default Yes Opt-in (streaming_mode=True)

Both modes share the same operator evaluator and configuration surface, so a fact that fires a rule in one mode fires the same rule in the other on first sight.

docs.title: Stateless mode (default)
docs.text:
Algorithm: Lazy, on-demand evaluation. Rules are loaded once; each evaluate call matches the fact map it is given and returns the complete fired set.

Best for: - API/request-response (HTTP, batch) - Rules added/removed dynamically - Low memory footprint preferred

Example: 

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule1 = Rule(name="rule1", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag")
rule2 = Rule(name="rule2", conditions=F("country") == "US", action="allow")
rules = [rule1, rule2]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Single evaluation
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "country": "US"})
print(f"Fired: {result.fired_rules}")

# Multiple independent evaluations
facts = [{"amount": 3000, "country": "NG"}, {"amount": 7000, "country": "US"}]
for fact in facts:
    result = engine.evaluate(fact)  # Fresh evaluation each time
    print(f"Fact {fact}: Fired {result.fired_rules}")

Memory profile: O(1) per evaluation (rules loaded once, facts evaluated independently).

docs.title: Streaming mode
docs.text:
Algorithm: The same PHREAK network, but working memory persists across calls. A fact seen for the first time reports the full fired set; re-evaluating an unchanged fact reports an empty delta.

Best for: - Long-lived sessions (repeated assert/retract) - Event streams where only changes matter

Example: 

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine(streaming_mode=True)
engine.load_rules(rules)

# First sight of a fact reports the full fired set
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "country": "US"})

See Working Memory for the streaming contract in full.

docs.title: Reference evaluator (correctness oracle)
docs.text: fluxrules.services.reference_evaluator.ReferenceEvaluator is a small, deterministic, dependency-free evaluator. It is not a selectable engine. It is the default RuleService engine and an independent oracle the test suite checks PHREAK against, so shared-code defects cannot hide behind a single implementation.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Choosing a mode: See Choosing an Evaluation Mode to pick between the two modes
  • Streaming in depth: See Working Memory
  • Engine limits: See Engine Scope and Limits

docs.title: Engine Scope and Limits
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The PHREAK Engine.

Documented constraints and capabilities of FluxRules engines.

docs.title: Single-fact evaluation
docs.text:
Scope: Both engines evaluate one fact dict per call.

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
# Each evaluate() is independent
result1 = engine.evaluate({"amount": 5000})
result2 = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500})
# result1 and result2 have no shared state

Limitation: Engines do not join facts, aggregate over collections, or correlate across time.

Workaround: Pre-aggregate facts upstream, then pass combined dict to evaluate().

For a deployment where unsupported cross-fact or temporal rule shapes must fail at startup instead of logging a warning, enable the strict guardrail:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine(strict_scope=True)
engine.load_rules(
    [
        Rule(
            name="amount_check",
            conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
            action="review",
            persist=False,
        )
    ]
)

Use the separate Cross-Fact Rules engine when the rule semantics genuinely require joins, windows, or truth maintenance.

docs.title: Rule complexity
docs.text:
Scope: Conditions support arbitrary nesting of AND/OR/NOT operators.

Limits enforced by the code: - Rules: default cap of 50,000 per engine (GlobalRuleRepository); configurable via PhreakEngine(max_rules=...). Exceeding the cap raises ValueError("Repository full"). - Conditions per rule and nesting depth: no fixed cap in the engine; arbitrary AND/OR/NOT nesting is supported (deep nesting is exercised in the test suite). Depth is ultimately bounded by Python's recursion limit.

Performance: Evaluation time scales roughly with rule count and condition complexity; measure your own workload (see Load Testing).

docs.title: Capacity and selectivity guidance
docs.text:
The default per-engine capacity is 50,000 rules. Raising max_rules only removes the repository guard; it does not make a low-selectivity workload cheap. PHREAK first reduces candidates with field presence and the alpha prefilter, then evaluates the remaining candidates. Rules sharing few indexed predicates or matching a hot field can therefore approach rule-count work per fact.

For a production rollout, load the complete ruleset once, measure a representative fact sample, and record the candidate and latency metrics before choosing a worker count:

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
from fluxrules import F, Rule

rules = [
    Rule(
        name="amount_check",
        conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
        action="review",
        persist=False,
    )
]
representative_facts = [{"amount": 1500}, {"amount": 50}]

engine = PhreakEngine(max_rules=50000, enable_metrics=True)
engine.load_rules(rules)
for fact in representative_facts:
    engine.evaluate(fact)

metrics = engine.get_observability_metrics()
print(
    metrics["rules_loaded"],
    metrics["candidates_per_fact_out"],
    metrics["alpha_prune_ratio"],
    metrics["eval_latency_ms_p95"],
)

Treat a low alpha_prune_ratio, high candidates_per_fact_out, or rising eval_latency_ms as a signal to split rulesets, improve selective predicates, or scale stateless workers. Do not infer capacity from the 50,000-rule limit alone.

docs.title: Fact size
docs.text:
Scope: Facts are flat dicts after the flattening pipeline.

Limits enforced by the code: - Fact keys: no fixed limit in the engine (bounded by available memory). - Value size: large strings/numbers supported. - Nested depth: Flatten() converts nested dicts to dot notation up to max_depth=100 (default) and raises ValueError beyond that.

docs.title: Working memory
docs.text:
Scope: PHREAK has optional working memory for fact storage.

Limits: - Stateless mode: No persistent network overhead, working memory is optional - Streaming mode: Working memory persists across calls

Working memory size: Limited by available RAM. No fixed limit.

Use case: Store intermediate facts during multi-step workflows with sessions.

docs.title: Streaming mode
docs.text:
Scope: PhreakEngine supports streaming mode via streaming_mode=True.

Limitation: Streaming returns deltas (changes since last evaluation), not absolute matches.

Requirement: Sticky routing (same stream → same engine instance).

Streaming state is local to one PhreakEngine instance. Do not send one ordered stream through ordinary round-robin HTTP workers: each worker would have a different previous-fact state and could emit incorrect deltas. Use stateless mode for independently load-balanced requests. For independent batch facts, process-based parallel evaluation is available through engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=N). It refuses a streaming engine when workers is more than 1, because the workers would split the stream's state. A streaming workload must instead shard by stream identity and keep each shard ordered on one owner.

docs.title: Ways to Evaluate a Fact
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (rules, facts, results).

A fact is the data you want to check, such as one payment: {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}. Evaluating a fact means running your rules against it and finding out which ones match.

FluxRules gives you several ways to do this. They all use the same rules and the same matching logic, so the same fact always matches the same rules. They differ in how the fact reaches the engine: one at a time, many at once, as a stream, from the command line, or over HTTP.

This page shows each way with a small example and says when to use it. To see what happens inside one evaluation, read From Fact to Action.

docs.title: The rules used on this page
docs.text:
Every example on this page uses these two rules:

from fluxrules import F, Rule

RULES = [
    Rule(id=1, name="big_payment", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review", priority=10),
    Rule(id=2, name="german_payment", conditions=F("country") == "DE", action="add_vat"),
]
FACT = {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}

priority decides the order of the results: higher numbers come first. The fact above matches both rules, so the answer is always rule 1, then rule 2.

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
Most ways return an EvaluationResult. These are the fields you will use most:

Field What it holds fired_rules The ids of the rules that matched, highest priority first. This is the answer. actions The action names of the matched rules, in the same order. FluxRules does not run them; your code does. explanations One sentence per matched rule saying why it matched. rules_by_domain, rules_by_tag The matched rule ids grouped by each rule's domain and tags. latency_ms How long the evaluation took, in milliseconds.

docs.title: Pick a way
docs.text: Way Use it when Keeps state between facts? 1. fluxrules.evaluate() A script, a test, or a one-off check No 2. engine.evaluate() Your application checks facts one by one. The usual choice. No 3. A model as the fact Your facts already have a Pydantic model or dataclass No 4. engine.evaluate_batch() You have a list of facts, such as rows from a table No 5. Streaming mode The same entity is sent again and again, and only changes matter Yes 6. DedupEvaluator Many facts are exact repeats A cache of results 7. CrossFactEngine A rule must compare two facts, such as a payment and its customer Yes 8. Sessions You build a fact up piece by piece, or save and restore it Yes 9. The command line You want to try rules from a file, or check them in CI No 10. HTTP Another service sends facts to a FluxRules server No

docs.title: 1. One call: fluxrules.evaluate()
docs.text:
import fluxrules

result = fluxrules.evaluate(RULES, FACT)

assert result.fired_rules == [1, 2]
assert result.actions == ["review", "add_vat"]

fluxrules.evaluate(rules, fact) takes one rule or a list of rules, and one fact. It prepares the rules, evaluates the fact, and returns the result.

Use it when you check a fact once: in a script, a notebook or a test.

Avoid it when you check many facts against the same rules. It prepares the rules on every call. An engine (way 2) prepares them once.

It reads the process-wide engine settings (fluxrules.engine.configuration.get_config()). To give it different settings, use an engine instead.

docs.title: 2. An engine: engine.evaluate()
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(RULES)

result = engine.evaluate(FACT)
assert result.fired_rules == [1, 2]

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 50, "country": "US"})
assert result.fired_rules == []

Create the engine once and load the rules once, when your application starts. After that, engine.evaluate(fact) is cheap: load_rules builds indexes, so each evaluation only looks at rules that can match the fact.

Use it when your application checks facts one by one, for example one per web request. This is the usual choice. One engine can be shared by many threads.

Related methods on the same engine:

  • engine.evaluate_by_domain(fact, ["tax"]) and engine.evaluate_by_tags(fact, ["fraud"]) only consider rules in those domains or with those tags. See Domains and Tags.
  • engine.evaluate(fact, strict_facts=True) checks the shape of the fact first (a dict with string keys and flat values) and raises a clear error if it is wrong.

The engine reads its settings from the EngineConfig you pass (or the process-wide one). If you change a field on that object later, the engine uses the new value from its next evaluation on. See Configuration.

docs.title: 3. A model as the fact
docs.text:
If your facts already have a model, pass an instance of it directly:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine


class Payment(BaseModel):
    amount: float
    country: str


engine = PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Payment)
engine.load_rules(RULES)

result = engine.evaluate(Payment(amount=4200, country="DE"))
assert result.fired_rules == [1, 2]

The engine turns the model into a plain dict before it checks the rules. A Pydantic model, a dataclass, an attrs class or a msgspec Struct all work, with or without fact_schema.

fact_schema=Payment is optional. With it, load_rules checks that every field a rule names exists in Payment, so a rule with a typo is refused when it loads instead of quietly never matching.

The engine can also clean facts that arrive as dicts before it checks the rules:

  • fact_pipeline= reshapes each dict, for example to flatten it or fill in defaults. See Fact Pipeline.
  • validate_facts="normalize" validates each dict against fact_schema and converts values, so "4200" becomes 4200.0. on_invalid= decides what happens to a fact that fails. See Typed Facts.

These steps run in that order (pipeline, then validation) and apply to every way on this page that uses an engine.

docs.title: 4. Many facts at once: engine.evaluate_batch()
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(RULES)

facts = [
    {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"},
    {"amount": 50, "country": "US"},
    {"amount": 9000, "country": "FR"},
]
results = engine.evaluate_batch(facts)

assert [r.fired_rules for r in results] == [[1, 2], [], [1]]

evaluate_batch(facts) returns one result per fact, in the same order as the input. On its own it does the same as [engine.evaluate(f) for f in facts].

Add workers=4 to spread the facts over 4 processes, so they use 4 CPU cores:

results = engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=4)

Each worker process builds a copy of your engine, with the same rules and settings, so the results are exactly the same. Starting processes takes time, so this pays off for thousands of facts, not for a few.

Use it when you have a list of facts, such as rows from a database table or lines from a file.

Many facts at once explains the rules for workers and shows how to evaluate rows from a database.

docs.title: 5. A stream of updates: streaming mode
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine(streaming_mode=True)
engine.load_rules(RULES)

assert engine.evaluate(FACT).fired_rules == [1, 2]  # first time: full answer
assert engine.evaluate(FACT).fired_rules == []  # same fact again: skipped
changed = {**FACT, "amount": 10}
assert engine.evaluate(changed).fired_rules == [2]  # changed: evaluated again

streaming_mode=True makes the engine remember the previous fact. A fact identical to the previous one is skipped and returns no matches. A changed fact is evaluated again.

Use it when the same entity, such as an account, is sent again and again, and you only care when something changes.

Avoid it when each fact is independent, such as one request per payment. Because the engine remembers, one stream must always go to the same engine. Splitting a stream between servers or processes gives wrong answers, which is why evaluate_batch with workers refuses a streaming engine.

See Choosing an Evaluation Mode.

docs.title: 6. Repeated facts: DedupEvaluator
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
from fluxrules.engine.runtime import DedupEvaluator, LRUDedupBackend

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(RULES)
dedup = DedupEvaluator(engine, backend=LRUDedupBackend(max_entries=10_000))

first = dedup.evaluate(FACT)  # evaluated by the engine
again = dedup.evaluate({"country": "DE", "amount": 4200})  # same content: from the cache

assert again.fired_rules == first.fired_rules == [1, 2]
assert (dedup.stats.hits, dedup.stats.misses) == (1, 1)

DedupEvaluator wraps an engine and remembers the result for each fact it has seen. When the same fact arrives again, it returns the remembered result without running the rules. Two dicts with the same keys and values count as the same fact, whatever the order of their keys.

  • backend=LRUDedupBackend(max_entries=10_000) keeps at most 10,000 results in memory and forgets the least recently used one when it is full. This is also the default backend (with 100,000 entries). RedisDedupBackend shares the cache between processes; it needs the redis extra.
  • dedup.stats counts cache hits and misses.

A result from the cache is the original result object, so its latency_ms and execution_id are those of the first evaluation.

Use it when your input repeats a lot, such as retried events or polling. It needs a stateless engine: it refuses a streaming one. Call dedup.clear() after you load new rules, or old answers stay in the cache.

docs.title: 7. Facts that relate to each other: CrossFactEngine
docs.text:
The ways above check one fact at a time. When a rule must compare two facts, such as "a payment over 2000 from a customer whose account is less than 14 days old", use CrossFactEngine:

from fluxrules.engine.cross_fact import CrossFactEngine, CrossFactRule, Pattern

engine = CrossFactEngine()
engine.load_rules(
    [
        CrossFactRule(
            id=1,
            name="large_payment_from_new_account",
            action="manual_review",
            patterns=[
                Pattern("p", "Payment", constraints=[("amount", ">", 2000)]),
                Pattern(
                    "c",
                    "Customer",
                    constraints=[("account_age_days", "<", 14)],
                    joins=[("id", "==", "p", "customer_id")],
                ),
            ],
        )
    ]
)

engine.insert("Payment", {"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 4200})
delta = engine.insert("Customer", {"id": "c1", "account_age_days": 5})
assert [a.rule_name for a in delta.added] == ["large_payment_from_new_account"]

Each Pattern matches one type of fact. constraints compare a field with a value. joins compare a field with a field of a fact matched by an earlier pattern: here, the customer's id must equal the payment's customer_id.

The engine keeps every inserted fact. insert, update and retract each return a CrossFactDelta, whose added and removed lists say which matches appeared or disappeared because of that change. It does not return an EvaluationResult.

See Cross-Fact Rules.

docs.title: 8. Saved rule sets and sessions
docs.text:
RuleService stores rule sets by name. A session collects a fact piece by piece and evaluates it against one named rule set:

from fluxrules.domain.models import Ruleset
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
service.persist(
    Ruleset(
        group="payments",
        rules=tuple(rule.to_engine_rule(group="payments") for rule in RULES),
    )
)

session = service.create_session("payments")
session.add_fact("amount", 4200)
session.add_fact("country", "DE")
assert session.evaluate().fired_rules == [1, 2]

snapshot = session.save()  # a JSON string you can store and restore later
  • Ruleset(group="payments", ...) names the rule set. to_engine_rule(group=...) converts each Rule to the stored form.
  • create_session("payments") starts an empty session for that rule set.
  • add_fact(key, value) adds one field. session.evaluate() checks all fields added so far.
  • save() and EvaluationSession.restore(snapshot, service) let you pause and continue later.

service.evaluate_ruleset("payments", fact) evaluates a whole fact against a stored rule set in one call, without a session.

RuleService.create() keeps rule sets in memory. Storing them in a database needs the sql extra. See Sessions and Persistence.

docs.title: 9. The command line
docs.text:
With the cli extra installed, evaluate a fact from a JSON file against rules in a JSON or YAML file:

fluxrules evaluate rules.yaml event.json
fluxrules evaluate rules.yaml event.json --format json
fluxrules evaluate rules.yaml event.json --schema models.py:Payment --validate-facts normalize
  • --format json prints the matched rules and actions as JSON instead of a table.
  • --schema models.py:Payment checks the rules against the Payment model first, and stops with exit code 1 if a rule names a field the model lacks.
  • --validate-facts normalize also validates and converts the event against that model before evaluating it.

Use it when you want to try rules without writing code, or check rule files in CI. See CLI.

docs.title: 10. HTTP
docs.text:
The FluxRules server (the api extra) evaluates facts sent as JSON:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/evaluate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"facts": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}, "ruleset_id": "payments"}'
  • facts is the fact to evaluate.
  • ruleset_id is optional. It picks a stored rule set; without it, all stored rules are used. rule_ids picks individual rules instead.

The response lists the matched rule ids as matched_rules, plus actions and an execution_id. POST /api/v1/evaluate/bulk takes a list under facts and returns one result per fact. A session can also collect facts over several requests and evaluate them later with POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/evaluate.

Use it when another service, possibly not written in Python, needs answers. See HTTP API Reference and Deployment.

docs.title: Examples and Learning Path
docs.text:
The examples/ folder holds runnable scripts that build on each other, from the first rule to fact pipelines. This page describes each one in the order we suggest you read them.

Every example uses the same payment-risk triage data, defined in examples/shared_use_case.py. Because the data stays the same, you can focus on the feature each example teaches.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text: FluxRules is extended through a small set of registries plus optional entry-point auto-discovery. This page is the catalog and the stability policy; the deep how-to guides live on their own pages and are linked below.

docs.title: The extension points
docs.text:
What you add Public entry point How-to guide Condition operator register_operator(name, func) Conditions Rule engine register_engine(name, cls) Custom Engines Action action_registry.register(...) Actions Pipeline transform pipeline.registry.register(cls) Custom Transforms Validator ValidationService.register_validator(...) Validation Framework

Each registry is a plain, importable object. There is no hidden framework. A custom engine, for example, becomes selectable everywhere the built-in engine is (the Python factory, the HTTP API, and the CLI --engine flag) the moment it is registered:

# python skip
from fluxrules import register_engine, get_engine
from fluxrules.engine.base import BaseEngine


class MyEngine(BaseEngine):
    def _evaluate_rules(self, rule_ids, facts):
        # Return (fired_rule_ids, actions, explanations)
        ...


register_engine("MYENGINE", MyEngine)
engine = get_engine("MYENGINE")  # now resolvable by name

Built-in engines (PHREAK) cannot be overridden or removed, so get_engine("PHREAK") is always stable.

docs.title: Proving a custom engine is correct
docs.text:
A third-party engine can prove it matches FluxRules semantics using the public conformance kit, which drives it against the independent, dependency-free ReferenceEvaluator across a battery of rule shapes:

# python skip
from fluxrules.testing import assert_engine_contract
from my_pkg import MyEngine


def test_my_engine_is_conformant():
    assert_engine_contract(MyEngine)

assert_engine_contract accepts an engine class, a zero-argument factory, or an instance, and raises AssertionError naming any case where the fired-rule set diverges from the reference. Pass cases= to supply your own battery.

docs.title: Entry-point auto-discovery
docs.text:
Packages can advertise extensions so they register automatically, without the host application importing them by hand. Declare entry points in the plugin package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."fluxrules.operators"]
within_range = "my_pkg.operators:within_range"

[project.entry-points."fluxrules.engines"]
myengine = "my_pkg.engine:MyEngine"

[project.entry-points."fluxrules.actions"]
slack_notify = "my_pkg.actions:slack_notify"

[project.entry-points."fluxrules.transforms"]
redact = "my_pkg.transforms:Redact"

Then, once, at application startup:

# python skip
from fluxrules.plugins.discovery import load_plugins

loaded = load_plugins()  # {"fluxrules.operators": ["within_range"], ...}

Discovery is explicit: it is never an import side effect, so applications stay in control of when third-party code is loaded. A plugin that fails to load is logged and skipped rather than aborting discovery.

docs.title: Stability policy
docs.text:
Extension points follow the project's semantic-versioning contract for the 0.x line:

  • Registry signatures (register_operator, register_engine, register_validator, the action and transform registries) and the entry-point group names (fluxrules.operators, fluxrules.engines, fluxrules.actions, fluxrules.transforms) are treated as public API. A breaking change to any of them is called out in the changelog under a Changed or Removed heading and accompanies a minor version bump while 0.x.
  • BaseEngine is the supported base class for custom engines. New optional hooks may be added in minor releases; the required _evaluate_rules contract is covered by assert_engine_contract, so a conformant engine keeps working across minor upgrades.
  • The conformance battery may gain cases in minor releases (a stricter oracle), but existing correct engines are expected to keep passing. If a case is tightened in a way that could fail a previously-conformant engine, it is documented as a Changed entry.

See Contributing to propose a new extension point.

docs.title: Fact Pipeline
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Fact) and Conditions.

A Fact Pipeline transforms facts before rule evaluation. Use pipelines to:

  1. Normalize: Convert nested structures to flat dicts
  2. Enrich: Add computed fields
  3. Validate: Ensure required fields exist
  4. Type coerce: Convert string values to proper types

docs.title: Pipeline or typed facts?
docs.text:
Typed facts also clean facts before evaluation. Pick by what you have:

You have Use A model class (Pydantic, dataclass, attrs, msgspec) for the fact Typed facts: fact_schema= plus validate_facts="normalize" No model, or facts from mixed sources (webhooks, queues, files) A fact pipeline Computed or default fields, or reusable composed stages (>>, \|) A fact pipeline Facts streamed from a source with dead-letter handling A fact pipeline with FactLoader

With a model, typed facts already cover several transforms. Key-style aliases replace Rename, model coercion replaces FieldType, required model fields replace Require, and nested models become dotted keys as with Flatten.

The two combine. With both set, the engine runs the pipeline first and then validates its output against fact_schema.

docs.title: Basic pipeline
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
from fluxrules.pipeline import Defaults, FactPipeline, Flatten, Rename, FieldType, Require

# Define pipeline stages
pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),  # Flatten nested objects (obj.field -> "obj.field")
        Rename({"user_id": ["user.id", "userId"]}),  # Normalize field names
        FieldType({"amount": float}),  # Convert types
        Require(["user_id", "amount"]),  # Validate required fields
    ],
    name="normalize_payment",
)

# Apply to fact
raw_fact = {
    "user": {"id": "user_123"},
    "amount": "5000",  # String needs conversion
    "country": "US",
}

normalized_fact = pipeline(raw_fact)
# Result: {"user_id": "user_123", "amount": 5000.0, "country": "US"}
normalize_pipeline = pipeline

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(
    [
        Rule(
            name="high_value",
            conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
            action="review",
            persist=False,
        )
    ]
)

# Now evaluate with engine
result = engine.evaluate(normalized_fact)

docs.title: Available transforms
docs.text: Transform Purpose Example Flatten() Nested dict → flat dict with dot notation {"user": {"id": 1}} → {"user.id": 1} Rename() Normalize field names {"user_id": ["userId", "uid"]} FieldType() Type coercion {"amount": float} Defaults() Fill missing fields {"country": "US"} Require() Validate required fields ["amount", "user_id"]

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
Pipelines compose with >> (sequence) and | (fallback):

# Sequence: run clean, then enrich
clean = FactPipeline([Flatten()], name="clean")
enrich = FactPipeline([Defaults({"channel": "web"})], name="enrich")
pipeline = clean >> enrich

# Fallback: try primary, then secondary
primary = FactPipeline([Require(["amount"])], name="primary")
secondary = FactPipeline([Defaults({"amount": 0})], name="secondary")
resilient = primary | secondary

# Apply
try:
    normalized = resilient(raw_fact)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Pipeline failed: {e}")

docs.title: Using pipelines with engines
docs.text:
Give the engine the pipeline as fact_pipeline, and evaluate() applies it to every fact:

engine = PhreakEngine(fact_pipeline=normalize_pipeline)
engine.load_rules(
    [Rule(name="high_value", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review", persist=False)]
)

result = engine.evaluate(raw_fact)  # normalized, then evaluated
  • Any callable that takes and returns a fact dict works, not only a FactPipeline.
  • The pipeline runs on dict (and other mapping) input. A model instance is already structured, so it skips the pipeline and goes straight to conversion and validation.
  • A fact the pipeline drops (Filter, or a transform whose error policy skips the record) returns an empty result. A Filter drop is a decision, not an error, so the error policy never retries it or replaces it with a fallback. Other pipeline errors propagate.
  • With fact_schema= and validate_facts, the pipeline runs first and its output is validated.
  • assert_fact() does not run the pipeline.
  • engine.evaluate_batch(facts) runs the pipeline on each fact, as evaluate() does. With workers=N, each worker process gets its own copy of the pipeline, so a step that remembers earlier facts (a duplicate filter, a counter) only sees its own worker's facts, and the pipeline object in your process does not change. A pipeline used with workers must also be picklable: a Filter(lambda f: ...) is refused with a clear error, so use a named function defined at the top level of a module. See Many facts at once.

To read facts from a source, use FactLoader instead:

from fluxrules.pipeline import FactLoader, IterableSource

# Create loader with pipeline
raw_facts = [raw_fact]
loader = FactLoader(
    source=IterableSource(raw_facts),
    pipeline=normalize_pipeline,  # Transform each fact
)

# Evaluate pipeline facts
for normalized_fact in loader:
    result = engine.evaluate(normalized_fact)
    print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: From Fact to Action
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts.

A fact can reach PhreakEngine in several shapes: a plain dict, a raw nested payload, a typed model, a batch of records, or a file passed to the CLI. This page follows one fact from arrival to the actions it produces, and names the feature that acts at each stage. Every stage marked opt-in costs nothing until you turn it on.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
flowchart TB

        direction LR
        DICT["Plain dict<br/>amount: 4200"]
        RAW["Raw nested payload<br/>webhook, queue message"]

docs.title: Stage by stage
docs.text:
Stage What happens Turn it on Read more 0. Rules load Rules from any source become one Rule type. With a schema, every field each rule names is checked against the model, and a bad rule is refused before anything loads. The engine then builds its indexes once. PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Model); fluxrules validate --schema in CI Authoring Rules, YAML Rules, Typed Facts, CLI 1. Arrival evaluate() takes a dict, any mapping, or a model instance. evaluate_batch() takes many at once, optionally across worker processes. FactLoader reads batches; the CLI and HTTP API pass a parsed JSON dict. Always on Concepts, Ways to Evaluate a Fact, Fact Pipeline, HTTP API Reference 2. Pipeline Raw input is reshaped: flatten, rename, coerce, fill defaults, require fields, filter. A filtered fact returns an empty result. A model instance skips this stage. fact_pipeline=FactPipeline([...]) Fact Pipeline 3. Validation The fact is validated against the model: userAge and user-age become user_age, "42" becomes 42 (in normalize). An invalid fact is raised, skipped or quarantined. validate_facts="normalize" or "strict", on_invalid= Typed Facts 4. Flat dict Rules read flat keys, so nested models become dotted keys (account.age_days). Always on Nested Facts 5. Discovery Only rules that can match are kept: the alpha index drops rules whose values provably fail, the linker drops rules whose fields are absent, and optional domain or tag filters narrow further. In streaming mode only changed fields are re-linked. Always on; evaluate_by_domain, evaluate_by_tags; streaming_mode=True Architecture, Domains and Tags, Choosing an Evaluation Mode 6. Conditions Surviving rules are evaluated. Identical sub-conditions are computed once per call. A rule naming Amount against a fact with amount raises FieldNotFoundError instead of silently not matching; with a fact schema, so does userAge against user_age. With missing_field="unknown", a NOT rule does not fire just because the fact lacks the field. Always on; compile_conditions=True; EngineConfig(missing_field=...) Conditions, Complex Conditions 7. Order Fired rules are ordered by priority, highest first, then by rule id. Rule(priority=...) Rule Types 8. Result One EvaluationResult for every path: which rules fired, their actions in order, grouping by domain and tag, an explanation per rule, and latency. Always on; enable_metrics=True for percentiles Concepts, Observability 9. Act evaluate() never runs side effects: it returns action names. Your code dispatches them, for example by calling action_registry.execute(name, **fact) for each name. @action handlers Actions

Rules that join several facts (an order and its customer) take a different engine, CrossFactEngine, with its own insert and retract contract. See Cross-Fact Rules.

docs.title: One fact, end to end
docs.text:
A payment model, three rules in two domains, and an engine with the opt-in fact stages switched on. The rules use fields(Payment), which names fields through the model; see Conditions.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

from fluxrules import Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
from fluxrules.facts import fields, lenient_aliases
from fluxrules.pipeline import Defaults, FactPipeline


class Account(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=lenient_aliases())

    age_days: int
    country: str


class Payment(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=lenient_aliases())

    amount: float
    channel: str
    account: Account


p = fields(Payment)  # checked field references: a typo fails here
rules = [
    Rule(
        id=1,
        name="block_high_risk_country",
        priority=100,
        domain="fraud",
        conditions=p.account.country.isin(["NG", "RU"]) & (p.amount > 1000),
        action="block",
    ),
    Rule(
        id=2,
        name="review_new_account",
        priority=50,
        domain="fraud",
        conditions=(p.amount > 2000) & (p.account.age_days < 14),
        action="manual_review",
    ),
    Rule(
        id=3,
        name="tag_api_traffic",
        priority=10,
        domain="ops",
        conditions=p.channel == "api",
        action="tag_api",
    ),
]

engine = PhreakEngine(
    fact_schema=Payment,
    validate_facts="normalize",
    on_invalid="quarantine",
    fact_pipeline=FactPipeline([Defaults({"channel": "web"})]),
)
engine.load_rules(rules)

What each option does here:

Option Stage Meaning fact_schema=Payment 0 load_rules checks every field the rules name against Payment. A rule that names a field Payment does not have is refused. fact_pipeline=... 2 Before anything else, each incoming dict passes through the pipeline. Here Defaults adds channel: "web" when the fact has no channel. validate_facts="normalize" 3 Each fact is checked against Payment and cleaned up: Amount and ageDays are renamed to amount and age_days (the models use lenient_aliases()), and "4200" becomes 4200.0. on_invalid="quarantine" 3 Decides what happens to a fact that fails that check, such as an amount of "lots". The engine does not raise an error. It returns an empty result and keeps the fact, with the reason it failed, in engine.quarantined_facts, so you can inspect or replay it later. The other choices are "raise" (the default) and "skip", which logs a warning and drops the fact.

One more option belongs to stage 6 but is not needed here, because none of these rules use NOT: EngineConfig(missing_field="unknown"). A condition on a field the fact does not have is false, so a rule such as "not blocked" (~(F("blocked") == True)) fires even when the fact has no blocked field at all. With missing_field="unknown" the engine treats the missing field as unknown and the rule does not fire. See Missing fields and NOT.

A raw webhook payload, with camelCase keys, numbers as strings, nesting, and no channel, takes every stage:

webhook = {"Amount": "4200", "account": {"ageDays": "3", "country": "NG"}}

result = engine.evaluate(webhook)
assert result.fired_rules == [1, 2]  # priority 100 before 50
assert result.actions == ["block", "manual_review"]
assert result.rules_by_domain == {"fraud": [1, 2]}

A model instance is already structured, so it skips the pipeline and is not re-validated:

order = Payment(amount=50, channel="api", account=Account(age_days=400, country="US"))
assert engine.evaluate(order).actions == ["tag_api"]

Discovery can be narrowed to the rules of one domain:

assert engine.evaluate_by_domain(webhook, ["ops"]).fired_rules == []

A fact that fails validation is quarantined instead of raised. The stored fact already has channel, because the pipeline ran before validation:

assert engine.evaluate({"amount": "lots"}).fired_rules == []

[rejected] = engine.quarantined_facts
assert rejected.facts == {"amount": "lots", "channel": "web"}
print(rejected.error)  # what failed: amount is not a number, account is missing

The same rules can live in a YAML file that names fact_schema, and fluxrules validate rules.yaml checks them in CI before any of this runs. See CLI.

docs.title: ID Generation
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule).

FluxRules automatically generates rule IDs. By default, IDs are sequential integers (1, 2, 3, ...).

docs.title: Auto-generated IDs
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule

rule1 = Rule(
    name="check_1",
    conditions=F("amount") > 0,
    persist=False,
)
print(rule1.id)  # 1

rule2 = Rule(
    name="check_2",
    conditions=F("amount") > 0,
    persist=False,
)
print(rule2.id)  # 2

docs.title: Custom IDs
docs.text:
Override auto-generation with the id parameter:

from fluxrules import F

rule = Rule(
    id=999,  # Custom ID
    name="custom_id_rule",
    conditions=F("amount") > 0,
    persist=False,
)
print(rule.id)  # 999

docs.title: ID persistence
docs.text:
• persist=False (default): In-memory auto-increment per Rule instance
  • persist=True: ID from database auto-increment. Rule.save() does the same thing for a rule that already exists in memory.

When you persist rules to the database, the database assigns final IDs:

from fluxrules import F
from fluxrules.domain.models import Ruleset
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
rule = Rule(
    name="will_be_persisted",
    conditions=F("amount") > 0,
    persist=True,  # Will store in database
)

service.persist(Ruleset(group="default", rules=(rule.to_engine_rule(),)))
# After persist, rule.id is set from database

docs.title: ID uniqueness
docs.text:
• Within a process: Rule IDs are unique
  • Across persistence: Database ensures uniqueness per ruleset
  • Conflict handling: Pass explicit id= to avoid conflicts

  • Persistence: See Persistence for database ID management

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer. FluxRules 1.x is tested on Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14.
  • Python 3.10 and older are not supported. On those versions pip will not install FluxRules 1.x and reports that no matching distribution was found. Upgrade Python, or pin fluxrules<1.0 to stay on the last release that supported 3.10.

Check your version before installing:

python --version  # must print 3.11 or higher

docs.title: Install with uv
docs.text:
uv is the recommended tool. Add FluxRules to your project from PyPI:

uv add fluxrules

To try it in a fresh virtual environment without a project:

uv venv
uv pip install fluxrules

docs.title: Install with pip
docs.text:
Create a virtual environment and install the release from PyPI:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install fluxrules

That is all you need to start. You do not need to clone the repository.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
The base package is enough to write and evaluate rules. Each extra adds one integration:

Extra What it adds api FastAPI HTTP server, SQLAlchemy ORM, JWT login sql SQLAlchemy and Alembic for database storage redis Redis-backed storage adapter otel OpenTelemetry tracing yaml Loading rules from YAML files cli The fluxrules command-line tool all Everything above

Install one or more extras by name:

pip install 'fluxrules[api]'
pip install 'fluxrules[yaml,cli]'
