docs.title: FluxRules Load Testing & Scalability Analysis
docs.text:
This document addresses production scalability concerns: Can PHREAK handle millions of facts daily with 50K+ rules?

How to read these numbers. Throughput and daily-capacity figures below come from the realistic-rule benchmark (tests/performance/perf_realistic_rules.py), measured on a pre-loaded engine (the per-request reload defect was fixed in the P0 trust work: the engine is built once and hot-swapped, never rebuilt per fact). They are measured, not extrapolated from idealized batch throughput. Your numbers depend on your rules' selectivity, so measure your real set with the harness before sizing.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Short answer: Yes for millions/day; the path to tens-to-hundreds of millions is horizontal (more processes/pods), not a single magic thread.

  • Single process: A pre-loaded PHREAK engine evaluates one fact against the surviving candidate rules. Per-fact cost scales with surviving candidates, which the always-on alpha pre-filter minimizes on realistic (selective) rules.
  • Throughput (measured, realistic mixed rules): order 10²-10³ facts/sec per process at 10K-100K rules, depending on selectivity. Run the harness for your set: python tests/performance/perf_realistic_rules.py.
  • Daily volume (one process): reported as measured sustained throughput × 86,400 s with the method stated. That is typically single-digit to low-tens of millions/day per process on realistic rules. (No "billions/day single-thread" claim: that was idealized batch math and has been removed.)
  • For tens-to-hundreds of millions daily: deploy N processes/pods behind a queue (Kafka, Redis Streams) with sticky routing for any streaming state.
  • Honest worst case: if most rules test one low-selectivity field that every fact carries, the alpha filter cannot prune and per-fact cost is O(rules). Measure this case (--adversarial) and size for it if your rules look like that.

docs.title: Realistic-rule benchmark (the honest path)
docs.text:
Run: python tests/performance/perf_realistic_rules.py [--rules N ...] [--adversarial] [--parallel]

This harness generates rule sets with mixed fields, ranges, in-sets, ==, and AND/OR depth at a configurable match rate, then reports per-fact p50 / p95 / p99, candidates/fact before and after the alpha layer, the cumulative alpha prune ratio, throughput, and an honest daily-capacity projection. A process-pool run (--parallel) reports multi-core scaling, and --adversarial measures the low-selectivity hot-field worst case.

A CI smoke subset (tests/engine/test_realistic_rules_smoke.py) gates a p95 budget on every regular CI run so scaling regressions fail the build.

Record your own measured table here from a pinned machine (median of N runs):

Scale p50 / p95 / p99 (ms/fact) Throughput (facts/s) Alpha prune Daily / process 10K measure measure measure measure 50K measure measure measure measure 100K measure measure measure measure

docs.title: Committed readiness run (million-fact + horizontal scaling)
docs.text:
A pinned, machine-stamped result is committed at benchmarks/readiness_2026-09-11.json (regenerate with python tests/performance/perf_realistic_rules.py --readiness --readiness-rules 1000 --readiness-facts 1000000 --parity-facts 100000 --parallel-facts 400000 --workers 8 --json benchmarks/<date>.json). It streams 1,000,000 facts through a pre-loaded 1,000-rule engine (memory-flat via a fact generator) and records p50/p95/p99, throughput, peak RSS, the alpha-on-vs-off correctness parity check, plus a process-pool scaling run, so the "millions/day" and "horizontal scaling" claims are backed by a reproducible artifact, not extrapolation.

Measured on the environment stamped in the artifact (CPython 3.11.13, arm64, 12 cores):

Run Result Streaming, 1,000 rules × 1,000,000 facts p50 0.89 ms / p95 1.12 ms / p99 1.25 ms; 1,107 facts/s; peak RSS 77.2 MiB Correctness parity (alpha on vs off) 0 mismatches / 100,000 facts Horizontal scaling, 400,000 facts, 8 workers 6.39× speedup, 889 facts/s/core, fired-facts parity OK (400,000 == 400,000)

The alpha layer pruned 84.1% of candidates on this selective set. These are this machine's numbers; regenerate on your target hardware before sizing.

docs.title: Legacy micro-benchmark (PHREAK vs reference evaluator)
docs.text:
Run: pytest tests/performance/test_benchmark.py -v -s

Scenario Rules Facts per Eval Reference PHREAK Micro 10 5 0.004 ms 0.003 ms Small 100 20 0.028 ms 0.063 ms Medium 1,000 50 0.324 ms 0.598 ms Large 10,000 100 3.391 ms 6.286 ms XL 50,000 200 33.745 ms 102.640 ms

These use single-field synthetic rules (every fact carries the hot field), which is the easy case but not representative of production selectivity. Use the realistic-rule harness above for capacity planning; use this table only to compare PHREAK against the naive reference evaluator.

Key insight: PHREAK stays within a small constant factor of the naive reference evaluator while scaling to 50K rules.

docs.title: Single-process capacity (measured, not extrapolated)
docs.text:
Per-fact cost is linear in the number of surviving candidate rules, not the total rule count. The always-on alpha pre-filter drops rules whose necessary conditions provably fail before any per-rule evaluation. So capacity depends on your rules' selectivity, which is why we measure rather than assert a single number.

Methodology (§7):

  1. Build the engine once (production uses a versioned hot-swap holder, with no per-request reload).
  2. Warm up, then time each fact individually; report p50/p95/p99, not just a mean.
  3. Pause GC during the timed loop so numbers reflect matcher cost.
  4. Daily capacity = measured sustained throughput × 86,400 s, reported with the method stated (never idealized batch throughput × a day).
Single process, realistic rules:
- Measure per-fact p50/p95/p99 with perf_realistic_rules.py on your rule set.
- Daily/process  = sustained facts/sec × 86,400.
- Typical range  = single-digit to low-tens of millions/day per process,
                   driven by selectivity (alpha prune ratio).

Removed claim. Earlier revisions stated "2.6 billion facts/day single-thread" and "8-26 billion/day per process." Those multiplied an idealized batch throughput by 86,400 and assumed away per-request reload, real selectivity, GC, and I/O. They are not defensible and have been replaced by the measured methodology above.

docs.title: Adversarial caveat (the honest worst case)
docs.text:
If most rules test one low-selectivity field that every fact carries, the alpha pre-filter cannot prune, so every fact reaches O(rules) per-rule evaluations. The harness measures this directly:

python tests/performance/perf_realistic_rules.py --adversarial

Plan capacity for this number, not the selective best case, if your rule set looks like that. (FluxRules is a high-throughput single-fact matcher; cross- fact joins/temporal correlation are out of scope; see Engine Scope & Limits.)

docs.title: Multi-core scaling
docs.text:
Python's GIL serializes CPU-bound condition evaluation within a process, so multi-core throughput comes from processes, not threads. Use engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=N). It starts N worker processes, and each one rebuilds your engine with the same settings and rules:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine


def main() -> None:
    engine = PhreakEngine()
    engine.load_rules([Rule(id=1, name="big", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review")])
    facts = [{"amount": n} for n in range(0, 5000, 500)]
    results = engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=4)
    print(sum(1 for r in results if r.fired_rules), "facts matched")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The if __name__ == "__main__": guard matters. On macOS and Windows, each worker process imports your script again, and without the guard it would start the batch again. See Many facts at once for the full rules.

The benchmark harness measures parallel throughput:

python tests/performance/perf_realistic_rules.py --parallel --workers 8

The harness reports parallel throughput, per-core throughput, and the speedup, with a fired-facts parity check proving results are identical to single-process.

docs.title: Distributed architecture
docs.text:
For millions of facts daily (1-10M/day):

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Message Queue (Kafka/Redis)          │
│  (Buffer: 100K-1M facts waiting)            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
              │
              ├────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
              │        │          │          │
              ▼        ▼          ▼          ▼
         ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐
         │Instance1│ │Instance2│ │Instance3│ │Instance4│
         │PHREAK   │ │PHREAK   │ │PHREAK   │ │PHREAK   │
         │Network  │ │Network  │ │Network  │ │Network  │
         │(50K)    │ │(50K)    │ │(50K)    │ │(50K)    │
         └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘
              │        │          │          │
              └────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌──────────────────┐
              │  Results DB      │
              │ (PostgreSQL)     │
              └──────────────────┘

Capacity (illustrative; substitute your measured per-process number): - N processes × (your measured facts/sec) = aggregate facts/sec - aggregate facts/sec × 86,400 = facts/day - Scaling is ~linear in processes for stateless evaluation; verify with perf_realistic_rules.py --parallel.

docs.title: 1. Delta Evaluation (Field-Level Dirty Tracking)
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()

# Compile ruleset once
engine.load_rules(ruleset)

# Evaluate many facts with incremental updates
facts = {"customer_id": 123, "amount": 5000}
result = engine.evaluate(facts)

# Next fact: only "amount" changed
facts_updated = {"customer_id": 123, "amount": 6000}
result = engine.evaluate(facts_updated, prev_facts=facts)
# PHREAK recomputes only alphas for "amount" field

Impact: 5-10× faster for incremental updates vs. full re-evaluation.

docs.title: 2. Batch Evaluation with Working Memory
docs.text:
# python skip
# Accumulate facts in working memory (streaming_mode=True engine)
for i, fact in enumerate(facts_stream):
    engine.assert_fact(fact)
    if i % 1000 == 0:
        # Flush: evaluate the current working-memory fact set
        result = engine.evaluate(fact)
        results.append(result)

Impact: Amortizes compilation overhead, ~50K facts/batch.

docs.title: 3. Horizontal Scaling with Load Balancing
docs.text:
# python skip
# Deploy with Docker Compose
# Each instance: 1 CPU, 1GB RAM
# Network: Redis/Kafka queue

import redis
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

app = FastAPI()
queue = redis.Redis(host="redis", port=6379)
engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(ruleset)

@app.post("/evaluate")
def evaluate_fact(fact: dict):
    result = engine.evaluate(fact)
    queue.rpush("results", result.to_json())
    return {"status": "queued"}

docs.title: Scenario 1: Fraud Detection (1M facts/day, 5K rules)
docs.text:
Daily Volume: 1,000,000 facts  (≈ 12 facts/sec average)
Rules: 5,000 (fraud detection patterns)

Setup:
- 1 process is ample: 1M/day ≈ 12 facts/sec average; even the adversarial
  worst case at 5K rules clears this with wide headroom.
- Deploy on a small instance (1 CPU, 4GB RAM).

Architecture:
API ──────▶ PHREAK Engine ──────▶ Results DB

docs.title: Scenario 2: E-commerce (100M facts/day, 50K rules)
docs.text:
Daily Volume: 100,000,000 facts  (≈ 1,160 facts/sec average;
                                   higher at peak; size for peak, not average)
Rules: 50,000 (pricing, promotions, inventory)

Setup:
- Multiple processes/pods behind a queue. Size N from YOUR measured per-process
  throughput: N ≈ peak facts/sec ÷ (measured facts/sec/process), plus headroom.
- Run perf_realistic_rules.py on your 50K rule set (and --adversarial) first.
- Load balancer (nginx/HAProxy); message queue: Kafka (fault tolerance);
  results store: PostgreSQL with replication.

Architecture:
         Kafka Queue
            │
    ┌───────┼───────┐
    ▼       ▼       ▼       ▼
  API1   API2   API3   API4
  (PHREAK)
    │       │       │       │

docs.title: Scenario 3: Financial Risk (500M facts/day, 100K rules)
docs.text:
Daily Volume: 500,000,000 facts  (≈ 5,800 facts/sec average; size for peak)
Rules: 100,000 (regulatory, risk, compliance)

Per-fact latency: MEASURE at 100K rules with perf_realistic_rules.py. Per-fact
cost scales with surviving candidates (post-alpha), not raw rule count, so the
number depends on selectivity. Do not assume a fixed multiple of the 50K case.

Setup:
- Many processes/pods (size from measured per-process throughput + headroom).
- Pre-load the rule network per pod; hot-swap on rule change (no per-request
  reload).
- Deploy across multiple availability zones.

Architecture:
    Kafka Cluster (distributed)
           │
    ┌──────┼──────┬──────┬──────┐
    ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
  K8s Pod × 20 (auto-scaling)
  PHREAK Engine (100K rules)
    │      │      │      │      │
    └──────┼──────┘      └──────┘
           │
      PostgreSQL (sharded)
      + Redis Cache

docs.title: Recommended Test Suite for Production Validation
docs.text: To validate your specific workload (millions of facts, 50K+ rules), implement:

docs.title: 1. Streaming Benchmark
docs.text:
# tests/performance/test_streaming.py
import pytest
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
import time

def test_phreak_streaming_1m_facts():
    """Validate 1M facts/day throughput with 50K rules."""
    engine = PhreakEngine()
    engine.load_rules(ruleset_50k)

    # Simulate 1M facts arriving over 24 hours
    fact_rate = 1_000_000 / (24 * 3600)  # ~12 facts/sec

    start = time.time()
    for i in range(1_000_000):
        fact = generate_fact(i)
        result = engine.evaluate(fact)
        assert result is not None

    elapsed = time.time() - start
    throughput = 1_000_000 / elapsed

    assert throughput > 10_000, f"Expected >10K facts/sec, got {throughput}"
    print(f"Throughput: {throughput:.0f} facts/sec")

docs.title: 2. Batch Processing Benchmark
docs.text:
# tests/performance/test_batch_processing.py
def test_phreak_batch_1m_facts():
    """Validate batch processing of 1M facts."""
    engine = PhreakEngine()
    engine.load_rules(ruleset_50k)

    batch_size = 1000
    total_facts = 1_000_000

    start = time.time()
    for batch_idx in range(total_facts // batch_size):
        batch = [generate_fact(i) for i in range(batch_idx * batch_size, (batch_idx + 1) * batch_size)]
        for fact in batch:
            engine.assert_fact(fact)
        # Evaluate the last fact in the batch to flush working memory
        engine.evaluate(batch[-1])

    elapsed = time.time() - start
    throughput = total_facts / elapsed

    assert throughput > 50_000, f"Expected >50K facts/sec, got {throughput}"
    print(f"Batch Throughput: {throughput:.0f} facts/sec")

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
Before deploying PHREAK to handle millions of facts:

  • [ ] Baseline: Run pytest tests/performance/test_benchmark.py with your ruleset
  • [ ] Streaming: Implement test for your expected fact rate (e.g., 10K facts/sec)
  • [ ] Batching: Measure throughput with batch processing
  • [ ] Memory: Monitor RSS (resident memory) during load test
  • [ ] Latency: Track p50, p95, p99 latencies with latency_tracking=True
  • [ ] Database: Stress-test your persistence layer (PostgreSQL/SQLite)
  • [ ] Caching: Consider Redis for rule network sharing across instances
  • [ ] Monitoring: Set up Prometheus metrics and alerting
  • [ ] Horizontal Scaling: Test load balancer failover and auto-scaling

docs.title: Current Limitations
docs.text:
1. Single-Process Baseline: Standard benchmarks measure one Python process

  2. Workaround: Run multiple instances behind a queue (Kafka/Redis)

  3. Working Memory Limits: Not tested with >1M facts in memory

  4. Workaround: Batch evaluation with periodic cleanup

  5. 100K+ Rules: Extrapolated linearly; direct testing pending

  6. Workaround: Shard rules by domain (fraud vs. promotions) across instances

  7. Real-Time Validation: Benchmarks are offline; streaming latency untested

  8. Workaround: Use latency_tracking=True in production

docs.title: Nested Facts
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Fact) and Fact Pipeline.

FluxRules engines evaluate flat dictionaries. Use the Flatten transform to work with nested fact structures, or pass a model: nested models are flattened for you (see From a model).

A dotted rule field such as user.profile.country checked against an unflattened fact ({"user": {...}}) raises FieldNotFoundError with a hint to flatten, rather than silently not matching.

docs.title: Nested fact structure
docs.text:
fact = {
    "user": {"id": "user_123", "profile": {"country": "US", "tier": "premium"}},
    "transaction": {"amount": 5000, "currency": "USD"},
}

docs.title: Flattening nested facts
docs.text:
Use FactPipeline with Flatten() to convert to dot notation:

from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten, Require

pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),  # Converts nested to dot notation
        Require(["user.id", "transaction.amount"]),  # Validate required fields
    ],
    name="normalize",
)

flat_fact = pipeline(fact)
# Result:
# {
#     "user.id": "user_123",
#     "user.profile.country": "US",
#     "user.profile.tier": "premium",
#     "transaction.amount": 5000,
#     "transaction.currency": "USD"
# }

docs.title: Writing rules for nested facts
docs.text:
After flattening, write rules using dot notation:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule = Rule(
    name="premium_users_high_value",
    conditions=(F("user.profile.tier") == "premium") & (F("transaction.amount") > 10000),
    action="require_approval",
    persist=False,
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

# Evaluate flattened fact
result = engine.evaluate(flat_fact)
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Full workflow
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten, FieldType, Defaults
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# 1. Define pipeline for nested facts
pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),
        Defaults({"user.country": "US"}),  # Fill missing nested fields
        FieldType({"transaction.amount": float}),  # Type coercion on nested fields
    ],
    name="prepare_facts",
)

# 2. Load rules
engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

# 3. Process nested fact
flat = pipeline(fact)

# 4. Evaluate
result = engine.evaluate(flat)

docs.title: From a model
docs.text:
When facts arrive as Pydantic models, dataclasses, attrs classes or msgspec structs, pass them to the engine directly. Nested models become dotted keys, the same shape Flatten() produces:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from fluxrules import F, Rule, to_fact_dict
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine


class Profile(BaseModel):
    country: str
    tier: str


class User(BaseModel):
    id: str
    profile: Profile


user = User(id="user_123", profile=Profile(country="US", tier="premium"))
assert to_fact_dict(user)["profile.country"] == "US"

model_engine = PhreakEngine()
model_engine.load_rules(
    [Rule(id=1, name="us_premium", conditions=F("profile.tier") == "premium", action="flag")]
)
assert model_engine.evaluate(user).fired_rules == [1]

Plain dict values inside a model are kept as values, not flattened. See Typed Facts for checking rules against the model.

docs.title: External Observability Exporters
docs.text: The FactPipeline framework provides out-of-the-box support for integrating with popular observability backends via the extensible ObservabilityHook protocol. This page documents the built-in exporters for Prometheus and OpenTelemetry.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The observability system is built on the ObservabilityHook protocol, a minimal, Python protocol that any class can implement to receive pipeline events. This design ensures:

  • No coupling between core pipeline logic and external backends
  • Graceful degradation if a backend is misconfigured or unavailable
  • Easy extension for custom backends (datadog, newrelic, etc.)
# The protocol (from fluxrules.pipeline.observability)
from typing import Protocol

from fluxrules.pipeline import Transform


class ObservabilityHook(Protocol):
    def on_pipeline_start(self, pipeline_name: str, fact: dict) -> None: ...
    def on_transform_start(self, transform: Transform, fact: dict) -> None: ...
    def on_transform_end(self, transform: Transform, fact: dict, duration: float) -> None: ...
    def on_transform_error(self, transform: Transform, fact: dict, error: Exception) -> None: ...
    def on_pipeline_end(self, pipeline_name: str, fact: dict, duration: float) -> None: ...
    def on_pipeline_error(self, pipeline_name: str, fact: dict, error: Exception) -> None: ...

Both PrometheusHook and OpenTelemetryHook implement this protocol. They are optional dependencies, so use only what you need.

docs.title: Prometheus Exporter
docs.text: Export metrics to Prometheus for time-series monitoring and alerting.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install prometheus_client

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten
from fluxrules.pipeline import PrometheusHook

# Create the exporter
prometheus_hook = PrometheusHook(namespace="myapp", subsystem="pipeline")

# Attach to pipeline
pipeline = FactPipeline([Flatten()], hooks=[prometheus_hook], name="normalize_facts")

# Use the pipeline: metrics are automatically recorded
fact = pipeline({"user": {"id": "u_1"}})

# Expose metrics (standard approach)
from prometheus_client import start_http_server

start_http_server(0)  # Use an available port; production deployments may choose a fixed port.

docs.title: Metrics Exported
docs.text:
The PrometheusHook registers the following metrics in the global Prometheus registry:

Metric Type Labels Description myapp_pipeline_pipeline_runs_total Counter pipeline_name Total pipeline executions myapp_pipeline_pipeline_errors_total Counter pipeline_name Total pipeline failures myapp_pipeline_pipeline_duration_seconds Histogram pipeline_name Pipeline execution duration myapp_pipeline_transform_invocations_total Counter transform_name Transform invocation count myapp_pipeline_transform_errors_total Counter transform_name Transform error count myapp_pipeline_transform_duration_seconds Histogram transform_name Transform execution duration

The histogram buckets are optimized for typical fact-processing latencies: - Pipelines: [0.001s, 0.01s, 0.05s, 0.1s, 0.5s, 1.0s, 5.0s] - Transforms: [0.001s, 0.01s, 0.05s, 0.1s, 0.5s, 1.0s]

docs.title: Example: Querying with Prometheus
docs.text:
# Pipeline success rate
rate(myapp_pipeline_pipeline_runs_total[1m]) / rate(myapp_pipeline_pipeline_errors_total[1m])

# Average pipeline latency
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(myapp_pipeline_pipeline_duration_seconds_bucket[1m]))

# Transform-level insights
topk(5, rate(myapp_pipeline_transform_invocations_total[1m]))

docs.title: Metric Caching & Custom Registries
docs.text:
Prometheus forbids registering two collectors with the same name in one registry. PrometheusHook handles this by caching collectors per (registry, namespace, subsystem), so constructing the hook repeatedly is safe and never raises a Duplicated timeseries in CollectorRegistry error:

hook1 = PrometheusHook(namespace="myapp")
hook2 = PrometheusHook(namespace="myapp")  # Reuses the same cached collectors
assert hook1._pipeline_runs_total is hook2._pipeline_runs_total

By default metrics are registered in the global prometheus_client.REGISTRY. For test isolation or multi-tenant setups, pass your own CollectorRegistry:

from prometheus_client import CollectorRegistry

registry = CollectorRegistry()
hook = PrometheusHook(namespace="tenant_a", registry=registry)
# Metrics for tenant_a are isolated from the global registry.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Exporter
docs.text: Export traces and metrics to OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing, correlation, and context propagation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Core OpenTelemetry API + SDK
pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk

# Add an exporter (choose one or more)
pip install opentelemetry-exporter-otlp          # OTLP: Jaeger, Tempo, Collector, etc.
pip install opentelemetry-exporter-zipkin        # Zipkin

Tip: Modern Jaeger ingests OTLP natively, so the OTLP exporter is the recommended path. The standalone opentelemetry-exporter-jaeger package is deprecated and removed in recent OpenTelemetry releases.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten
from fluxrules.pipeline import OpenTelemetryHook

# Create the exporter
otel_hook = OpenTelemetryHook(service_name="my_rule_engine", version="1.0.0")

# Attach to pipeline
pipeline = FactPipeline([Flatten()], hooks=[otel_hook], name="normalize_facts")

# Use the pipeline: traces are automatically recorded
fact = pipeline({"user": {"id": "u_1"}})

# Traces appear in your configured OpenTelemetry backend
# (Jaeger, Tempo, DataDog, New Relic, etc.)

docs.title: Span Structure
docs.text:
The OpenTelemetryHook creates a single parent span per pipeline execution, recording transform events as child events within that span:

Span: pipeline.normalize_facts
  ├─ Event: transform.start (Flatten)
  ├─ Event: transform.end (Flatten, duration: 0.0012s)
  ├─ Event: transform.start (Rename)
  ├─ Event: transform.end (Rename, duration: 0.0008s)
  ├─ Status: OK
  └─ Attributes:
      pipeline.name: normalize_facts
      pipeline.duration_seconds: 0.0021
      fact.keys: ["user", "order"]

The span is created with tracer.start_span(...) (not start_as_current_span) because the hook holds a single span across several discrete callbacks rather than within one with block. Success and failure are reported through the native span status (StatusCode.OK / StatusCode.ERROR), and failures additionally call span.record_exception(error), the idiomatic OpenTelemetry way to attach an exception, which your backend renders as an exception event with stack trace.

docs.title: Span Attributes
docs.text:
Each pipeline span includes:

Attribute Type Example pipeline.name string "normalize_facts" pipeline.duration_seconds float 0.0021 fact.keys list[str] ["user", "order"]

The span status conveys success/failure:

Outcome Span status Extra success StatusCode.OK none error StatusCode.ERROR (description = error message) record_exception(error) emits an exception event

Transform events include:

Event Attributes transform.start transform.name, transform.version transform.end transform.name, duration_seconds transform.error transform.name, error.type, error.message

docs.title: Example: Exporting via OTLP (Jaeger, Tempo, Collector)
docs.text:
# python skip
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

# Configure the OTLP exporter (points at a Collector / Jaeger / Tempo OTLP endpoint)
otlp_exporter = OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint="http://localhost:4317", insecure=True)

trace_provider = TracerProvider()
trace_provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(otlp_exporter))

# Set as the global provider BEFORE constructing the hook so it picks up this tracer
trace.set_tracer_provider(trace_provider)

# Now create your pipeline
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten, OpenTelemetryHook

hook = OpenTelemetryHook(service_name="my_app")
pipeline = FactPipeline([Flatten()], hooks=[hook])
pipeline({"user": {"id": "u_1"}})

# Spans automatically appear in your backend (Jaeger/Tempo UI, etc.)

Testing tip: For unit tests, swap the OTLP exporter for the SDK's InMemorySpanExporter and assert on exporter.get_finished_spans(). This is how tests/unit/pipeline/test_exporters.py validates this hook end-to-end.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The OpenTelemetryHook degrades gracefully if OpenTelemetry is misconfigured:

# python skip
# If the tracer is not properly initialized, the hook
# swallows exceptions and continues silently
hook = OpenTelemetryHook()
pipeline = FactPipeline([...], hooks=[hook])

# Even if OTEL is broken, your pipeline runs normally
pipeline({"data": "here"})  # Works fine

docs.title: Combining Exporters
docs.text:
Use multiple exporters simultaneously to send metrics and traces to different backends:

from fluxrules.pipeline import (
    FactPipeline,
    Flatten,
    MetricsHook,
    PipelineMetrics,
    PrometheusHook,
    OpenTelemetryHook,
)

# Create exporters
metrics_obj = PipelineMetrics()
hooks = [
    MetricsHook(metrics_obj),  # In-memory metrics
    PrometheusHook(),  # Prometheus metrics
    OpenTelemetryHook(),  # Distributed tracing
]

# Single pipeline, multiple backends
pipeline = FactPipeline([Flatten()], hooks=hooks, name="multi_backend")

# All three backends receive events simultaneously
pipeline({"user": {"id": "u_1"}})

# Query metrics locally
print(metrics_obj.as_dict())

# Prometheus: http://localhost:8000/metrics
# OpenTelemetry: Check your Jaeger/Tempo/etc.

docs.title: Building Custom Exporters
docs.text:
The ObservabilityHook protocol makes it easy to build custom exporters. Example: exporting to Datadog:

from fluxrules.pipeline.observability import ObservabilityHook
from fluxrules.pipeline.base import Transform
from typing import Any


class DatadogHook:
    """Send pipeline events to Datadog."""

    def __init__(self, api_key: str):
        self.api_key = api_key
        # Initialize Datadog client

    def on_transform_end(self, transform: Transform, fact: dict[str, Any], duration: float) -> None:
        """Send transform completion metric to Datadog."""
        datadog_client.metric(
            f"pipeline.transform.duration", duration, tags=[f"transform:{transform.metadata.name}"]
        )

    # ... implement other protocol methods

Then use it:

hook = DatadogHook(api_key="...")
pipeline = FactPipeline([...], hooks=[hook])

docs.title: 1. Use Namespacing
docs.text:
Avoid metric collisions in Prometheus by using a unique namespace:

# Good: namespaced by service
PrometheusHook(namespace="user_service", subsystem="pipeline")

# Good: namespaced by environment
PrometheusHook(namespace="prod_ml_engine", subsystem="pipeline")

docs.title: 2. Combine Local + Remote Metrics
docs.text:
Track local metrics for debugging + remote metrics for production monitoring:

metrics = PipelineMetrics()  # Local, in-memory
hooks = [
    MetricsHook(metrics),
    PrometheusHook(),  # Production monitoring
]

pipeline = FactPipeline([...], hooks=hooks)

docs.title: 3. Instrument with Custom Transforms
docs.text:
Combine exporters with custom transforms to add business logic instrumentation:

from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Transform


class BusinessLogicTransform(Transform):
    """Track domain-specific events (e.g., fraud flags)."""

    def __call__(self, fact):
        if fact.get("fraud_score", 0) > 0.8:
            print(f"HIGH RISK: {fact['user_id']}")  # Or emit custom metric
        return fact

docs.title: 4. Monitor Error Rates
docs.text:
Use Prometheus queries to monitor transform-level error rates:

# Transform error rate
rate(myapp_pipeline_transform_errors_total[1m]) 
  / ignoring(instance) rate(myapp_pipeline_transform_invocations_total[1m])

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Prometheus: Minimal overhead; metrics are incremented atomically.
  • OpenTelemetry: Span creation has measurable overhead (~microseconds per event); use sampled tracing in high-throughput scenarios.

To reduce overhead in production, consider:

# python skip
# Only use OpenTelemetry if tracing is enabled
hooks = [MetricsHook()]
if TRACING_ENABLED:
    hooks.append(OpenTelemetryHook())

pipeline = FactPipeline([...], hooks=hooks)

docs.title: Prometheus metrics not appearing
docs.text:
• Ensure prometheus_client is installed: pip install prometheus_client
  • Call start_http_server(port) to expose metrics
  • Check http://localhost:PORT/metrics

docs.title: OpenTelemetry spans not appearing
docs.text:
• Ensure OpenTelemetry SDK and exporter are installed
  • Configure a global TracerProvider before creating the hook
  • Check that your exporter backend (Jaeger, Tempo, etc.) is running

docs.title: Import errors
docs.text:
Both exporters are optional. If you see ImportError, install the required library:

pip install prometheus_client opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Deployment.

Monitor FluxRules with engine metrics, pipeline hooks, logs, and optional Prometheus/OpenTelemetry exporters. Exporters are opt-in; the core engine does not start a metrics server or emit external telemetry by default.

docs.title: PHREAK engine metrics
docs.text:
Enable the bounded in-process collector when you need candidate, selectivity, latency, or streaming-cache signals:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule = Rule(
    name="amount_check",
    conditions=F("amount") > 100,
    action="review",
    persist=False,
)
engine = PhreakEngine(enable_metrics=True)
engine.load_rules([rule])
engine.evaluate({"amount": 150})

metrics = engine.get_observability_metrics()
print(metrics["alpha_prune_ratio"])
print(metrics["eval_latency_ms_p95"])

The collector is bounded and advisory. Useful operational signals include candidates_per_fact_out, alpha_prune_ratio, eval_latency_ms_p95, linked_rules_avg, node_memory.hit_rate in streaming mode, and working_memory_size.

With engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=N), only per-fact latency reaches the engine's metrics. The other counters are counted inside the worker processes and are not added here.

docs.title: Metrics (Prometheus)
docs.text:
Prometheus export is optional and is attached to a FactPipeline through a PrometheusHook:

from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten
from fluxrules.pipeline.exporters import PrometheusHook

hook = PrometheusHook(namespace="fluxrules")
pipeline = FactPipeline([Flatten()], hooks=[hook])
pipeline({"user": {"id": "u1"}})

The hook exposes pipeline and transform metrics such as pipeline run/error counters, pipeline duration, transform invocation/error counters, and transform duration histograms.

The hook records pipeline and transform counters/histograms in the registry provided to it. A /metrics HTTP endpoint requires an application-owned Prometheus exposition route; the core pipeline does not start one automatically.

# The host application exposes its configured Prometheus registry.
curl http://localhost:8000/metrics

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Logs are output to stdout (structured for container environments):

# Set log level
export FLUXRULES_LOG_LEVEL=INFO

# Redirect to logging backend
docker run -v /var/log/fluxrules:/app/logs fluxrules:latest

docs.title: Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry)
docs.text:
If extras include [otel], attach OpenTelemetryHook to a pipeline and configure the exporter/provider in the host application:

# Enable OpenTelemetry
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc
export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=fluxrules

from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten
from fluxrules.pipeline.exporters import OpenTelemetryHook

hook = OpenTelemetryHook(service_name="fluxrules")
pipeline = FactPipeline([Flatten()], hooks=[hook])
pipeline({"user": {"id": "u1"}})

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Liveness/readiness endpoint:

GET /health

Response: 

{
  "status": "healthy",
  "version": "1.1.2"
}

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule) and Sessions (RuleService).

FluxRules rules can be persisted to a database. Use persistence when you need to:

  1. Store rules permanently: survive application restarts
  2. Share rules across instances: load the same ruleset in multiple processes
  3. Audit trail: track rule evaluation for compliance

docs.title: Quick start: Store and load rules
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Create rules
rules = [
    Rule(
        name="high_value_transaction",
        conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
        action="require_approval",
    ),
]

# Load and evaluate with engine
engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000})
print(f"Matched rules: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Persist flag
docs.text:
Every rule has a persist flag (default: False):

  • persist=False (default): Constructing the rule does no I/O. The rule is in-memory only and gets a locally generated ID.
  • persist=True: The rule is written to the database during construction and adopts the database-assigned ID.

Constructing a Rule is a pure operation by default, so importing a module that defines rules never opens a database connection. To store a rule you built in memory, call Rule.save():

from fluxrules import F

rule = Rule(
    name="production_rule",
    conditions=F("x") > 10,
    action="act",
)
rule.save()  # now in the database, rule.id is the stored ID

save() is an insert, not an upsert: calling it twice stores the rule twice and does not update an existing row. Use the repository or service layer when you need update semantics.

# Persisted rule (stored in database)
from fluxrules import F

rule1 = Rule(
    name="production_rule",
    conditions=F("x") > 10,
    action="act",
    persist=True,  # Database storage
)

# Temporary rule (in-memory only)
rule2 = Rule(
    name="test_rule",
    conditions=F("y") == "test",
    action="test_act",
    persist=False,  # No database storage
)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set the database environment during initialization:

from fluxrules.initialization import initialize_persistence

# Development (SQLite, default)
initialize_persistence(env="dev")

# Production (PostgreSQL)
initialize_persistence(env="prod", db_url="postgresql://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules")

# Custom URL
initialize_persistence(db_url="postgresql://localhost/my_rules")

Using environment variables:

export FLUXRULES_ENV=prod
export FLUXRULES_DB_URL=postgresql://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules

FluxRules auto-initializes the database on first use if not called explicitly.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Every rule evaluation produces an audit trail automatically:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Setup engine and rules
rule = Rule(name="test", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag")
engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

fact = {"amount": 6000}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)

# Audit trail built-in to result
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")      # Rule IDs that matched
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")          # Actions executed
print(f"Time: {result.latency_ms}ms")        # Execution time

# Log for audit
import json
audit_record = {
    "fact_id": fact.get("id"),
    "matched_rules": result.fired_rules,
    "actions": result.actions,
    "latency_ms": result.latency_ms,
}
print(json.dumps(audit_record))

Persist audit records to your logging backend as needed.

docs.title: Supported databases
docs.text:
• SQLite (default, development, single-file)
  • PostgreSQL (production, scales to 100K+ rules)
  • MySQL, SQL Server, and any other SQLAlchemy-supported dialect: via the ServiceFactory path below; see the note on backend in that section

docs.title: Using a different SQL provider (Postgres, SQL Server, etc.)
docs.text:
By default persist=True writes through the DBConnectionManager path, which is configured via initialize_persistence() or the FLUXRULES_DB_URL / FLUXRULES_ENV environment variables.

In real applications you typically configure a connection once at startup (e.g. in a FastAPI lifespan handler). When you register a persistence adapter with ServiceFactory, persist=True automatically delegates to that adapter instead of the default SQLite path. No other changes are needed.

docs.title: FastAPI + PostgreSQL example
docs.text:
# python skip
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from fastapi import FastAPI

from fluxrules.config import PersistenceConfig, RuntimeConfig
from fluxrules.di import ServiceFactory
from fluxrules import F, Rule

DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules"
engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL, pool_size=10, max_overflow=20)
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Register the Postgres-backed adapter once at startup.
    ServiceFactory.create_persistence_adapter(
        session_provider=SessionLocal,
        config=RuntimeConfig(persistence=PersistenceConfig(backend="postgres")),
    )
    yield
    ServiceFactory.reset()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

# Anywhere in your app: persist=True now writes to Postgres, not SQLite.
rule = Rule(
    name="kyc_verified",
    domain="compliance",
    conditions=F("kyc_status") == "verified",
    action="proceed",
    persist=True,
)

SQLAlchemyPersistenceAdapter is dialect-agnostic: it works with any database SQLAlchemy supports (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite). The key thing to know: backend="postgres" is the configuration value that activates the SQLAlchemy path in ServiceFactory, regardless of the actual database dialect. Change the DATABASE_URL scheme for your target database but keep backend="postgres":

# MySQL
DATABASE_URL = "mysql+pymysql://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules"

# SQL Server
DATABASE_URL = "mssql+pyodbc://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules?driver=ODBC+Driver+17+for+SQL+Server"

The rest of the setup (session_provider, ServiceFactory.create_persistence_adapter()) is identical.

docs.title: Priority order
docs.text:
When persist=True is used, fluxrules checks in this order:

  1. ServiceFactory adapter: if one is registered and it is not the in-memory fallback, it is used. This covers any SQLAlchemy-backed dialect (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server) as long as backend="postgres" was set at registration time.
  2. DBConnectionManager: the initialize_persistence() / env-var path. Used when no ServiceFactory adapter is registered (the common case for standalone scripts and simple deployments).
  3. Fallback: if neither is reachable, a locally generated ID is assigned and an INFO-level log entry is emitted ("No database configured; using in-memory mode"). The rule is still usable in-memory.

Note on table creation: ServiceFactory does not create database tables. When using the ServiceFactory path you are responsible for running schema migrations before the application starts (e.g. via Alembic). The initialize_persistence() helper creates tables automatically and is the right choice when you want a zero-config startup with SQLite or a simple PostgreSQL setup.

docs.title: Pydantic Rule Guide
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule) and Conditions (condition tree).

The Rule class is a Pydantic v2 model. This guide covers all fields and validation.

docs.title: Rule fields
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule

rule = Rule(
    # Core (required)
    name="high_value_transaction",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,

    # Core (optional)
    domain="fraud_detection",                     # Logical grouping (default: "default")
    tags=frozenset(["tier_1", "manual_review"]),  # Searchable keywords
    action="require_approval",                    # Single action (string)
    # action=("act1", "act2"),                   # Multiple actions (tuple)
    priority=10,                                  # Higher = first (default: 0)
    persist=True,                                 # Store in database (default: False)
)

docs.title: Field Reference
docs.text: Field Type Required Default Notes name str Yes none Human-readable rule name conditions dict Yes none Rule logic (condition tree format) domain str No "default" Organizational grouping tags frozenset[str] No frozenset() Search/filter keywords action str \| tuple[str, ...] No None Action(s) when rule fires priority int No 0 Evaluation order persist bool No False Store in the database during construction; see Rule.save()

docs.title: Condition tree format
docs.text:
The conditions field defines rule logic. Write it with F expressions:

from fluxrules import F

# Simple condition
F("amount") > 5000

# AND/OR grouping
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

# NOT operator
~(F("verified") == True)

Each expression is stored as a dictionary tree. A plain dictionary is accepted anywhere an F expression is, for example when rules come from YAML or a database:

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"},
    ],
}

See Conditions and Complex Conditions for details.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Pydantic automatically validates rules:

from pydantic import ValidationError

# Missing required field
try:
    Rule(conditions={...})  # Missing `name`
except ValidationError as e:
    print(f"Validation error: {e}")

# Invalid conditions
try:
    Rule(
        name="test",
        conditions={"type": "invalid", "field": "x"},  # Invalid type
        persist=False
    )
except ValidationError as e:
    print(f"condition validation error: {e}")

docs.title: Add tags
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules import F

rule = Rule(
    name="check",
    conditions=F("status") == "pending",
    tags=frozenset(["tier_1", "fraud", "manual_review"]),
    persist=False,
)

# tags are frozenset (immutable)
print(rule.tags)  # frozenset({'tier_1', 'fraud', 'manual_review'})

docs.title: Multiple actions
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule

# Action is a single string
rule = Rule(
    name="suspicious",
    conditions=F("risk_score") > 75,
    action="block",  # Single action
    persist=False,
)

print(rule.action)  # "block"

docs.title: Priority for ordering
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule

rules = [
    Rule(name="urgent", conditions=F("status") == "critical", priority=100, persist=False),
    Rule(name="normal", conditions=F("status") == "warning", priority=10, persist=False),
    Rule(name="low", conditions=F("status") == "info", priority=1, persist=False),
]

# Higher priority evaluated first

Equal priorities

All matching rules fire; priority only controls order. When two rules share a priority (in the same group or in different groups), the engine currently orders them by rule ID, highest first. This is an implementation detail, not a guaranteed contract, so don't rely on it. Give rules distinct priorities if their relative order matters. Same-group, same-priority rules also raise a priority_conflict validation warning.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Convert Rule to/from JSON:

import json

# To JSON
rule_dict = rule.model_dump()
rule_json = rule.model_dump_json()

# From JSON
restored = Rule(**json.loads(rule_json))

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This page takes you from an empty script to working rules in a few minutes.

Prerequisites: Python 3.11 or newer, and FluxRules installed (see Installation).

docs.title: Your first rule
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule, evaluate

rule = Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("age") >= 18, action="allow")

result = evaluate(rule, {"age": 30})
print(result.fired_rules)  # [1], the id of the rule that matched
print(result.actions)      # ['allow']

A rule pairs a condition with an action. F("age") >= 18 is the condition: it holds when the field age is 18 or more. The dictionary {"age": 30} is a fact, the data you want to check. evaluate() runs the rule against the fact and returns a result that lists the rules that matched (fired_rules) and the actions they ask for (actions).

Concepts explains rules, facts and results in more detail.

docs.title: Using an engine
docs.text:
evaluate() is handy for a quick check. When you evaluate many facts against the same rules, load the rules into an engine once and reuse it:

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, Rule

rule = Rule(
    id=1,
    name="high_value_transaction",
    domain="fraud_detection",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="manual_review",
    priority=100,
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000})
print(f"Matched rules: {result.fired_rules}")
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")

Output: 

Matched rules: [1]
Actions: ['manual_review']

This rule uses three more options:

  • id gives the rule a fixed id. Without it, FluxRules numbers rules in the order you create them, counting across your whole program. This page sets ids so the printed output stays the same however you run the examples.
  • domain names the problem area the rule belongs to. You can use it to load or filter a group of rules. See Domains and Tags.
  • priority sets the order in which matching rules fire. A higher number fires first. Every matching rule still fires; priority only sets the order.

docs.title: Combining checks with AND, OR and NOT
docs.text:
A condition can combine several checks:

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, Rule

rule = Rule(
    id=1,
    name="risky_payment",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        & ((F("country").isin(["NG", "SN"])) | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70))
        & ~(F("verified_user") == True)
    ),
    action="block_payment",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "country": "NG", "verified_user": False})
print(result.fired_rules)  # [1]

& means both sides must hold, | means either side is enough, and ~ means the check must not hold. Wrap each comparison in parentheses, because &, | and ~ bind more tightly than > and == in Python. Complex Conditions covers nesting in depth.

docs.title: Several rules at once
docs.text:
Pass a list to load_rules. Each fact is checked against every rule:

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, Rule

rules = [
    Rule(id=1, name="high_value", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="manual_review"),
    Rule(
        id=2,
        name="high_risk_country",
        conditions=F("country").isin(["NG", "SN"]),
        action="block_payment",
    ),
]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "country": "NG"})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")  # [2] (high_risk_country)
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")      # ['block_payment']

Only the second rule matches, because the amount is not over 5000.

docs.title: HTTP API Reference
docs.text:
Prerequisites: HTTP API (starting the server).

This page lists the main endpoints of the FluxRules server, with the request and response of each. The server needs the api extra (pip install "fluxrules[api]"). Start it with fluxrules serve.

The full, always current list is generated by the server itself: open http://localhost:8000/docs while it runs.

docs.title: Endpoints at a glance
docs.text:
Method Path Purpose GET /health Health check POST /api/v1/auth/token Log in and get a token POST /api/v1/rules Store a rule GET /api/v1/rules List stored rules POST /api/v1/evaluate Evaluate one fact against stored rules POST /api/v1/evaluate/bulk Evaluate several facts GET /api/v1/explain/{execution_id} Look up an earlier evaluation POST /api/v1/rules/simulate Dry run with explanations POST /validate Check a rule set without storing it POST /api/v1/sessions Create a session that stores facts POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/evaluate Evaluate each fact stored in a session POST /api/v1/engines/evaluate Evaluate a fact, with an explanation per matched rule

Each one is described in full below.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• Requests and responses are JSON (Content-Type: application/json), except the login form below.
  • Rules are stored in the server's database. Add them with POST /api/v1/rules before you evaluate anything.
  • A matched rule is reported by its id in a list called matched_rules. (The Python API calls the same list fired_rules.)
  • Endpoints marked (login) need a token in the Authorization header.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
Create a user once, then ask for a token:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/auth/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "password": "Str0ng-Passw0rd!"}'

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/auth/token \
  -d "username=alice&password=Str0ng-Passw0rd!"

The token endpoint takes a form (username=...&password=...), not JSON. It answers with:

{"access_token": "eyJhbGciOi...", "token_type": "bearer", "role": "business"}

Send the token with every request marked (login):

curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/rules -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi..."

docs.title: POST /api/v1/rules (login)
docs.text:
Store a new rule.

Request: 

{
  "name": "big_payment",
  "group": "payments",
  "priority": 10,
  "action": "review",
  "conditions": {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 1000}
}

  • name, conditions and action are required.
  • group collects rules into a rule set. Evaluate one group with ruleset_id (see below).
  • priority orders the matches: higher numbers come first. It defaults to 0.
  • conditions uses the condition format described in Conditions.
  • evaluation_mode ("stateless" by default) is stored and returned as a label only. No evaluation reads it: a rule marked "stateful" is evaluated like any other.

Response: the stored rule, with its new id, a current_version of 1 and timestamps.

Before storing it, the server checks the new rule against the rules already in its group. If it finds a conflict, such as the same name or the same priority, it answers 400 with the list of conflicts and keeps the rule aside for review instead of storing it. Add ?skip_conflict_check=true to store it anyway. POST /api/v1/rules/validate runs the same check without storing anything. See Rule Analysis.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/rules (login)
docs.text: List the stored rules.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/evaluate (login)
docs.text:
Evaluate one fact against the stored rules.

Request: 

{
  "facts": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"},
  "ruleset_id": "payments"
}

  • facts is the fact to evaluate. Required.
  • ruleset_id is optional. It limits the evaluation to the rules of that group. Without it, all stored rules are used.
  • rule_ids is optional. It limits the evaluation to those rule ids, such as [1, 4].

Response: 

{
  "execution_id": "8ac723da-c93d-40ec-809c-64a244003e9e",
  "ruleset_group": "payments",
  "matched_rules": [1, 2],
  "actions": ["review", "add_vat"],
  "facts": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}
}

  • matched_rules: the ids of the rules that matched, highest priority first.
  • actions: their actions, in the same order. The server does not run them; the caller does.
  • execution_id: an id for this evaluation. Use it with GET /api/v1/explain/{execution_id}.
  • ruleset_group: the ruleset_id you sent, or "all".

docs.title: POST /api/v1/evaluate/bulk (login)
docs.text:
Evaluate several facts against the same rules in one request.

Request: 

{
  "facts": [
    {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"},
    {"amount": 50, "country": "US"}
  ],
  "ruleset_id": "payments"
}

facts is a list here. ruleset_id and rule_ids work as for a single fact.

Response: 

{
  "count": 2,
  "ruleset_group": "payments",
  "results": [
    {"index": 0, "execution_id": "1105cdb5-...", "matched_rules": [1, 2], "actions": ["review", "add_vat"]},
    {"index": 1, "execution_id": "9c24bea9-...", "matched_rules": [], "actions": []}
  ]
}

results has one entry per fact, in the order you sent them. index is the position of the fact in your list.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/explain/{execution_id} (login)
docs.text:
Look up an earlier evaluation by its execution_id. The response has the same fields as POST /api/v1/evaluate, including the facts that were evaluated. An unknown id answers 404.

The server keeps only the most recent records: 10,000 by default, set by the EXPLAIN_STORE_MAX_RECORDS environment variable (0 keeps none). An older execution_id answers 404. The records live in the server's memory, so they are lost when it restarts, and with several server processes each one has its own.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/rules/simulate (login)
docs.text:
Evaluate a fact as a dry run and get an explanation for each matched rule.

Request: 

{
  "event": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"},
  "rule_ids": [1, 2]
}

event is the fact. rule_ids is optional and limits the run to those rules.

Response: 

{
  "matched_rules": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "big_payment", "priority": 10},
    {"id": 2, "name": "german_payment", "priority": 0}
  ],
  "execution_order": [1, 2],
  "explanations": {
    "1": "Rule big_payment (1) matched via PHREAK (segments: seg_amount, seg_country)",
    "2": "Rule german_payment (2) matched via PHREAK (segments: seg_amount, seg_country)"
  },
  "dry_run": true,
  "stats": {
    "total_rules": null,
    "candidates_evaluated": 2,
    "rules_matched": 2,
    "evaluation_time_ms": 0.41,
    "optimization": null
  }
}

  • matched_rules: each matched rule's id, name and priority, in the order they fired. execution_order lists the same ids.
  • explanations: why each rule matched.
  • stats: how many rules the engine looked at closely after filtering (candidates_evaluated), how many matched (rules_matched), and how long it took in milliseconds (evaluation_time_ms). total_rules and optimization are not filled in.

docs.title: Engine endpoints
docs.text: These endpoints under /api/v1/engines need no login.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/engines/evaluate
docs.text:
Evaluate a fact against the stored rules and get an explanation for each matched rule.

Request: 

{"event": {"amount": 4200, "country": "DE"}, "rule_ids": [1, 2]}

  • event is the fact. Required.
  • rule_ids is optional and limits the run to those rules.
  • engine_type is optional. "PHREAK", the only engine, is the default; any other name answers 400.

Response: 

{
  "matched_rules": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "big_payment", "priority": 10},
    {"id": 2, "name": "german_payment", "priority": 0}
  ],
  "execution_order": [1, 2],
  "explanations": {
    "1": "Rule big_payment (1) matched via PHREAK (segments: seg_amount, seg_country)",
    "2": "Rule german_payment (2) matched via PHREAK (segments: seg_amount, seg_country)"
  },
  "stats": {"latency_ms": 1.68, "rules_evaluated": 2, "rules_matched": 2},
  "engine_type": "PHREAK",
  "dry_run": false
}

The fields are the same as for POST /api/v1/rules/simulate, except for the names in stats: rules_evaluated is the number of rules the engine looked at closely after filtering, and latency_ms is the time taken.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/engines/simulate
docs.text: The same request and response as /api/v1/engines/evaluate, with "dry_run": true. Neither endpoint runs actions or changes anything, so the two give the same answers.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/engines/config and GET /api/v1/engines/available
docs.text: Report the engine in use and the engines available (only "PHREAK"), with a short description of each.

docs.title: Endpoints that are not finished
docs.text:
These endpoints answer, but do not yet do what their names say:

  • POST /api/v1/engines/switch and POST /api/v1/engines/reload check the engine name and answer "status": "success", but change nothing on the server. Without Redis, rules stored with /api/v1/rules are used from the next request on. With Redis, these engine endpoints (and /api/v1/rules/simulate) read the rule list from a Redis cache that lasts up to 5 minutes, so a new or changed rule can take that long to appear there. /api/v1/evaluate always reads the stored rules directly.
  • POST /api/v1/engines/benchmark times a new engine with no rules loaded on generated events, so it does not measure your rules.
  • GET /api/v1/engines/stats reports a new engine with no rules loaded, so rules_loaded is always 0.

docs.title: POST /validate
docs.text:
Check a rule set for problems without storing it. No login needed.

Request: 

{
  "ruleset": {
    "group": "payments",
    "rules": [
      {
        "id": 1,
        "name": "big_payment",
        "conditions": {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 1000}
      }
    ]
  }
}

Response: 

{"issues": []}

issues lists each problem as a sentence, such as "Ruleset is empty". An empty list means the rule set is fine. A condition the server cannot read at all, such as an unknown operator, answers 422 instead (see Errors).

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Sessions store facts on the server under a session id, so you can collect facts over several requests and evaluate them later. A session holds at most 100 facts and is visible only to the user who created it.

Sessions live in the memory of one server process. They are lost when the server restarts, and if you run several server processes, each one has its own sessions: send all requests for a session to the same process.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/sessions (login)
docs.text:
Create a session.

Request: 

{"metadata": {"channel": "web"}}

Both fields are optional. metadata is any data you want to keep with the session. session_id lets you choose the id yourself; otherwise the server makes one.

Response (201): 

{
  "id": "a43cdf91-61f3-41ac-a55d-526d6e806ab6",
  "user_id": 1,
  "metadata": {"channel": "web"},
  "fact_count": 0,
  "created_at": "2026-10-31T23:19:46.484674Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-31T23:19:46.484674Z"
}

docs.title: POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/facts (login)
docs.text:
Add a fact to a session.

Request: 

{"fact_id": "txn_123", "fact": {"amount": 5000}}

fact is the fact. fact_id is optional; sending the same fact_id again replaces that fact.

docs.title: POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/evaluate (login)
docs.text:
Evaluate every fact stored in the session against the stored rules. Each fact is evaluated on its own, and you get one result per fact. Facts are never combined, so two transactions with the same fields each get their own answer.

Request (optional; send no body to use all stored rules): 

{"ruleset_id": "payments"}

ruleset_id and rule_ids work as for POST /api/v1/evaluate.

Response: 

{
  "session_id": "a43cdf91-61f3-41ac-a55d-526d6e806ab6",
  "count": 2,
  "ruleset_group": "payments",
  "results": [
    {"index": 0, "fact_id": "txn_1", "execution_id": "1105cdb5-...", "matched_rules": [1, 2], "actions": ["review", "add_vat"]},
    {"index": 1, "fact_id": "txn_2", "execution_id": "9c24bea9-...", "matched_rules": [], "actions": []}
  ]
}

  • results are in the order the facts were first added. Replacing a fact (sending the same fact_id again) keeps its place.
  • fact_id says which stored fact each result belongs to.
  • Each execution_id works with GET /api/v1/explain/{execution_id}.

The answers are the same as sending the facts to POST /api/v1/evaluate/bulk. Evaluating only reads the session: its facts stay as they were.

Also available: GET /api/v1/sessions/{id} and GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/facts to read a session back, DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{id}/facts/{fact_id} to remove one fact, and DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{id} to remove the session.

docs.title: GET /health
docs.text: Answers {"status": "healthy"} while the server runs. No login needed.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/system/status
docs.text:
The version and the state of each part of the server. No login needed.

{
  "status": "running",
  "version": "1.1.2",
  "engine": "fluxrules",
  "healthy": true,
  "components": {
    "queue": {"healthy": true, "message": "Queue not configured (embedded mode)"},
    "cache": {"healthy": true, "message": "Cache not configured (embedded mode)"},
    "persistence": {"healthy": true, "message": "Persistence is healthy"}
  }
}

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Most errors use FastAPI's format, with the reason under detail:

{"detail": "Execution 'abc' not found"}

A request whose body has the wrong shape answers 422, and detail lists each problem with its location:

{
  "detail": [
    {"type": "missing", "loc": ["body", "facts"], "msg": "Field required", "input": {"fact": {}}}
  ]
}

Errors raised by the rule engine itself use an error code and a message:

{"error": "DSL_PARSE_ERROR", "message": "..."}

Status codes you will see:

  • 400: the request was understood but refused, for example a rule conflict.
  • 401: the token is missing, wrong or expired.
  • 404: the rule, session or execution does not exist.
  • 422: the request body has the wrong shape.
  • 500 or 503: a problem on the server, such as the database being unavailable.

docs.title: Rule Analysis
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule).

Analyze rules for coverage, conflicts, and dead rules.

docs.title: Rule coverage
docs.text:
Check which rules are actually firing:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule1 = Rule(name="rule1", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="allow")
rule2 = Rule(name="rule2", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag")
rules = [rule1, rule2]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Track rule matches across facts
coverage = {}
facts = [{"status": "active", "amount": 3000}, {"status": "active", "amount": 6000}]
for fact in facts:
    result = engine.evaluate(fact)
    for rule_id in result.fired_rules:
        coverage[rule_id] = coverage.get(rule_id, 0) + 1

# Find unused rules
all_rule_ids = set(r.name for r in rules)
covered_ids = set(coverage.keys())
unused = all_rule_ids - covered_ids
print(f"Unused rules: {unused}")

docs.title: Conflict detection
docs.text:
Rules may fire for the same fact:

result = engine.evaluate(fact)

if len(result.fired_rules) > 1:
    print(f"Multiple rules matched: {result.fired_rules}")
    # May indicate conflicting logic

docs.title: Dead rule detection
docs.text:
Rules that never fire under any condition:

from fluxrules import Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Setup rules and engine
rules = [
    Rule(name="rule1", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="allow"),
    Rule(name="rule2", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag"),
]
engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Evaluate against diverse fact set
comprehensive_facts = [
    {"status": "active", "amount": 3000},
    {"status": "inactive", "amount": 6000},
    {"status": "active", "amount": 10000},
]

coverage = {}
for fact in comprehensive_facts:
    result = engine.evaluate(fact)
    for rule_id in result.fired_rules:
        coverage[rule_id] = True

# Dead rules
all_ids = set(r.name for r in rules)
dead = [r for r in rules if r.name not in coverage]

print(f"Dead rules: {[r.name for r in dead]}")

  • Rule Lifecycle: See Rule Lifecycle for rule management

docs.title: Rule Builder
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule), Authoring Rules and Conditions (condition tree).

RuleBuilder is a fluent API for constructing rules step by step. It validates as you go and build() returns the same canonical Rule every other authoring path produces, so the result goes straight into an engine with no conversion.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
.condition() accepts an F expression or a raw dict; both compile to the same condition tree.

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, RuleBuilder

rule = (
    RuleBuilder()
    .name("high_value_transaction")
    .group("fraud_detection")
    .tag("tier_1", "manual_review")
    .priority(10)
    .condition(F("amount") > 5000)
    .action("require_approval")
    .build()
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500})
print(f"Fired: {result.fired_rules}")

build() returns a Rule, so it also works with the top-level evaluate():

from fluxrules import F, RuleBuilder, evaluate

rule = (
    RuleBuilder()
    .name("adult")
    .condition(F("age") >= 18)
    .action("allow")
    .build()
)

print(evaluate(rule, {"age": 30}).fired_rules)

docs.title: Fluent API
docs.text:
Method Purpose Returns .name(str) Set rule name (required) Builder .condition(F(...) or dict) Set the condition tree from an F expression or a raw dict (required) Builder .action(str) Append an action; call repeatedly for several Builder .priority(int) Set priority, higher evaluates first Builder .group(str) Set the group/domain Builder .description(str) Set a human-readable description Builder .tag(*str) Add tags Builder .enabled(bool) Set the enabled flag Builder .persist(bool) Store the built rule in the database Builder .status(RuleStatus) Set lifecycle status Builder .created_by(str) Record the author Builder .build() Create the rule Rule .build_engine_rule() Create the internal representation EngineRule .to_dict() Create the canonical rule mapping dict

RuleBuilder() generates an ID automatically; pass one explicitly with RuleBuilder(42) when you need a specific ID.

docs.title: Multiple actions
docs.text:
Call .action() once per action. They fire in the order added.

from fluxrules import F, RuleBuilder, evaluate

rule = (
    RuleBuilder()
    .name("escalate")
    .condition(F("risk") > 90)
    .action("notify_compliance")
    .action("freeze_account")
    .build()
)

result = evaluate(rule, {"risk": 95})
print(result.actions)

docs.title: Building complex conditions
docs.text:
Compose conditions with &, |, and ~ directly on F expressions:

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, RuleBuilder

rule = (
    RuleBuilder()
    .name("complex_rule")
    .condition(
        (F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").isin(["NG", "GH"]))
    )
    .action("review")
    .build()
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])
print(f"Fired: {engine.evaluate({'amount': 6000, 'country': 'NG'}).fired_rules}")

ConditionBuilder is still available for dict-based composition but is superseded by the F DSL for new code.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The builder fails at the point of the mistake rather than at evaluation time. .condition() parses the condition tree immediately, and .build() enforces that the required fields are present.

from fluxrules import F, RuleBuilder
from fluxrules.exceptions import RuleValidationError

try:
    RuleBuilder().condition(F("x") > 1).build()
except RuleValidationError as e:
    print(f"Invalid rule: {e}")

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Building a rule performs no I/O. Pass .persist(True) to store it as it is built, or call Rule.save() later:

# python skip
rule = RuleBuilder().name("r").condition(dsl).action("a").persist(True).build()

# equivalently, decide after the fact:
rule = RuleBuilder().name("r").condition(dsl).action("a").build()
rule.save()

docs.title: Rule Lifecycle
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule) and Persistence (database).

A rule's lifecycle consists of: Create → Load → Validate → Evaluate → Delete.

docs.title: Create a rule
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule = Rule(
    name="high_value_transaction",
    domain="fraud_detection",
    tags=frozenset(["tier_1", "manual_review"]),
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="require_approval",
    priority=10,
    persist=True,  # Enable database persistence
)

print(f"Rule created: {rule.name} (ID: {rule.id})")

Core Rule fields:

Field Type Required Purpose name str Yes Descriptive rule name domain str No Logical grouping (default: "default") tags frozenset[str] No Searchable keywords conditions dict Yes Rule logic (condition tree format) action str \| tuple[str, ...] No Action when rule fires priority int No Evaluation priority (higher first) persist bool No Store in database (default: False)

docs.title: From Python code (temporary)
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule

rules = [
    Rule(
        name="rule1",
        conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
        action="act1",
        persist=False,
    ),
    Rule(
        name="rule2",
        conditions=F("country") == "US",
        action="act2",
        persist=False,
    ),
]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

docs.title: From database (persistent)
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
loaded_rules = service.load_ruleset(ruleset_id=1)

docs.title: From YAML file
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.adapters.loaders import load_rules_from_yaml

rules_dicts = load_rules_from_yaml("rules.yaml")
rules = [Rule(**r) for r in rules_dicts]

docs.title: Validate a rule
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F
from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import validate_conditions, ConditionValidationError

# Validate condition tree syntax before creating a rule
dsl = (F("amount") > 5000).to_dict()

try:
    validate_conditions(dsl)
    print("Conditions are valid")
except ConditionValidationError as e:
    print(f"Invalid conditions: {e}")

Invalid DSLs raise ConditionValidationError. See Validation Framework for details.

docs.title: Evaluate rules
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Single evaluation
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500, "country": "US"})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")

# Multiple evaluations
facts_list = [{"amount": 7500, "country": "US"}, {"amount": 100, "country": "CA"}]
for fact in facts_list:
    result = engine.evaluate(fact)
    # Process result...

docs.title: From database
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
service.delete_rule(rule_id=1)

Deleted rules are removed from the database. In-memory rules loaded via engine.load_rules() must be reloaded.

docs.title: From memory
docs.text:
In-memory rules (rules loaded via code, not persisted) cannot be deleted after loading. Create a new engine instance and reload without the unwanted rule:

# Original engine
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Create a new engine with only the first rule
new_engine = PhreakEngine()
new_engine.load_rules([rules[0]])

docs.title: Rule state
docs.text:
Rules are immutable once created. To change a rule, create a new Rule with the updated fields:

# python skip
# Original rule
from fluxrules import F

old_rule = Rule(
    name="check_amount",
    conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
    action="flag",
    persist=True,
)

# Updated rule (new instance)
new_rule = Rule(
    name="check_amount",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="flag",
    persist=True,
)

# Delete old, persist new
service.delete_rule(old_rule.id)
service.persist(Ruleset(group="default", rules=(new_rule.to_engine_rule(),)))

docs.title: Rule Types
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts.

This page explains the boundary between the public Rule authoring type and the internal EngineRule representation. Condition syntax belongs to Conditions, and engine-mode selection belongs to Choosing an Engine.

docs.title: Public Rule
docs.text:
Rule is the public type for authoring and serialization. Its conditions tree is the source of truth for boolean logic. Set persist=False in examples and tests to avoid writing to the configured database.

from fluxrules import F, Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="adult",
    conditions=F("age") >= 18,
    actions=("allow", "audit"),
    persist=False,
)

assert rule.action == "allow"  # compatibility view of actions[0]
assert rule.actions == ("allow", "audit")

See Concepts and the Pydantic Rule Guide for the complete field reference.

docs.title: RuleBuilder
docs.text:
RuleBuilder is a fluent adapter for workflows that assemble a rule incrementally. Its build() method returns the public Rule, so a built rule needs no conversion before evaluation. Use build_engine_rule() when an internal boundary needs the EngineRule shape instead.

from fluxrules import F, RuleBuilder

rule = (
    RuleBuilder(rule_id=1)
    .name("High Value Transaction")
    .group("fraud_detection")
    .priority(10)
    .condition(F("amount") > 10000)
    .action("flag_for_review")
    .build()
)

assert rule.conditions["type"] == "condition"
assert rule.domain == "fraud_detection"

engine_rule = RuleBuilder(rule_id=2).name("internal").condition(
    F("amount") > 1
).action("flag").build_engine_rule()
assert engine_rule.conditions["type"] == "condition"

Implementation: src/fluxrules/domain/rule_builder.py.

docs.title: Internal EngineRule
docs.text:
EngineRule is immutable and is used by the reference evaluator, persistence adapters, and internal services. Its authoritative logic is always the full conditions tree. Its .conditions member is a derived flat leaf view for compatibility; it cannot preserve OR, NOT, or nesting and must not be used to rebuild rule logic.

Convert explicitly at an internal integration boundary:

from fluxrules import F, Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="adult",
    conditions=F("age") >= 18,
    action="allow",
    persist=False,
)

engine_rule = rule.to_engine_rule()
round_tripped = Rule.from_engine_rule(engine_rule, persist=False)

assert round_tripped.conditions == rule.conditions

Implementation: src/fluxrules/domain/models.py; conversion methods: src/fluxrules/domain/unified_rule.py.

docs.title: Engine Input Contracts
docs.text:
API Accepted input Output or behavior PhreakEngine.load_rules(rules) Public Rule objects or rule dictionaries Loads rules for stateless or streaming PHREAK evaluation ReferenceEvaluator.evaluate(ruleset, facts) A Ruleset containing EngineRule objects Returns EvaluationResult with fired_rules and ordered actions fluxrules.evaluate(rules, facts) A Rule, an iterable of rules, or a Ruleset Returns EvaluationResult with fired_rules and ordered actions Rule.to_engine_rule() One public Rule Produces the immutable internal representation Rule.from_engine_rule(engine_rule) One EngineRule Produces a public Rule; persistence is disabled by default

For normal application code, create Rule objects and pass them to PhreakEngine.load_rules(). Use EngineRule and ReferenceEvaluator at internal adapter, persistence, or parity-test boundaries.
