docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Prerequisites: API and Deployment.

Security considerations for running FluxRules in production.

docs.title: Authentication (API)
docs.text:
By default, the API has no authentication. Add it for production:

# python skip
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer

app = FastAPI()
security = HTTPBearer()


@app.post("/api/v1/evaluate")
async def evaluate(request: EvaluateRequest, credentials=Depends(security)):
    """Endpoint requiring valid bearer token."""
    token = credentials.credentials
    if not validate_token(token):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)

    # Proceed with evaluation
    return engine.evaluate(request.facts)

For production, use OAuth2 or API keys via a gateway (nginx, AWS API Gateway, etc.).

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
All facts are validated before evaluation:

# python skip
from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import validate_conditions, ConditionValidationError
from fastapi import HTTPException

# Validate rule conditions before accepting from API
try:
    validate_conditions(rule.conditions)
except ConditionValidationError as e:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=str(e))

docs.title: Database security
docs.text:
If using persistence, secure the database:

# Use SSL for database connections
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://user:pass@db.example.com/fluxrules?sslmode=require"

# Restrict database access to app instances only
# Use VPC/security groups to isolate database

docs.title: Audit logging
docs.text:
Track all rule changes and evaluations:

# Enable audit trail (requires [sql])
from fluxrules.initialization import initialize_persistence

initialize_persistence(env="prod")  # Enables audit logging

Check audit logs:

# Via REST API (if available)
curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/audit?limit=100

docs.title: Secrets management
docs.text:
Use environment variables for secrets, never hardcode:

import os

db_url = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL")  # From environment
api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")  # From secret store

# Never do this:
# db_url = "postgresql://user:password@db.example.com/db"

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: A short, honest model of the surfaces an operator is responsible for. FluxRules is a library plus an optional HTTP service; most controls are the operator's to apply.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text: Boundary Who is trusted Primary risk Rule authors Whoever can create/modify rules A malicious or buggy rule can match/act incorrectly; custom operators/actions/engines run arbitrary Python in-process Fact producers Callers of evaluate() / the HTTP API Malformed or oversized facts; injection into downstream actions HTTP clients API consumers Unauthenticated access, DoS via large payloads/rulesets Persistence The database Tampered rules loaded from storage; connection credentials

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
• Rule definitions and their execution results/audit trail.
  • The evaluation process (availability and correctness).
  • Persistence credentials and the API SECRET_KEY.

docs.title: Threats and mitigations
docs.text: Threat Mitigation in FluxRules Operator responsibility Arbitrary code via custom operators/actions/engines Extension registration is explicit; entry-point discovery is opt-in (never an import side effect) Only load trusted plugins; review load_plugins() sources Malicious rule conditions validate_conditions / ValidationService reject malformed logic; the engine evaluates data, not eval Validate rules at the API boundary before persisting SQL injection ORM + parameterized queries; internal DDL uses constant table names (bandit/ruff-gated) Use least-privilege DB accounts Unauthenticated API access Auth primitives shipped (bcrypt, PyJWT) Enforce auth + network restrictions (no auth by default) Tampered stored rules Audit trail with integrity hashing Restrict who can write to the rule store Supply-chain compromise Pinned dev tooling, Dependabot, CI security job (bandit + pip-audit), signed releases + SBOM Verify release signatures/SBOM before deploying Denial of service Working-memory high-water mark; bounded evaluation Rate-limit and size-limit inputs at the gateway

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: FluxRules does not sandbox custom Python extensions, does not provide authentication middleware by default, and does not manage secrets. These are delegated to the deployment environment and the guidance above.

docs.title: Dependency advisory status
docs.text:
The API extra was installed non-editably in a clean Python 3.11 environment and audited with pip-audit on 2026-09-30. The audit found no known vulnerabilities in its resolved dependencies (FastAPI 0.142.2, Starlette 1.7.0, and PyJWT 2.15.1). The API now uses PyJWT rather than python-jose, removing the ECDSA dependency path. The Starlette lower bound excludes the versions identified by the current audit advisories.

Starlette 1.x represents included routers lazily, so app.routes is no longer a flat inventory of endpoint routes. FluxRules verifies the stable API contract through OpenAPI paths/methods and integration tests rather than Starlette's internal route representation. CI separately audits a fresh non-editable install of the api extra; the core package still does not install the API/web dependencies by default.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Working Memory (fact accumulation) and Concepts (Rule, Engine).

Sessions provide stateful, multi-step evaluation with snapshot support. Use sessions when you need to:

  1. Accumulate facts across multiple steps
  2. Save/restore state for recovery
  3. Isolate rule evaluation in separate execution contexts

docs.title: Creating and using a session
docs.text:
Create a session via RuleService, then accumulate facts and evaluate:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.domain.models import Ruleset
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()

# Build rules and register them as a named ruleset
rules = [
    Rule(
        id=1,
        name="verify_kyc",
        conditions=F("kyc_status") == "verified",
        action="proceed_to_payment",
    ),
    Rule(
        id=2,
        name="check_amount",
        conditions=F("amount") > 10000,
        action="require_approval",
    ),
]
ruleset = Ruleset(
    group="order_rules",
    rules=tuple(r.to_engine_rule(group="order_rules") for r in rules),
)
service.persist(ruleset)

# Create a session bound to that ruleset and accumulate facts
session = service.create_session("order_rules")
session.add_fact("kyc_status", "verified")
session.add_fact("amount", 15000)
result = session.evaluate()
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")  # actions whose rules matched
assert sorted(result.fired_rules) == [1, 2]

Key point: Sessions accumulate facts. You evaluate once against all accumulated facts, not after each add_fact().

docs.title: Session lifecycle
docs.text:
A session has these phases:

  1. Create: service.create_session(ruleset_id) initializes an empty session bound to that ruleset
  2. Accumulate: add_fact(), add_facts(), remove_fact(), clear_facts()
  3. Evaluate: evaluate() matches rules against accumulated facts
  4. Save: save() exports to JSON snapshot
  5. Restore: EvaluationSession.restore(json, service) reconstructs from snapshot

Evaluations are independent: each evaluate() is stateless. The session remembers facts but not evaluation history.

# Multiple evaluations with different facts
session.add_fact("amount", 500)
result1 = session.evaluate()
assert result1.fired_rules == [1]  # only the KYC rule

session.add_fact("amount", 50000)  # add_fact replaces the old value
result2 = session.evaluate()
assert sorted(result2.fired_rules) == [1, 2]  # different result due to the updated fact

docs.title: Snapshot: save and restore
docs.text:
Serialize a session to JSON for checkpointing or recovery:

from fluxrules.services.session import EvaluationSession

# Checkpoint current state
snapshot = session.save()  # Returns JSON string

# Later: restore in a new process/thread
restored = EvaluationSession.restore(snapshot, service)
result = restored.evaluate()

# The restored session has the same facts and metadata
print(restored.facts)  # Same as original session
assert restored.facts == session.facts

Snapshots include: - execution_id: unique session identifier - facts: all accumulated fact key-value pairs - timestamp: when the snapshot was created - metadata: optional custom data (application-specific)

Use snapshots to: - Pause workflows: save after step 1, restore in step 2 - Recover failures: restart from a known state - Audit trail: keep JSON copies of evaluation context

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
Each session is isolated. Facts in one session do not affect another:

# Each session is independent: same ruleset, different fact sets
session1 = service.create_session("order_rules")
session1.add_fact("amount", 20000)

session2 = service.create_session("order_rules")
session2.add_fact("amount", 100)

result1 = session1.evaluate()  # Evaluates with 20000
result2 = session2.evaluate()  # Evaluates with 100
# No cross-contamination
assert (result1.fired_rules, result2.fired_rules) == ([2], [])

Use sessions to evaluate the same ruleset independently for different users, transactions, or workflows.

docs.title: Sessions over HTTP
docs.text:
The HTTP API has its own sessions, under /api/v1/sessions. They work differently from the Python sessions on this page:

  • Python session: each add_fact(key, value) adds one field to a single fact, and evaluate() checks that one fact.
  • HTTP session: each POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/facts stores a whole fact under a fact_id, and POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/evaluate evaluates every stored fact on its own, returning one result per fact.

See HTTP API Reference: Sessions.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Prerequisites: API and Deployment.

Common issues and solutions.

docs.title: API server won't start
docs.text:
Problem: Address already in use or connection refused.

Solution: 

# Check if port 8000 is in use
lsof -i :8000

# Use a different port
python -m fluxrules.api.app --port 8001

docs.title: Rules not matching
docs.text:
Problem: Expected rule matches, but fired_rules is empty.

Solutions: 1. Validate condition tree syntax: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/validate \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"conditions": {...}}'

  1. Check fact format: Ensure fact keys match condition field names 
    # python skip
   from fluxrules import F, Rule

   # Rule expects "amount" field
   rule = Rule(
       conditions=F("amount") > 5000
   )

   # Fact must have "amount"
   result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500})  # matches
   result = engine.evaluate({"value": 7500})   # does not match
   ```

   If the fact carries the field in another case (`amount` for a rule on
   `Amount`), evaluation raises `FieldNotFoundError` naming the key it found.
   Another key style (`user_age` for a rule on `userAge`) raises only when the
   engine has a [fact schema](typed-facts.md); without one the rule just does
   not match. Rename the rule field, or declare a fact schema with
   `lenient_aliases()` and `validate_facts="normalize"` so incoming keys are
   renamed for you.

3. **Check operator:** Verify operator spelling and case
   - Valid: `"=="`, `"!="`, `">"`, `"<"`, `"in"`, `"contains"`

## A NOT rule fires unexpectedly, or warns `MissingFieldNotWarning`

**Problem:** A rule such as `~(F("blocked") == True)` fires for facts that do
not carry `blocked` at all, and a `MissingFieldNotWarning` is logged.

**Cause:** A missing field makes its condition `False`, so `NOT` over it is
`True`. From 2.0 such a `NOT` will not fire.

**Solutions:**
- Opt in to the 2.0 behaviour now: `EngineConfig(missing_field="unknown")`.
- If firing on absence is intended, say so with `~F("blocked").exists() | ~(F("blocked") == True)`
  and set `missing_field="false"` to silence the warning.

See [Missing fields and NOT](conditions.md#missing-fields-and-not).

## `UnknownFieldError` from `load_rules`

**Problem:** `load_rules` raises `UnknownFieldError: Rule '...' references unknown field ...`.

**Cause:** The engine was built with `fact_schema=Model` and a rule names a
field the model does not have. Nothing was loaded.

**Solution:** Fix the rule field (the message suggests the closest name), or
add the field to the model. Nested models are addressed with dotted paths
(`customer.age`).

## High latency

**Problem:** Evaluations are slow.

**Solutions:**
1. **Filter rules by domain/tags:** Evaluate only the rules that apply to the fact
2. **Profile with latency_ms:** Check the returned latency
3. **Reduce rule complexity:** Simpler conditions evaluate faster

## Memory leaks

**Problem:** Memory usage keeps growing.

**Solutions:**
1. **Use PHREAK (default):** Lower memory footprint
2. **Check working_memory:** If asserting many facts, retract old ones
   ```python
   fact_id = engine.assert_fact(fact)
   # Later
   engine.retract_fact(fact_id)
   ```

## Database connection errors

**Problem:** `connection refused` or `database unavailable`.

**Solutions:**
```bash
# Check connection string
echo $DATABASE_URL

# Test database connectivity
psql -h db.example.com -U user -d fluxrules -c "SELECT 1"

# Use fallback (in-memory mode)
export FLUXRULES_FALLBACK_MODE=true

docs.title: Typed Facts
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Fact) and Conditions.

Facts reach the engine as a flat dict. When your facts already have a shape, for example a Pydantic model behind an API, you can hand that shape to FluxRules and get three things in return:

  1. Pass models straight in. engine.evaluate(order) works for Pydantic models, dataclasses, attrs classes and msgspec structs.
  2. Rules checked against the model. With fact_schema=Order, load_rules refuses a rule that names a field Order does not have. This costs nothing per fact.
  3. Incoming keys normalized (opt-in). With validate_facts="normalize", each dict is validated by Pydantic, so userAge, UserAge and user-age all arrive as user_age, and "42" arrives as 42.

Everything is opt-in. Engines without a fact_schema behave as before, and plain dicts stay the fastest input.

No model for your facts, or need enrichment and composed stages? Use a fact pipeline instead, or alongside via fact_pipeline=.

What a schema can and cannot promise

A schema guarantees that rules agree with the model: that is checked completely when rules load. It cannot guarantee that incoming data agrees with the model, because an upstream service can still rename a key or send "abc" for a number. What it does guarantee is that such a mismatch is never silent: it fails at load_rules, or at evaluate under the policy you choose with on_invalid.

docs.title: Pass a model to the engine
docs.text:
Nested models become dotted keys, the same shape the Flatten transform produces. Keys are the Python field names, not aliases, because rules use field names.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

from fluxrules import F, Rule, to_fact_dict
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine
from fluxrules.facts import lenient_aliases


class Customer(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=lenient_aliases())

    user_age: int
    country: str = "US"
    blocked: bool | None = None


class Order(BaseModel):
    amount: float
    customer: Customer


order = Order(amount=250, customer=Customer(user_age=30))
assert to_fact_dict(order) == {
    "amount": 250.0,
    "customer.user_age": 30,
    "customer.country": "US",
    "customer.blocked": None,
}

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(
    [Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("customer.user_age") >= 18, action="allow")]
)
assert engine.evaluate(order).fired_rules == [1]

fluxrules.evaluate(rules, facts) accepts the same inputs.

docs.title: Check rules against a schema
docs.text:
Give the engine the model as fact_schema. Every field each rule references, including exists() fields, is checked once when the rules load. A rule naming an unknown field raises UnknownFieldError with a suggestion, and nothing from that load_rules call is loaded:

from fluxrules import UnknownFieldError

checked = PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Order)

try:
    checked.load_rules(
        [Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("customer.userAge") >= 18, action="allow")]
    )
except UnknownFieldError as exc:
    print(exc)
    # Rule 'adult' references unknown field 'customer.userAge' (not in fact
    # schema Order). Did you mean 'customer.user_age'? Known fields: [...]

checked.load_rules(
    [Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("customer.user_age") >= 18, action="allow")]
)

fact_schema accepts a Pydantic model, dataclass, attrs class, msgspec Struct or TypedDict. One engine checks against one schema, so keep rules for different fact shapes in different engines.

How the check reads the model:

  • A nested model is flattened into its fields, so rules name those fields (customer.user_age). The model itself is not a field: a rule on customer is refused with a hint, because a fact never has a customer key. To test whether a nested model is set, use one of its fields: F("customer.user_age").exists().
  • A field that can hold several models (owner: Person | Company) accepts the fields of each. If it can also hold a plain value (contact: Person | str), the field itself is accepted too.
  • A field typed Any or object accepts any dotted path below it, because a model stored there is flattened like any other.
  • A model that refers to itself (child: Node | None) is flattened to any depth, so any dotted path below that field is accepted (child.v, child.child.v).
  • Computed fields (@computed_field) are fields like any other.

docs.title: Write rules with checked field references
docs.text:
fields(Model) catches the typo even earlier, at the line that writes the rule. Each attribute is an ordinary F reference, so every operator works:

from fluxrules.facts import fields

o = fields(Order)
rule = Rule(
    id=2,
    name="big_us_order",
    conditions=(o.amount > 100) & (o.customer.country == "US"),
    action="review",
)
assert rule.conditions["children"][0]["field"] == "amount"

try:
    o.customer.contry  # noqa: B018
except UnknownFieldError as exc:
    assert "Did you mean 'customer.country'" in str(exc)

print(dir(o.customer))  # ['blocked', 'country', 'user_age']: IDE-style discovery

Rules built this way serialize to the usual condition dict, so they store and load exactly like F rules.

docs.title: Normalize incoming keys
docs.text:
lenient_aliases() is a Pydantic alias generator. For each field it accepts the snake_case, camelCase, PascalCase, kebab-case and all-lowercase spellings (user_age, userAge, UserAge, user-age, userage). The spellings are listed per field, so a key that is not a spelling of a declared field is never folded into one.

Turn on per-fact validation to apply it on every evaluate:

normalizing = PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Customer, validate_facts="normalize")
normalizing.load_rules(
    [Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("user_age") >= 18, action="allow")]
)

for payload in ({"user_age": 30}, {"userAge": "30"}, {"UserAge": 30}, {"user-age": 30}):
    assert normalizing.evaluate(payload).fired_rules == [1]
validate_facts What happens to a dict fact Cost "off" (default) Used as-is none "normalize" Validated by Pydantic in lax mode: aliases rename keys, values are coerced ("30" → 30), defaults fill in about 2-4 µs per fact "strict" Validated in Pydantic strict mode: aliases still apply, no type coercion about 2-4 µs per fact

A model instance of fact_schema is already valid and skips validation. A nested dict payload is validated against the nested model, then flattened. Validation needs a schema Pydantic can validate: a Pydantic model, a dataclass or a TypedDict (from typing_extensions on Python 3.11).

docs.title: How a fact reaches the engine
docs.text:
Input to evaluate() validate_facts="off" (default) validate_facts="normalize" / "strict" dict Used as-is Validated against fact_schema, then flattened. Flat dotted keys (customer.user_age) are accepted too. Instance of fact_schema Converted with to_fact_dict Already valid: converted, not re-validated Any other model (Pydantic, dataclass, attrs, msgspec) Converted with to_fact_dict Converted, then validated against fact_schema Other Mapping (e.g. MappingProxyType) Copied to a dict Validated against fact_schema, then flattened

The same path serves evaluate_by_domain, evaluate_by_tags, evaluate_all, evaluate_with_actions and streaming mode, since they all call evaluate(). With strict_facts=True, the structural flat-fact check runs on the converted (or validated) dict.

Two entry points do not validate:

  • engine.assert_fact(...) converts a model but never validates it. Working memory is not read by evaluate().
  • fluxrules.evaluate(rules, facts) converts a model but has no fact_schema, so aliases are not applied. Use an engine with fact_schema when incoming keys need normalizing.

Indicative costs per fact, measured on CPython 3.11 with a five-field model (order of magnitude, not a guarantee):

Step Cost dict passed through ~0.07 µs Flat Pydantic model converted ~0.9 µs (a model_dump() is ~0.7 µs) Nested Pydantic model converted ~1.9 µs Dataclass converted ~1.1 µs validate_facts on a flat dict ~2.3 µs validate_facts on a nested dict ~3.6 µs fact_schema rule check once per load_rules, nothing per fact

docs.title: Decide what happens to invalid facts
docs.text:
on_invalid sets the policy when validation fails:

from fluxrules import FactValidationError

strict = PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Customer, validate_facts="normalize")
strict.load_rules([Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("user_age") >= 18, action="allow")])

try:
    strict.evaluate({"userAge": "abc"})
except FactValidationError as exc:
    assert exc.errors[0]["type"] == "int_parsing"  # Pydantic error code and location

tolerant = PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Customer, validate_facts="normalize", on_invalid="quarantine")
tolerant.load_rules([Rule(id=1, name="adult", conditions=F("user_age") >= 18, action="allow")])

assert tolerant.evaluate({"userAge": "abc"}).fired_rules == []
[rejected] = tolerant.quarantined_facts
assert rejected.facts == {"userAge": "abc"}
on_invalid Result "raise" (default) FactValidationError with .errors (field location and error code for each problem) "skip" Empty result, and a warning is logged "quarantine" Empty result; the fact and its error are kept in engine.quarantined_facts (the most recent 1000)

Whether unknown keys are allowed is the model's choice: Pydantic ignores them by default and rejects them with model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid").

evaluate_batch follows the same policy for every fact in the batch:

batch = [{"userAge": "40"}, {"userAge": "x"}, {"userAge": "12"}, {"userAge": "y"}]
results = tolerant.evaluate_batch(batch)

assert [r.fired_rules for r in results] == [[1], [], [], []]
assert [q.facts for q in tolerant.quarantined_facts][-2:] == [{"userAge": "x"}, {"userAge": "y"}]

With workers=N, the rejected facts from all workers are added to quarantined_facts in input order, as above. With on_invalid="raise", the error for the first invalid fact in the batch is raised, as a loop over evaluate() would. The model is sent to the workers by pickling, so define it at the top level of a module. See Many facts at once.

docs.title: Check rule files in CI
docs.text:
Rules kept in JSON or YAML files can be checked against the model before they reach an engine. fluxrules validate (from pip install 'fluxrules[cli]') reports every field the model lacks, not only the first:

fluxrules validate rules/payments.yaml --schema myapp.models:Payment

{
  "valid": false,
  "issues": [
    "Rule 'large_payment_new_account' references unknown field 'account.ageDays' (not in fact schema Payment). Did you mean 'account.age_days'?"
  ],
  "schemas": [
    {"file": "rules/payments.yaml", "fact_schema": "myapp.models:Payment", "source": "--schema"}
  ]
}

The command exits 0 when the rules are valid, 1 when it finds an issue (an unknown field or a structural problem such as a duplicate id), and 2 when a rule file or the schema cannot be loaded. Pass several files at once (fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml ...); issues are then prefixed with their file.

The schema is named by an import string, myapp.models:Payment (a module) or models/payment.py:Payment (a file), and comes from --schema, else a fact_schema key in the rule file, else fact_schema in fluxrules.yaml. fluxrules evaluate takes the same options plus --validate-facts. A schema named inside a file is loaded only with --trust-schema, because loading it runs its code. See CLI for the forms, the lookup order and the exit codes.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
load_rules_from_yaml checks a rule file's own fact_schema when it loads the file (with trust_schema=True, since loading the schema runs its code), and raises UnknownFieldError on the first unknown field. Pass fact_schema= (a class or an import string) to choose the model yourself:

# python skip
from fluxrules.adapters.loaders.yaml_loader import load_rules_from_yaml
from fluxrules.facts import load_schema, schema_info

rows = load_rules_from_yaml("rules/payments.yaml", fact_schema=Payment)

# Every problem at once, as the CLI does:
info = schema_info(load_schema("myapp.models:Payment"))
for error in info.unknown_fields(rows):
    print(error.rule, error.field, error.suggestion)

docs.title: Without a schema
docs.text: With no schema, the engine still reports case mismatches: a rule on Amount against a fact carrying amount raises FieldNotFoundError. Other key styles (userAge against user_age) are reported only with a schema, because without one the engine cannot tell a typo from a second kind of fact that spells the field differently. See Field names are exact.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: Real-world scenarios where FluxRules excels.

docs.title: Fraud Detection
docs.text:
Scenario: Bank processes transactions and needs to flag suspicious ones.

Rules: - High-value transactions (>$10,000) - Transactions from high-risk countries - Unusual velocity (5+ transactions in 1 hour) - Cross-border with high-risk IP

FluxRules advantage: Simple condition trees for complex business logic, millisecond latency.

Example: Example 22: Real-World Workflow

docs.title: Compliance Automation
docs.text:
Scenario: E-commerce platform enforces compliance rules.

Rules: - Block sales to restricted countries - Require identity verification for large orders - Flag duplicate customer accounts - Require 2FA for high-value orders

FluxRules advantage: Rules externalized from code, changeable without deployment.

docs.title: Risk Scoring
docs.text:
Scenario: Insurance company scores claims automatically.

Rules: - Tier 1: Low-risk claims (auto-approve) - Tier 2: Medium-risk claims (manual review) - Tier 3: High-risk claims (investigation)

FluxRules advantage: Tiered logic with explicit rule evaluation.

docs.title: Workflow Routing
docs.text:
Scenario: API gateway routes requests based on rules.

Rules: - Route large requests to high-capacity workers - Route priority customers to expedited queue - Route test traffic to staging environment

FluxRules advantage: Fast (ms-level) routing decisions.

docs.title: Order Management
docs.text:
Scenario: E-commerce system automates order processing.

Rules: - Orders < $100: Auto-ship - Orders > $1000: Require approval - International orders: Require customs clearance - VIP orders: Rush shipping

FluxRules advantage: Multi-tier logic with conditional actions.

docs.title: Validation Framework
docs.text:
Validation in FluxRules catches errors in condition logic before rules are deployed.

Prerequisites: Familiarity with Conditions and condition condition tree structure (see Complex Conditions).

docs.title: What Gets Validated
docs.text:
When you create or load rules, FluxRules validates the condition tree:

  • Syntax: Structure, types, required fields
  • Semantics: Valid operators, valid values
  • Logic: No impossible conditions (e.g., age > 18 AND age < 18)

The validation system catches errors early with clear error messages.

Source: src/fluxrules/domain/conditions/validation.py

docs.title: Validate a Single Rule's Conditions
docs.text:
from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import validate_conditions, ConditionValidationError
from fluxrules.domain import Rule

# Define a rule: F DSL is the recommended authoring format
from fluxrules import F

rule = Rule(
    name="high_amount_check",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").isin(["US", "CA"])),
    action="review",
)

# Validate the condition tree
try:
    validate_conditions(rule.conditions)
    print("Rule is valid")
except ConditionValidationError as e:
    print(f"Validation error: {e}")

docs.title: Common Validation Errors
docs.text:
These examples are written as dictionaries on purpose: F expressions can only build valid nodes, so a hand-written dictionary is how an invalid one appears.

Invalid operator: 

invalid_dsl = {
    "type": "condition",
    "field": "amount",
    "op": "__unknown__",  # not in VALID_OPERATORS
    "value": 100
}
# Raises: ConditionValidationError: '__unknown__' is not a valid operator

Impossible logic: 

impossible_dsl = {
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "age", "op": ">", "value": 18},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "age", "op": "<", "value": 18}  # impossible
    ]
}
# Note: validate_conditions validates structure; dead-rule detection is on the roadmap

Missing required fields: 

invalid_condition = {
    "type": "condition",
    "field": "amount"
    # missing 'op' and 'value'
}
# Raises: ConditionValidationError: missing required 'op' key

docs.title: Condition Node Types and Validation Rules
condition
docs.text:
Tests a single field against a value using an operator.

Required fields: type, field, op, value

Valid operators: ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, in, not_in, contains, not_contains

from fluxrules import F

F("amount") >= 1000
# stored as:
{"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">=", "value": 1000}

docs.title: group
docs.text:
Combines multiple conditions with AND or OR logic.

Required fields: type, op, children

Valid op values: "AND", "OR" (case-insensitive; both uppercase and lowercase work)

from fluxrules import F

(F("amount") > 100) & (F("status") == "active")
# stored as:
{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 100},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "status", "op": "==", "value": "active"}
    ]
}

docs.title: not
docs.text:
Negates a condition.

Required fields: type, condition

from fluxrules import F

~(F("status") == "blocked")
# stored as:
{
    "type": "not",
    "condition": {"type": "condition", "field": "status", "op": "==", "value": "blocked"}
}

docs.title: exists, sequence, accumulate
docs.text: Additional node types for advanced features (documented in Nested Facts and Working Memory).

docs.title: Validation Modes
docs.text:
The validation happens automatically at rule creation. If validation fails, behavior depends on context:

  • Rule creation in code: Validate explicitly before use
  • REST API: Validation is automatic (returns 400 Bad Request on error)
  • YAML loader: Validation is automatic (raises exception on error)
  • Engine load: No validation (assumes rules are pre-validated)

docs.title: Using the Shared Dataset
docs.text:
The shared payment-risk dataset includes a validation example in Example 04:

from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate
from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import ConditionValidationError, validate_conditions

# Author with F DSL, validate with the top-level API
rule = Rule(
    name="fraud_check",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 5000)
        & (
            (F("country").isin(["CN", "RU"]))
            | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 85)
        )
    ),
    action="block",
)

issues = validate([rule])
assert issues == []  # passes

# Or validate the underlying condition tree directly
validate_conditions(rule.conditions)  # passes

See Example 04: Validation for complete working code.

For error handling with validation, see Example 14: Error Handling.

docs.title: Condition Validation Errors
docs.text:
When validation fails, you get a ConditionValidationError with context about what went wrong.

Example: Invalid operator

from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import validate_conditions, ConditionValidationError

try:
    validate_conditions({
        "type": "condition",
        "field": "amount",
        "op": "is_greater_than",  # not a valid operator
        "value": 100
    })
except ConditionValidationError as e:
    print(e)  # "is_greater_than is not a valid operator..."

Example: Missing required field

try:
    validate_conditions({
        "type": "condition",
        "field": "amount"
        # missing 'op' and 'value'
    })
except ConditionValidationError as e:
    print(e)  # "Condition missing required 'op' key"

docs.title: Valid Operators Reference
docs.text:
The 13 valid operators are below. The comparison operators also accept the word aliases eq, ne, gt, gte, lt and lte in dictionary and YAML rules.

"op" F expression Use case == F("x") == v Exact match != F("x") != v Not equal > F("x") > v Greater than (numeric) >= F("x") >= v Greater or equal (numeric) < F("x") < v Less than (numeric) <= F("x") <= v Less or equal (numeric) in F("x").isin([...]) One of several values not_in F("x").not_in([...]) Not one of several values contains F("x").contains(v) Collection or string contains a value not_contains F("x").not_contains(v) Does not contain a value starts_with F("x").starts_with(v) String prefix ends_with F("x").ends_with(v) String suffix regex F("x").regex(p) Regular expression match

Source: src/fluxrules/engine/operators.py (VALID_OPERATORS)

docs.title: When Validation Happens
docs.text:
• Explicit call: validate_conditions(dsl), synchronous, raises on error
  • Rule creation: Rules are structurally validated on instantiation
  • Engine load: No automatic validation (engine.load_rules() assumes pre-validated rules)
  • REST API (if enabled): Automatic validation before saving
  • YAML loader (if enabled): Automatic validation on load

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
What validation covers: - Condition tree syntax and structure - Operator validity - Required fields - Type checking (values match operator expectations)

What validation does NOT cover: - Semantic logic (does your business rule make sense?) - Dead rule detection (rules that can never match) - Rule conflicts (multiple rules matching same input) - Coverage gaps (uncovered input spaces)

For advanced validation, use manual review or rule analysis tools (see Rule Analysis).

  • Examples 04 & 14: Working validation examples

docs.title: Working Memory and State
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule, Engine, Fact) and Conditions (condition tree format).

FluxRules evaluates fact maps against rules. This page describes:

  1. Single-fact evaluation: how engines match one fact at a time
  2. Working memory: how to store and retrieve facts
  3. Stateful sessions: how to accumulate facts across multiple evaluations

Each engine evaluates independently. If you need multi-fact correlation, see Cross-Fact Rules.

docs.title: Single-fact evaluation
docs.text:
PhreakEngine evaluates one fact dict per call:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule = Rule(
    name="high_value_flag",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="flag_for_review",
    persist=False,
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

# Evaluate a single fact
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500})
print(f"Matched rules: {result.fired_rules}")  # [1]

Each call to evaluate() is independent-engines do not correlate facts across time or aggregate over collections. Pass pre-aggregated facts to the engine.

docs.title: Working memory (fact store)
docs.text:
Every engine has a built-in fact store accessed via assert_fact and retract_fact:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([
    Rule(name="test", conditions=F("x") > 10, action="act", persist=False)
])

# Assert facts into the store
fact_id_1 = engine.assert_fact({"x": 15})  # Returns a fact ID
fact_id_2 = engine.assert_fact({"x": 5})

# Retrieve fact_id_1: still in working memory
# But evaluate() does not automatically use stored facts
result = engine.evaluate({"x": 20})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")  # [1] (matches the evaluate() call, not stored facts)

# Remove a fact from storage
engine.retract_fact(fact_id_1)

Key insight: assert_fact and retract_fact manage storage only. They do not trigger rule matching. Use evaluate() to match facts against rules.

docs.title: Stateful sessions
docs.text:
For workflows that accumulate facts across multiple steps, use EvaluationSession:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.domain.models import Ruleset
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
rules = [
    Rule(id=1, name="kyc_verified", conditions=F("kyc_status") == "verified", action="proceed"),
    Rule(id=2, name="high_risk", conditions=F("amount") > 10000, action="review"),
]
service.persist(
    Ruleset(group="onboarding", rules=tuple(r.to_engine_rule(group="onboarding") for r in rules))
)

session = service.create_session("onboarding")
session.add_fact("kyc_status", "verified")  # step 1: KYC check finishes
session.add_fact("amount", 15000)  # step 2: the payment request arrives
result = session.evaluate()
assert sorted(result.fired_rules) == [1, 2]  # both rules match

service.persist(Ruleset(...)) stores the rules under the name "onboarding", and create_session("onboarding") starts an empty session for that rule set.

Session methods:

  • add_fact(key, value): set or update one field
  • add_facts(dict): merge multiple fields
  • remove_fact(key): remove one field (no error if missing)
  • clear_facts(): remove all facts
  • evaluate(): evaluate ruleset against accumulated facts

docs.title: Snapshot save and restore
docs.text:
Sessions can be serialized to JSON snapshots for recovery:

from fluxrules.services.session import EvaluationSession

snapshot_json = session.save()  # a JSON string

# Later, for example in another process: rebuild the session from the string
restored = EvaluationSession.restore(snapshot_json, service)
assert restored.facts == session.facts
assert restored.evaluate().fired_rules == result.fired_rules

The snapshot includes facts, session ID, timestamp, and optional metadata. Use this to checkpoint multi-step workflows.

  • Sessions in production: See Sessions for session lifecycle and lifecycle management
  • Streaming mode: See example 23_streaming_vs_stateless.py for delta behavior

docs.title: YAML Rules
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Authoring Rules, Conditions and Rule Types.

FluxRules provides a YAML file loader. It returns rule mappings; the canonical Rule model remains the validation boundary before rules are passed to PhreakEngine.

docs.title: YAML
docs.text:
A YAML rule file holds one of three shapes, using the canonical Rule fields. conditions is the full condition tree.

A list of rules:

- id: 7
  name: high_value
  action: review
  conditions:
    type: condition
    field: amount
    op: ">"
    value: 100

A single rule mapping (the same fields, without the leading -).

Or a mapping with a rules list and an optional fact_schema, naming the model the rules are written against (see Check rules against a fact schema):

fact_schema: myapp.models:Payment
rules:
  - id: 7
    name: high_value
    action: review
    conditions: {type: condition, field: amount, op: ">", value: 100}

Load and validate the mappings explicitly:

# python skip
from fluxrules import Rule
from fluxrules.adapters.loaders.yaml_loader import load_rules_from_yaml
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rows = load_rules_from_yaml("rules.yaml")
rules = [Rule.model_validate_yaml({**row, "persist": False}) for row in rows]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 150})
assert result.fired_rules == [7]

The loader requires the yaml extra:

pip install 'fluxrules[yaml]'

load_rules_from_yaml returns the rule mappings in every case. To read a file as JSON or YAML by its extension and also get its fact_schema, use read_rule_file:

# python skip
from fluxrules.adapters.loaders import read_rule_file

document = read_rule_file("rules.yaml")
document.rules  # list of rule mappings
document.fact_schema  # "myapp.models:Payment", or None

docs.title: Canonical validation boundary
docs.text:
The raw loader intentionally returns dictionaries so applications can inspect, merge, or annotate imported rules. Always pass each mapping through the canonical validator before loading it:

from fluxrules import Rule

rule = Rule.model_validate_yaml(
    {
        "name": "country_check",
        "conditions": {
            "type": "condition",
            "field": "country",
            "op": "==",
            "value": "US",
        },
        "action": "review",
        "persist": False,
    }
)

This rejects empty logic, unknown operators, malformed condition tree structure, and conflicting action fields at the authoring boundary.

docs.title: Check rules against a fact schema
docs.text: A rule that names a field the facts never carry (account.ageDays instead of account.age_days) loads fine and then never matches. Naming the fact model catches it when the file is loaded.

docs.title: In the file
docs.text:
Put fact_schema next to rules, as above. load_rules_from_yaml then checks every field each rule references, including exists fields, and raises UnknownFieldError with a suggestion before returning anything:

UnknownFieldError: Rule 'high_value' references unknown field 'amout' (not in
fact schema Payment). Did you mean 'amount'? Known fields: [...]

fact_schema is an import string in one of two forms:

Form Example Loads Module myapp.models:Payment Payment from the module myapp.models; the current directory is searched File models.py:Payment Payment from that file, resolved against the YAML file's directory

Loading the schema imports its module, which runs that module's code. So load_rules_from_yaml loads a schema the file names only when you say you trust the file:

# python skip
rows = load_rules_from_yaml("rules.yaml", trust_schema=True)

Without trust_schema=True it raises ValueError naming the file and the schema. Passing fact_schema= yourself needs no flag, because then you chose the model. A file that names a schema is tied to that import path: moving or renaming the model class means updating the file.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
Pass fact_schema= to check against a model the file does not name, or to override the one it names. It takes a class or an import string:

# python skip
from myapp.models import Payment

from fluxrules.adapters.loaders.yaml_loader import load_rules_from_yaml

rows = load_rules_from_yaml("rules.yaml", fact_schema=Payment)

load_rules_from_yaml stops at the first unknown field. To list them all, use FactSchemaInfo.unknown_fields:

# python skip
from fluxrules.adapters.loaders import read_rule_file
from fluxrules.facts import load_schema, schema_info

document = read_rule_file("rules.yaml")
info = schema_info(load_schema(document.fact_schema, base_dir=document.path.parent))
for error in info.unknown_fields(document.rules):
    print(error.rule, error.field, error.suggestion)

An engine built with the same model checks again at load_rules: PhreakEngine(fact_schema=Payment). See Typed Facts.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml
fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml --schema myapp.models:Payment

fluxrules validate reads YAML and JSON rule files, reports every unknown field with a hint, and exits 1 when it finds one, so it can gate CI. The schema comes from --schema, else the file's fact_schema, else fact_schema in fluxrules.yaml. A schema named inside a file is loaded only with --trust-schema. See CLI.

docs.title: Operational guidance
docs.text:
Store YAML rule files in version control, validate them in CI (fluxrules validate rules/*.yaml), and record the generated rule-set version used by a deployment. The loader does not execute action handlers; evaluation returns action names and the application or action dispatcher owns side effects.

For persistence-backed rule management, use RuleService and Ruleset rather than treating a file loader as a database repository.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: Setup, testing, and contributing to FluxRules.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
• Contributing: Contribution guidelines
  • Testing: Running tests locally
  • Backlog: Designed but not yet shipped work

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: FluxRules uses uv for dependency management. As a published library, it does not commit uv.lock (it is gitignored), so a clean sync resolves the latest versions allowed by the ranges declared in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• uv ≥ 0.7 (curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh)
  • Python ≥ 3.11 (uv will download a matching interpreter if none is present)

docs.title: Dev environment
docs.text:
The project environment is the repository-root .venv. If your shell has VIRTUAL_ENV set to another project environment, clear it before running uv:

unset VIRTUAL_ENV

git clone https://github.com/saurabh2mishra/fluxrules.git
cd fluxrules

# Recommended: creates .venv, installs the dev + docs extras
# (including pytest-xdist for `pytest -n auto`), and wires up pre-commit hooks.
make dev

# Equivalent explicit command (dev group is installed by default):
uv sync --group docs

uv.lock is committed, so every contributor and CI resolve the same versions. Pass --locked to fail fast when pyproject.toml and the lock have drifted:

uv sync --group docs --locked      # use uv.lock exactly; error if it is stale

docs.title: Private index / offline mirrors
docs.text:
By default uv resolves packages from PyPI. Behind a corporate mirror, point uv (and pip fallbacks) at your index before syncing:

export UV_INDEX_URL="https://your-mirror/simple/"
export PIP_INDEX_URL="https://your-mirror/simple/"
uv sync --group docs

Use --offline to resolve entirely from uv's local cache when the network is unavailable.

docs.title: Library-only install
docs.text:
To use FluxRules as a dependency (no dev tooling):

pip install fluxrules            # from PyPI
pip install -e . --group dev     # editable, with dev tooling (pip >= 25.1)

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
1. Create feature branch
  2. Write tests for new behavior
  3. Implement feature
  4. Run full test suite
  5. Update documentation
  6. Submit pull request

See Contributing for more details.

docs.title: Backlog
docs.text: Planned work that is designed but not yet shipped. Each item names the release it is aimed at and why it is waiting. When an item ships, move it to CHANGELOG.md and delete it here.

docs.title: Typed facts and missing fields
docs.text: Shipped in 1.1.0: model input for every engine, fact_schema= with load-time rule checks, fluxrules.facts.fields() and lenient_aliases(), opt-in validate_facts / on_invalid, key-style-insensitive FieldNotFoundError, and EngineConfig.missing_field with MissingFieldNotWarning, and schema checks for JSON/YAML rule files in fluxrules validate and load_rules_from_yaml. See Typed Facts and Missing fields and NOT.

docs.title: Make missing_field="unknown" the default (2.0)
docs.text:
What: Flip EngineConfig.missing_field from None (1.x behaviour plus a warning) to "unknown", so NOT over a missing field no longer fires.

Why waiting: It changes which rules fire. 1.1.0 ships the opt-in and a MissingFieldNotWarning so users can find affected rules first.

Before flipping:

  • Audit stored rulesets (database and YAML) for NOT over fields that are often absent; the warning names the fields.
  • Remove the None mode and the warning.
  • Update tests/unit/test_field_not_found.py::TestEvaluateRaisesOnMissingField::test_not_does_not_raise_for_unrelated_absent_field, which pins today's firing behaviour.

docs.title: Strict missing-field mode (strict_fields)
docs.text:
What: An engine option that raises when a fact lacks any field a candidate rule needs, instead of evaluating the condition as False.

Why waiting: Multi-schema rulesets legitimately evaluate facts that lack other schemas' fields, so it needs scoping (per rule, per domain or via fact_schema) before it is useful. Phase 3 of the typed-facts plan.

docs.title: Check database rules against a fact schema
docs.text:
What: Extend fluxrules validate --schema to rules stored through the persistence layer, as it already does for JSON and YAML rule files.

Why waiting: The CLI has no way to point at a database yet (URL option or the configured persistence layer); that needs deciding first.

docs.title: Schema export for rule-authoring UIs
docs.text:
What: Export a fact schema's flat field paths and types (JSON Schema) so rule editors can offer field pickers and operator choices per type.

Why waiting: Depends on the shape the HTTP API wants. Phase 3.

docs.title: Rules stored with alias names (rule_names="alias")
docs.text:
What: An opt-in mode where fact_schema checks and matches rule fields by the model's aliases (for example camelCase) instead of its Python field names.

Why waiting: Only needed if stored rulesets use camelCase field names; count them first. Migrating stored rules to field names is the alternative.

docs.title: Typed facts in the HTTP API and cross-fact engine
docs.text:
What: Accept fact_schema for engines built by the API engine pool, and apply to_fact_dict / missing_field in the cross-fact engine.

Why waiting: The HTTP API receives JSON dicts, so model input does not apply; schema configuration needs an API design. The cross-fact engine does not evaluate NOT today.

docs.title: Tidy fluxrules.pipeline.schema
docs.text:
What: FactSchema / validate_facts there still treat Pydantic as optional and point to fluxrules[api], although Pydantic is a core dependency. Remove the fallback branch and the stale install hint, and consider building them on fluxrules.facts.

Why waiting: Cosmetic; no behaviour change.

docs.title: Comparing values
docs.text:
1.1.2 made every evaluation path give the same answer (Phases 0 and 1 of the comparison plan). The items below are the rest of that plan. They are aimed at 1.2.0, except the last, which changes defaults and waits for 2.0. How FluxRules Compares Values shows today's behaviour, and the comparison matrix (tests/engine/comparison_matrix.py) must keep every path in agreement as each item lands: run make docs-tables after any change to how values compare.

Decisions already made (2026-11-03):

  • A comparison that cannot be made keeps its answer (no match) in 1.x, but warns by default.
  • Text that looks like a number is converted only when a fact schema asks for it, never silently.
  • Under strict_type_comparison, values of different types are never equal, so 5 != "5" is a match. Only ordering (>, < and the like) across types cannot be made.
  • Safer defaults wait for 2.0.

docs.title: Close the remaining matrix gaps (1.2.0)
docs.text:
What: Add to the comparison matrix what 1.1.2 left out:

  • tuple fact values;
  • rules written as F expressions and loaded from YAML, not only as dicts;
  • evaluate_batch(workers=2), which runs in worker processes.

Also make the alpha prefilter call the same comparison functions as the engine (for example one operator.gt table in fluxrules.engine.operators) instead of its own copies.

Why waiting: The matrix already proves the paths agree, so these close coverage gaps rather than fix known bugs. Do them first in 1.2.0, so every later item is tested on every path.

docs.title: Report comparisons that cannot be made (1.2.0)
docs.text:
What: A comparison that cannot be made, such as "abc" > 5, None > 5, a date against a datetime, NaN or an invalid regex, is no match today, and NOT then fires. Make it visible:

  • Add EngineConfig.uncomparable, modelled on missing_field:
  • None (default): no match, as today, plus a warning once per field, operator and pair of types.
  • "false": no match, silently (1.1 behaviour).
  • "unknown": the check is unknown, so NOT over it does not fire, and AND / OR follow three-valued logic.
  • "raise": raise an error naming the field, operator and both types.
  • Add a ComparisonWarning class and list each case in the result (for example result.comparison_issues), with the field, operator, both types and the reason.
  • Apply it on every path. The comparison matrix grows a column per mode, and the reference page shows each mode.

Under strict_type_comparison, make != between different types a match (decided above). Today it is no match, so this changes the answer for anyone who set that flag.

Why waiting: It adds a setting and a warning that existing users will see, and the "unknown" mode needs three-valued logic in the engine, compiled conditions, streaming mode and the reference evaluator. Reuse the missing_field="unknown" machinery in fluxrules.domain.conditions.missing_fields rather than adding a second one.

docs.title: Check rule values when rules load (1.2.0)
docs.text:
What: Catch rules that can never match, before they run:

  • Value against operator: >, >=, < and <= need a number, text or a date; starts_with and ends_with need text; a regex must compile. Anything else warns when the rule is created.
  • Value against the fact schema: with fact_schema=, compare each rule value with its field's type. amount: float compared with "100.1" is an error that suggests writing 100.1. An ISO date string compared with a date field is converted to a date, because JSON rule files have no other way to write one. Unclear annotations (unions, Any) are skipped.
  • YAML traps: warn when a rule value in a YAML file was read differently from how it looks: NO / yes / on became a boolean, 0755 an octal number, 1:30 a number of seconds, or 1e3 text. Detect these from the YAML node text, before the values are built.
  • Report every one of these through validate() and fluxrules validate.

Why waiting: A rule that loaded quietly in 1.1 may now warn or, with a fact schema, refuse to load. That needs a minor release and a changelog entry under Changed.

docs.title: Make common comparisons easy (1.2.0)
docs.text:
What:

  • Floats and money: an approx operator, F("total").approx(0.3), using math.isclose with optional absolute and relative tolerances, plus guidance to keep money in Decimal.
  • Text: case-insensitive operators: equals_ignore_case, in_ignore_case, contains_ignore_case, starts_with_ignore_case and ends_with_ignore_case, comparing with str.casefold().
  • Dates and numeric text in facts: with a fact schema and validate_facts="normalize", ISO date strings already become dates and numeric text becomes numbers. Add tests and a section on the Comparing Values page; no conversion happens without a schema (decided above).

Every new operator needs an F method, a dict and YAML form, an entry in the matrix and the reference page, and a sound rule in the alpha prefilter (it may simply leave the rule unscreened).

Why waiting: New operators are new public API, so they belong in a minor release.

docs.title: Safer comparison defaults (2.0)
docs.text:
What: Flip the defaults that 1.2.0 makes opt-in:

  • uncomparable="unknown" by default, so NOT never fires because a comparison could not be made (alongside missing_field="unknown" above);
  • True no longer equals 1 (a boolean is not a number);
  • strict types whenever a fact schema is given.

Why waiting: Each one changes which rules fire. Ship the opt-in settings and warnings in 1.2.0 first, so users can find affected rules before the defaults change.

docs.title: Define what evaluation_mode="stateful" means for stored rules
docs.text:
What: Rules stored through the HTTP API have an evaluation_mode field ("stateless" by default, or "stateful"). It is saved and returned, but no evaluation path reads it, so a "stateful" rule fires like any other. Either give it a meaning (for example: such rules run only in a streaming engine or a session, and the stateless endpoints skip them) or remove the field.

Why waiting: Giving it a meaning changes which rules fire for anyone who set it, and needs a design for where stateful rules run in the HTTP API. Today's behaviour is documented in HTTP API Reference and pinned by tests/integration/test_e2e_admin_integration.py::TestExistingFeaturesRegression::test_simulate_event_evaluates_stateful_marked_rules.

docs.title: Compiled-rule cache: use the configured Redis server
docs.text:
What: src/fluxrules/services/validation/_compiled_cache.py connects with redis.Redis(), so it always uses localhost:6379, while the rest of the API reads REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT and REDIS_DB. A deployment with Redis on another host shares rule caches but not compiled rules between processes. Pass the connection settings in (the module is in services/, which must not import the api package), for example through a small setter the API calls at startup.

Why waiting: Behaviour is unchanged from 1.0, and a server without the cache still works (each process compiles its own rules). Documented in Deployment.

docs.title: Finish the /api/v1/engines endpoints, and clear the Redis rule cache
docs.text:
What: POST /api/v1/engines/switch and /reload answer "success" but change nothing; /benchmark and GET /stats describe a new engine with no rules. Either make them do what their names say or remove them. Related: RuleCache.clear() in src/fluxrules/api/engines/adapter.py empties only the in-process copy, so with Redis a rule change can take up to the cache's 5 minutes to reach /api/v1/engines/* and /api/v1/rules/simulate. Clearing should also delete the Redis keys.

Why waiting: Behaviour is unchanged from 1.0 and documented as it is in HTTP API Reference: Endpoints that are not finished, pinned by tests/integration/test_engine_endpoints.py. Removing endpoints or changing their answers is an API change that needs its own decision.
