docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Exact details for when you know what you are looking for.

  • Public API: the functions, classes and errors that fluxrules exports, with their stability labels.
  • HTTP API Reference: every endpoint of the HTTP server, with its request and response.
  • Configuration: engine settings and the extras that enable each integration.
  • CLI: the fluxrules command and its options.

To run FluxRules in production, see Deployment.

docs.title: Public API Reference
docs.text: Prerequisites: Concepts, Quickstart.

docs.title: Stability and Contract Labels
docs.text:
FluxRules has several deliberate contract families. They are coherent because each family has one entry point and one result shape; they are not intended to be interchangeable.

Label Meaning Stable Supported application-facing API covered by the compatibility tests in tests/contract/. Separate contract Supported capability with different semantics and lifecycle; use its dedicated entry point rather than swapping it into the single-fact API. Experimental Available for evaluation, but compatibility and operational behavior may change before 1.0. Internal Implementation detail. It may appear in stack traces or extension code, but applications should not depend on it.

docs.title: Contract map
docs.text:
Surface Label Entry point Input/output contract Canonical rule evaluation Stable Rule + PhreakEngine.load_rules() + engine.evaluate(facts) One fact in (a mapping or a typed model); EvaluationResult out (fired_rules, actions, explanations, metrics). Reference evaluation Stable reference ReferenceEvaluator.evaluate(ruleset, facts) or top-level fluxrules.evaluate() Rules plus facts in; the same EvaluationResult out (fired_rules, actions, trace). Used as the oracle for the single-fact subset. Cross-fact correlation Separate contract get_cross_fact_engine() insert/update/retract fact handles and activation deltas; not a BaseEngine replacement. Sessions and persistence Separate contract RuleService, persistence ports, session services Rulesets and snapshots are managed outside the direct PHREAK matcher. CLI Stable adapter fluxrules evaluate, validate, serve, init, version JSON/file-oriented command contract; uses the canonical public model and reports CLI exit/output semantics. HTTP API Stable adapter create_app() and documented routes HTTP request/response/error contract; deployment/authentication and optional extras apply. Custom engines/operators/transforms Experimental extension BaseEngine, register_engine, operator/transform registries Extension contracts are tested, but third-party compatibility is not promised before 1.0. EngineRule, infrastructure nodes, repositories Internal Internal conversion/persistence paths Do not use as the authoring API; Rule.to_engine_rule() is the explicit boundary.

The compatibility guarantee is per row. For example, PHREAK and the reference evaluator are parity-tested for the supported single-fact condition subset, while a Cross-Fact activation delta is intentionally not comparable to a stateless EvaluationResult.

docs.title: Top-Level Functions
docs.text:
From fluxrules:

  • evaluate(rules, facts) → EvaluationResult: Evaluate facts against rules. rules may be a single Rule, any iterable of Rule, or a Ruleset.
  • facts may be a plain python dict or a model: a Pydantic v2 model, dataclass, attrs class or msgspec Struct (a Pydantic v1 model is converted with .dict()). Nested models become dotted keys (customer.age). See Typed Facts.
  • to_fact_dict(facts) → dict: The conversion evaluate() and every engine apply to non-dict facts.
  • validate(rules) → list[str]: Validate rules and return issues; accepts the same shapes as evaluate
  • explain(execution_id: str) → dict[str, object]: Get an explanation payload for a past execution; keys: execution_id, fired_rules, actions, trace

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
From fluxrules.engine:

  • PhreakEngine (the single production engine, lazy evaluation): stateless (default) and streaming modes. evaluate() accepts a dict or a model. Optional typed-fact keywords: fact_schema= (check rule fields when rules load), validate_facts="off" | "normalize" | "strict" and on_invalid="raise" | "skip" | "quarantine"; rejected facts are listed in engine.quarantined_facts. See Typed Facts. fact_pipeline= applies a FactPipeline (or any dict-to-dict callable) to each fact in evaluate() before validation; see Fact Pipeline. evaluate_batch(facts, workers=None) evaluates many facts and returns one EvaluationResult per fact, in input order; workers=N spreads them over N processes, each rebuilt with the engine's settings. See Many facts at once. A change to the engine's EngineConfig object takes effect on its next evaluation, for interpreted and compiled rules alike.
  • BaseEngine (abstract base for custom engines); takes the same typed-fact and fact_pipeline= keywords. evaluate_batch works with workers=1; override _clone_settings() to allow more.

docs.title: Runtime Helpers
docs.text:
From fluxrules.engine.runtime:

  • evaluate_batch_parallel(rules, facts, num_workers=None, streaming_mode=False) → list[list[int]]: The older batch helper. Each worker builds a default PhreakEngine with only streaming_mode set, so other engine options (fact_schema, fact_pipeline, EngineConfig, ...) do not apply, and it returns only the fired rule ids per fact. It keeps working unchanged; for new code use engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=N), which keeps every option and returns full results.
  • DedupEvaluator(engine, backend=LRUDedupBackend()): Wraps a stateless engine and returns a cached result for a fact it has already seen. LRUDedupBackend(max_entries=100_000) keeps results in memory; RedisDedupBackend shares them between processes (needs the redis extra). See Ways to Evaluate a Fact.

docs.title: Typed Facts
docs.text:
From fluxrules.facts:

  • fields(Model): Checked field references: fields(Customer).age >= 18 builds the same condition as F("age") >= 18, and a field the model lacks raises UnknownFieldError.
  • lenient_aliases(): Pydantic alias generator accepting snake_case, camelCase, PascalCase, kebab-case and all-lowercase spellings of each field.
  • to_fact_dict(facts): Model or mapping to the flat fact dict.
  • schema_info(Model) → FactSchemaInfo: The flat field paths a rule may reference. check_rules(rules) raises on the first unknown field; unknown_fields(rules) returns every one as an UnknownFieldError (with .rule, .field, .suggestion and .summary).
  • load_schema(spec, base_dir=None) → type: Import a model class from "package.module:Class" or "path/to/models.py:Class". See Check rule files in CI.

From fluxrules.adapters.loaders:

  • load_rules_from_yaml(path, fact_schema=None): Rule mappings from a YAML file, checked against fact_schema or the file's own fact_schema key.
  • read_rule_file(path) → RuleFile: A JSON or YAML rule file as rules plus its optional fact_schema import string.
  • QuarantinedFact: Entry in engine.quarantined_facts (facts, error).

docs.title: Domain Models
docs.text:
From fluxrules:

  • Rule: Pydantic v2 model: id, name, domain, tags, conditions, action, actions, priority, enabled, persist
  • F (alias of Field) and Condition: the recommended way to write conditions: (F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"). See Authoring Rules.
  • RuleBuilder: Fluent authoring; RuleBuilder.build() returns a Rule. RuleBuilder.condition() accepts an F expression or a dictionary.
  • ConditionBuilder: Deprecated in favor of F; it will be removed in a future release.
  • Ruleset: Optional named collection of rules (group: str, rules: tuple[...]). evaluate() accepts bare rules, so you only need this to name a group.
  • EvaluationResult: The single result type for every evaluation path. fired_rules is what matched; actions are the collected actions. Also carries candidate_rule_ids (what discovery considered, always a superset of fired_rules), ruleset_group, trace, execution_id, latency_ms, engine_type, explanations, rules_by_domain, rules_by_tag, fired_segments.

fluxrules.engine.infrastructure.EvaluationResult is a re-export of this same class, not a second type.

docs.title: Service Layer
docs.text:
From fluxrules.services:

  • RuleService.create(): Factory for rule management
  • ValidationService(): Validate rules and conditions
  • EvaluationService(): Core evaluation
  • PersistenceService(): Database operations
  • AuditService(): Track rule executions

docs.title: Error Hierarchy
docs.text:
All errors derive from FluxRulesError:

from fluxrules import FluxRulesError

try:
    ...
except FluxRulesError as exc:
    logger.error("rule operation failed: %s (%s)", exc, exc.code)
Exception Base code Raised when FluxRulesError Exception FLUXRULES_ERROR Base of the taxonomy; not raised directly InvalidRuleError FluxRulesError INVALID_RULE A rule is structurally unusable UnknownOperatorError FluxRulesError UNKNOWN_OPERATOR A condition names an operator that does not exist CyclicDependencyError FluxRulesError CYCLIC_DEPENDENCY Rule dependencies form a cycle ConditionValidationError InvalidRuleError DSL_VALIDATION_ERROR A conditions tree fails strict validation FieldNotFoundError FluxRulesError FIELD_NOT_FOUND A condition's field is missing but a key in the fact is the same name in another key style (Amount / amount, userAge / user_age, user-age), or the field is a dotted path into a nested value that was not flattened UnknownFieldError InvalidRuleError, AttributeError UNKNOWN_FACT_FIELD A rule names a field the engine's fact_schema lacks (raised by load_rules), or fields(Model) is asked for one FactValidationError FluxRulesError, ValueError FACT_VALIDATION_ERROR With validate_facts on and on_invalid="raise", a fact fails validation; .errors holds each field location and error code EmptyRuleLogicError InvalidRuleError EMPTY_RULE_LOGIC A rule with no condition logic would be stored LossyConditionRebuildError InvalidRuleError LOSSY_CONDITION_REBUILD A condition tree would be rebuilt from a lossy .conditions view

Each carries a stable code intended for logging and API responses. Messages may be reworded; codes will not change.

docs.title: LossyConditionViewWarning
docs.text:
A UserWarning (not an error) emitted when reading .conditions on a rule whose logic uses OR/NOT/nesting. The leaves are still returned, but the boolean structure is not in the result; see Rule Types. To turn it into a hard failure:

import warnings

from fluxrules import LossyConditionViewWarning

warnings.simplefilter("error", LossyConditionViewWarning)

docs.title: MembershipValueWarning
docs.text: A UserWarning emitted when an in or not_in condition is given a single value instead of a list, such as F("country").isin("US"). The value is treated as a one-item list (["US"]) on every evaluation path, and the warning names the field and its position in the condition tree. Write the list, or use == / != for a single value, to silence it. See Conditions.

docs.title: MissingFieldNotWarning
docs.text: A FutureWarning emitted once per NOT condition when it fires only because a field it tests is missing from the fact. In 2.0 such a NOT will not fire. Choose the behaviour now with EngineConfig(missing_field=...): "unknown" adopts the 2.0 behaviour, "false" keeps the 1.x behaviour and silences the warning. See Conditions.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: • fluxrules.__version__

docs.title: Engine Configuration
docs.text:
Engine defaults are managed through fluxrules.engine.configuration.

from fluxrules.engine.configuration import get_config

cfg = get_config()
print(cfg.rule_engine_type)

docs.title: Changing settings after the engine is created
docs.text:
PhreakEngine uses the config object it was created with: the config you pass, or the process-wide config if you pass none. If you change a field on that object later, the engine uses the new value from its next evaluation on. This holds for rules run by the interpreter and for rules compiled with compile_conditions=True (the engine recompiles them when a condition setting changes):

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.configuration import EngineConfig
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

config = EngineConfig(missing_field="false")
engine = PhreakEngine(config=config, compile_conditions=True)
engine.load_rules([Rule(id=1, name="r", conditions=~(F("blocked") == True), action="allow")])  # noqa: E712
assert engine.evaluate({"amount": 1}).fired_rules == [1]

config.missing_field = "unknown"  # takes effect on the next evaluation
assert engine.evaluate({"amount": 1}).fired_rules == []

set_config(new_config) is different: it replaces the process-wide object instead of changing it. Engines created before the call keep the object they already had. Engines created afterwards use the new one. fluxrules.evaluate() and the HTTP API read the process-wide config on every call, so they follow set_config straight away.

The CLI reads the comparison settings from its config file; see CLI: Comparison settings.

evaluate_batch(facts, workers=N) sends the config's current values to its worker processes when you call it.

docs.title: Strict Fact Validation
docs.text:
Engine evaluation supports optional strict fact pre-flight validation:

from fluxrules import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 100}, strict_facts=True)

strict_facts=True checks the fact before any rule runs, and raises InvalidFactError (from fluxrules.pipeline.validators, a subclass of ValueError) when it is not a valid fact:

from fluxrules.pipeline.validators import InvalidFactError

try:
    engine.evaluate(["not", "a", "fact"], strict_facts=True)
except InvalidFactError as e:
    print(f"Rejected: {e}")

Without strict_facts, the same input raises TypeError instead. Catch the exception that matches the mode you use.

docs.title: Missing Fields Under NOT
docs.text:
EngineConfig.missing_field decides whether ~(F("blocked") == True) fires on a fact with no blocked key:

from fluxrules import EngineConfig
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine(config=EngineConfig(missing_field="unknown"))  # 2.0 behaviour
  • None (default): fires, and warns once per NOT with MissingFieldNotWarning.
  • "false": fires, no warning (1.x behaviour).
  • "unknown": does not fire; a missing field is unknown, as SQL treats NULL.

See Missing fields and NOT.

docs.title: Typed Facts
docs.text:
Engines take optional keywords for typed facts:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine


class Customer(BaseModel):
    user_age: int


engine = PhreakEngine(
    fact_schema=Customer,  # rules are checked against Customer at load_rules
    validate_facts="normalize",  # "off" (default) | "normalize" | "strict"
    on_invalid="quarantine",  # "raise" (default) | "skip" | "quarantine"
)

See Typed Facts.

docs.title: Dependency Extras
docs.text:
Configuration scope changes with installed extras:

  • api enables FastAPI server components.
  • sql enables SQLAlchemy and Alembic integration.
  • redis enables Redis adapters.
  • otel enables OpenTelemetry exporters.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: Prerequisites: Quickstart, Concepts.

docs.title: Quick Evaluation
docs.text:
Use the engine directly for simple cases:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Define rules
rule = Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
    action="flag"
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

# Evaluate
result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 2500})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")      # [1]
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")          # ["flag"]
print(f"Latency: {result.latency_ms} ms")    # ~2ms

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validate rules before use:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

# Create a rule and service
rule = Rule(
    name="check",
    conditions=F("status") == "active",
    action="proceed"
)

service = RuleService.create()
# Validation is automatic during evaluation

docs.title: Engines (Direct)
docs.text:
For more control, use engines directly:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule1 = Rule(name="rule1", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="flag")
rule2 = Rule(name="rule2", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="review")

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule1, rule2])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 2500})

docs.title: Many facts at once
docs.text:
engine.evaluate_batch(facts) evaluates a list of facts and returns a list of results, one per fact, in the same order. Each result is the same EvaluationResult that evaluate() returns, so you get the fired rules, their actions, the explanations and the latency for every fact:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([Rule(id=1, name="big", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review")])

facts = [{"amount": 50}, {"amount": 4200}, {"amount": 900}]
results = engine.evaluate_batch(facts)

assert [r.fired_rules for r in results] == [[], [1], []]
assert results[1].actions == ["review"]

Without workers, this is the same as writing [engine.evaluate(f) for f in facts]. It accepts any iterable, so a generator works too.

docs.title: Using several CPU cores
docs.text:
Python runs one thread of Python code at a time, so a single process uses one CPU core. To use more, pass workers:

results = engine.evaluate_batch(facts, workers=4)

This starts 4 worker processes and splits the facts between them. Each worker builds its own copy of your engine, with the same rules and the same settings: fact_schema, validate_facts, on_invalid, fact_pipeline, compile_conditions and the EngineConfig. The results are identical to the single-process ones and come back in input order.

Things to know when you use workers:

  • Starting processes takes time. Workers pay off for thousands of facts or expensive rules, not for a handful. workers larger than the number of facts is reduced to the number of facts.
  • Guard your script. On macOS and Windows each worker imports your script again. Put the code that calls evaluate_batch under if __name__ == "__main__":, or every worker would start the batch again.
  • Settings must be picklable. Workers receive the settings by pickling them. A lambda, or a class defined inside a function, cannot be pickled, so Filter(lambda f: ...) in a pipeline raises a clear ValueError before any worker starts. Use a named function defined at the top level of a module.
  • Invalid facts behave as in a loop. With on_invalid="quarantine", rejected facts get an empty result and are added to engine.quarantined_facts, in input order. With on_invalid="raise", the error for the first invalid fact is raised.
  • Not for streaming mode. A streaming engine remembers the previous fact, and splitting facts between processes would split that memory. A streaming engine accepts only workers=1.
  • Each worker has its own copy of the pipeline. A fact_pipeline step that remembers earlier facts, such as a filter that drops duplicates or a counter, only sees the facts sent to its own worker. Two duplicates that land in different workers are both evaluated, and the pipeline object in your process is not updated. Use workers=1 when the pipeline keeps state.
  • Metrics record latency only. With enable_metrics=True, your engine records each fact's evaluation time from the workers. The other counters (leaf-memo hits, linked rules, alpha prune ratio) are counted inside the workers and are not added to your engine's metrics.

docs.title: Facts from a database
docs.text:
Read the rows with your own query, build the engine once, and keep the row key next to each result. With SQLAlchemy, .mappings() gives each row as a dictionary:

from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

db = create_engine("sqlite://")
with db.begin() as conn:
    conn.execute(text("CREATE TABLE payments (id INTEGER, amount REAL, country TEXT)"))
    conn.execute(
        text("INSERT INTO payments VALUES (1, 50, 'US'), (2, 4200, 'DE'), (3, 9000, 'FR')")
    )

rules_engine = PhreakEngine()
rules_engine.load_rules(
    [Rule(id=1, name="big", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review")]
)

with db.connect() as conn:
    rows = conn.execute(text("SELECT id, amount, country FROM payments")).mappings().all()

results = rules_engine.evaluate_batch(rows)
flagged = [row["id"] for row, result in zip(rows, results, strict=True) if result.fired_rules]
assert flagged == [2, 3]

For a very large table, read and evaluate it in chunks (for example 10,000 rows at a time) instead of loading every row first.

docs.title: RuleService (Sessions & Persistence)
docs.text:
RuleService stores rule sets by name. A session collects the fields of one fact over several steps and evaluates them against a stored rule set:

from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.domain.models import Ruleset
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
payment_rules = [Rule(id=1, name="big", conditions=F("amount") > 1000, action="review")]
service.persist(
    Ruleset(
        group="payment_rules",
        rules=tuple(rule.to_engine_rule(group="payment_rules") for rule in payment_rules),
    )
)

session = service.create_session("payment_rules")
session.add_fact("customer_id", "c1")
session.add_fact("amount", 5000)
result = session.evaluate()
assert result.fired_rules == [1]
  • service.persist(Ruleset(...)) stores the rules under the name "payment_rules". to_engine_rule(group=...) converts each Rule to the stored form.
  • create_session("payment_rules") starts an empty session for that rule set.
  • add_fact(key, value) sets one field; session.evaluate() checks all fields added so far.

RuleService.create() keeps rule sets in memory. See Sessions for saving and restoring a session.
